subject: Chemistry
title: Hydrocarbons: Energy, Fuels, and Building Blocks
hook: Discover how hydrocarbons power India—from petrol pumps to plastic bags—and learn to name, classify, and predict their reactions.

characters.name: Arun
characters.role: Class 11 student curious about fuels and energy

characters.name: Ms. Verma
characters.role: Chemistry teacher with oil-refinery field trip experience

slides.title: Hydrocarbons: Fuels, Plastics, and Modern Life
slides.storyContext: Arun and Neha sit in Ms. Verma's classroom. 'Look around,' Ms. Verma says. 'Your pencil, the desk, the petrol in your scooter, the plastic bag in your pocket—all are hydrocarbons. They're compounds of only carbon and hydrogen. Today, we'll see how they're built, classified, and why they react so differently.'

image.alt: Hydrocarbons: Fuels, Plastics, and Modern Life — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: What Are Hydrocarbons? The Carbon–Hydrogen Bond
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma draws the simplest hydrocarbon: methane, CH₄. 'One carbon, four hydrogens. Carbon forms four C–H bonds. But carbon can also bond to other carbons, creating chains and rings. This is the foundation of all hydrocarbons and all organic molecules. The type and arrangement of these C–C bonds determine everything.'

points.text: Hydrocarbons contain only C and H
Can be classified by C–C bond type: single (–), double (=), or triple (≡)
Can be chain (open-ended) or cyclic (rings)
Most are nonpolar, hydrophobic, and found in crude oil and coal

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic molecules—just carbon and hydrogen bonding together in different patterns.

image.alt: What Are Hydrocarbons? The Carbon–Hydrogen Bond — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Hydrocarbons from the Earth
slides.storyContext: Neha researches the origins of hydrocarbons. 'Crude oil comes from ancient dead organisms. Coal is ancient vegetation. Both are underground treasure chests of energy—millions of years of sunlight stored as chemical bonds in C–C and C–H connections. When we burn hydrocarbons, we release that ancient solar energy.' Ms. Verma nods. 'And we use hydrocarbons not just for fuel, but for plastics, medicines, textiles, and thousands of products.'

points.label: Natural sources
points.text: Crude oil: mixture of alkanes and other hydrocarbons; coal: aromatic and aliphatic compounds

points.label: Refining
points.text: Crude oil is separated by boiling point into fractions: LPG, petrol, diesel, fuel oil, bitumen

points.label: Uses beyond fuel
points.text: Plastics (polyethylene from ethene), medicines, dyes, solvents, lubricants

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons are fossil fuels—ancient organic matter converted into energy and materials over millions of years.

image.alt: Hydrocarbons from the Earth — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Classification: Saturated vs. Unsaturated
slides.storyContext: Arun opens an old bottle of sesame oil and a bottle of vegetable oil from his kitchen. 'Ms. Verma, why does the sesame oil feel thicker and last longer?' Ms. Verma explains: saturated fats are like full trains—no more seats (C–C single bonds only). Unsaturated fats have gaps—they can still pick up passengers (double/triple bonds). This affects how tightly they pack and how they react.

points.label: Alkanes (Saturated)
points.text: Only C–C single bonds, formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Examples: CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈. Unreactive.

points.label: Alkenes (Unsaturated)
points.text: At least one C=C double bond, formula CₙH₂ₙ. Examples: C₂H₄ (ethene), C₃H₆ (propene). Reactive.

points.label: Alkynes (Unsaturated)
points.text: At least one C≡C triple bond, formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂. Examples: C₂H₂ (acetylene). Very reactive.

example.problem: Propane (C₃H₈) and propene (C₃H₆) have the same carbons but different formulas. Why, and how does that affect their properties?
example.solution: Propane has only C–C single bonds (saturated); propene has one C=C double bond (unsaturated). Propene is more reactive—it readily undergoes addition reactions (adding H₂, Br₂, etc.) because the double bond can break and form new bonds. Propane is inert unless heated or exposed to a catalyst.

slides.inSimpleWords: Saturated hydrocarbons are fully bonded and lazy; unsaturated ones have a double or triple bond, which makes them eager to react.

image.alt: Classification: Saturated vs. Unsaturated — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkanes: The Saturated Series
slides.storyContext: Neha researches hydrocarbon sources. 'Natural gas is mostly methane. Petrol is a mixture of alkanes. Coal is ancient alkanes and aromatics.' Ms. Verma nods. 'Alkanes are the most stable hydrocarbons. They're found in crude oil, and we refine them for energy. Let's look at their properties and reactions.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ for acyclic alkanes; CₙH₂ₙ for cycloalkanes

points.label: Bonding
points.text: All C–C and C–H bonds are sigma (σ) bonds; no π bonds

points.label: Properties
points.text: Nonpolar, hydrophobic, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, low reactivity

points.label: Main reactions
points.text: Combustion: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (+ heat); Free radical substitution (with Cl₂ or Br₂ under light)

example.problem: Complete combustion of octane (C₈H₁₈): write the balanced equation and explain why this is the basis of petrol's energy.
example.solution: 2 C₈H₁₈ + 25 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 18 H₂O. Petrol is mostly octane and similar alkanes. Combustion releases enormous energy (≈46 MJ/kg) because C–C and C–H bonds are relatively weak compared to C=O bonds in CO₂; the energy difference fuels our engines.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes are stable, nonreactive hydrocarbons found in crude oil. When you burn them, they release huge amounts of energy.

image.alt: Alkanes: The Saturated Series — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Combustion Reactions: Energy Release
slides.storyContext: Arun watches a demo: Ms. Verma lights ethane gas. A bright blue flame produces heat and light. 'Every hydrocarbon combusts this way,' she explains. 'Complete combustion to CO₂ and H₂O releases the maximum energy.'

example.problem: Balance the combustion of methane (CH₄) and calculate the energy change using bond energies.
example.solution: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Bond energies (kJ/mol): C–H = 413, O=O = 495, C=O = 799, O–H = 467. Bonds broken: 4(413) + 2(495) = 2642 kJ. Bonds formed: 2(799) + 4(467) = 2670 kJ. ΔH ≈ 2642 − 2670 = −28 kJ/mol (actually about −890 kJ/mol per mole of CH₄, showing combustion is highly exothermic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes burn completely in oxygen to produce CO₂ and H₂O, releasing large amounts of heat energy.

image.alt: Combustion Reactions: Energy Release — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkenes: The Unsaturated Players
slides.storyContext: Arun watches a demo: Ms. Verma adds bromine water to a test tube of ethene (C₂H₄). The orange-brown color vanishes instantly. 'The double bond opens up and captures the bromine. Alkenes are busy molecules—always ready to add something. This is why they're so useful in industry.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ (acyclic) or CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (cyclic with one ring)

points.label: Bonding
points.text: One or more C=C (sigma + pi bond); pi bond is the reactive site

points.label: Reactions
points.text: Addition: C=C + H₂, Cl₂, Br₂, H₂O, HCl → add across the double bond

points.label: Markovnikov rule
points.text: When HX (e.g., HCl) adds to an asymmetric alkene, H adds to the C with more H; X adds to the C with fewer H

example.problem: Propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂) reacts with HCl. Which product forms: 1-chloropropane or 2-chloropropane? Explain using Markovnikov's rule.
example.solution: 2-chloropropane (CH₃–CHCl–CH₃). By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the C with more H atoms (the CH₂ end), so Cl adds to the other C. The carbocation at the internal C is more stable (secondary) than at the terminal C (primary), so the reaction favors 2-chloropropane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes have a double bond that's eager to break apart and bond with other atoms. This makes them useful for making plastics and medicines.

image.alt: Alkenes: The Unsaturated Players — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Addition Reactions of Alkenes
slides.storyContext: Neha performs a series of tests on ethene (C₂H₄): adding bromine water, adding hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst, adding water in acidic solution.

example.problem: Write the products of these reactions with ethene: (1) + Br₂, (2) + H₂ (Ni catalyst), (3) + H₂O (H₂SO₄ catalyst)
example.solution: (1) C₂H₄ + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane (BrCH₂–CH₂Br, colorless). (2) C₂H₄ + H₂ → C₂H₆ (ethane). (3) C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH (ethanol). All are addition reactions—the double bond opens and new bonds form across it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes undergo addition reactions because the double bond is reactive and can break to form new bonds.

image.alt: Addition Reactions of Alkenes — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkynes: The Triple Bond Specialists
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma holds up a sample of acetylene (C₂H₂). 'This is used in welding torches because it burns at over 3000°C. The triple bond is even more strained and reactive than a double bond. Alkynes are powerful and rare in nature, but chemists use them to build complex molecules.'

points.label: General formula
points.text: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ for terminal alkynes; CₙH₂ₙ₋₄ for internal alkynes

points.label: Bonding
points.text: One C≡C (sigma + two pi bonds); the triple bond is very polarizable

points.label: Reactivity
points.text: Even more reactive than alkenes; can undergo addition, polymerization, and coupling

points.label: Terminal alkyne
points.text: Has an H on the triple-bonded C (—C≡C–H); weakly acidic, can form metal salts

example.problem: Acetylene (HC≡CH) reacts with Br₂. Write the product and explain the step-by-step addition.
example.solution: Step 1: HC≡CH + Br₂ → trans-1,2-dibromoethene (BrCH=CHBr, red color). Step 2: Further addition (if excess Br₂) → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane (BrCH₂–CHBr₂, colorless). Acetylene's triple bond opens in two stages, adding 2 Br at each step.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkynes have a triple bond—the strongest and most reactive C–C linkage. They're rare but incredibly useful in chemistry.

image.alt: Alkynes: The Triple Bond Specialists — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: The Special Ring
slides.storyContext: Neha brings a sample of charred wood from her cooking fire. 'Ms. Verma, I detect a sweet smell. What is it?' Ms. Verma explains: 'Benzene and other aromatics. They come from coal and petroleum. Unlike alkenes, benzene doesn't decolorize bromine easily—its π electrons are delocalized in a resonance-stabilized ring, making it unusually stable. Aromatic compounds are special.'

points.label: Benzene (C₆H₆)
points.text: Hexagonal ring with alternating double bonds (or resonance hybrid with delocalized π electrons)

points.label: Stability
points.text: Resonance delocalization makes benzene extra stable (aromatic); does not undergo addition like alkenes

points.label: Reactions
points.text: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (SEA): an electrophile replaces an H on the ring

points.label: Nitration example
points.text: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ (nitrobenzene); requires a catalyst and heat

example.problem: Explain why benzene (C₆H₆) does NOT decolorize bromine water like alkenes do, even though it has 'double bonds'.
example.solution: Benzene is aromatic: its 6 π electrons are delocalized equally around the ring, creating a resonance-stabilized structure. The 'double bonds' are not true C=C bonds ready to add Br₂. Instead, benzene undergoes substitution (SEA), where an H is replaced, not addition where Br₂ opens a double bond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Benzene and its cousins are 'aromatic'—their rings are so stable and special that they don't react like regular alkenes. They swap atoms rather than add them.

image.alt: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: The Special Ring — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Aromatic Substitution vs. Alkene Addition
slides.storyContext: Arun compares the behavior of benzene and ethene with bromine. Ethene decolorizes bromine water immediately (addition); benzene barely reacts (substitution only occurs with a catalyst).

example.problem: Contrast the reactions of ethene and benzene with Br₂. Why do they react so differently?
example.solution: Ethene (C₂H₄) + Br₂ → 1,2-dibromoethane (BrCH₂–CH₂Br) instantly. The C=C double bond is reactive and adds Br across. Benzene (C₆H₆) + Br₂ → NO REACTION (at room temperature). Requires a catalyst (FeBr₃) and heat for substitution: C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr. Benzene's aromatic ring is stabilized by resonance, so it resists disruption and only undergoes substitution, not addition.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes eagerly add bromine; benzene stubbornly refuses—its aromatic ring is just too stable.

image.alt: Aromatic Substitution vs. Alkene Addition — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Worked Example: Predicting Hydrocarbon Reactions
slides.storyContext: Arun is given a mystery hydrocarbon and asks Ms. Verma how to predict its reactions. Ms. Verma walks him through a full analysis: identify the type (alkane, alkene, alkyne, aromatic), predict the reactions, and explain the mechanism.

points.label: Sample: Pent-2-ene (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃)
points.text: Alkene; contains a C=C double bond in the middle chain

points.label: Add H₂ (hydrogenation)
points.text: CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃ + H₂ (catalyst: Ni/Pd) → CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ (pentane)

points.label: Add Br₂
points.text: Orange bromine is decolorized; product is 2,3-dibromopentane (or the two enantiomers)

points.label: Add HCl
points.text: Markovnikov: Cl adds to the internal C with fewer H, forming 2-chloropentane (secondary carbocation is more stable)

example.problem: Predict the product when pent-2-ene reacts with cold dilute KMnO₄ (oxidation).
example.solution: The double bond in pent-2-ene is cleaved by KMnO₄. Since the C=C is not at the end, products are two ketones: CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ rearranges to give 2-pentanone and some other oxidation products. A purple KMnO₄ solution turns brown (MnO₂) as the oxidation occurs.

slides.inSimpleWords: To predict how a hydrocarbon will react, first identify what type it is. Then apply the rules: alkanes burn or substitute; alkenes and alkynes add; aromatics substitute.

image.alt: Worked Example: Predicting Hydrocarbon Reactions — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Hydrocarbon Reaction Sequence
slides.storyContext: Arun is asked to design a lab procedure to convert ethane (C₂H₆) into ethanol (C₂H₅OH) using only hydrocarbon chemistry. He must plan the steps, predict products, and explain each reaction.

example.problem: Ethane cannot be directly converted to ethanol via addition reactions. Design a route: (a) substitute to form an alkene, (b) use the alkene to introduce oxygen functionality.
example.solution: Step 1: Ethane (C₂H₆) + Br₂ (UV light) → free radical substitution → bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) + HBr. Step 2: Bromoethane + KOH (alcoholic) → elimination → ethene (C₂H₄) + KBr + H₂O. Step 3: Ethene + H₂SO₄ (dilute) + H₂O (hydration) → ethanol (C₂H₅OH). The pathway uses substitution and elimination to form an alkene, then hydration to add the OH group.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons can be converted into each other through a series of well-planned reactions. Identify the starting point, the target, and the pathways in between.

image.alt: Challenge: Design a Hydrocarbon Reaction Sequence — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Classify Unknown Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Neha is given three unknown hydrocarbons and must classify each as alkane, alkene, alkyne, or aromatic based on their reactivity with bromine water and KMnO₄.

example.problem: Sample A: Does NOT decolorize Br₂ water at room temp, requires catalyst and heat. Sample B: Decolorizes Br₂ instantly, orange → colorless. Sample C: Burns to CO₂ and H₂O only, inert to Br₂. Classify each.
example.solution: Sample A: AROMATIC (benzene or derivative). It doesn't add Br₂ without catalyst (stable aromatic ring). Sample B: ALKENE or ALKYNE (most likely alkene). Immediately decolorizes Br₂ via addition. Sample C: ALKANE. Inert to Br₂, only reacts at high temp or with catalysts (substitution).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use bromine water and permanganate tests to distinguish alkanes, alkenes, and aromatic compounds.

image.alt: Challenge: Classify Unknown Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Polymerization: From Alkenes to Plastics
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma holds up a plastic bag. 'This started as ethene from crude oil. Through polymerization, thousands of ethene molecules link together to form polyethylene. This is how we make plastics.'

points.label: Addition polymerization
points.text: Monomers (alkenes) add across their double bonds repeatedly, forming long polymer chains.

points.label: Common polymers
points.text: Polyethylene (from ethene), polypropylene (from propene), polyvinyl chloride / PVC (from vinyl chloride)

points.label: Properties
points.text: Polymers are long-chain hydrocarbons; properties depend on chain length, branching, and cross-linking.

example.problem: Write the polymerization equation for ethene (C₂H₄) to form polyethylene.
example.solution: nC₂H₄ → [–CH₂–CH₂–]ₙ (polyethylene). The double bonds in ethene open and link repeatedly, creating a long saturated hydrocarbon chain.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkenes can link together to form long-chain polymers—the basis of plastics used in everything from bags to bottles.

image.alt: Polymerization: From Alkenes to Plastics — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Worked Example: Oil Refining and Fractional Distillation
slides.storyContext: Arun learns about the fractional distillation column at an oil refinery. Crude oil is separated into fractions based on boiling point, which depends on hydrocarbon chain length.

points.label: Fractional distillation
points.text: Crude oil is heated to 350°C, evaporated, and fed into a fractionating column where temperature decreases upward.

points.label: Fractions (top to bottom)
points.text: Petroleum gas (C₁–C₄), petrol (C₅–C₁₀), kerosene (C₁₀–C₁₆), diesel (C₁₆–C₂₀), fuel oil (C₂₀–C₅₀), bitumen (>C₅₀)

points.label: Why it works
points.text: Smaller molecules (lighter hydrocarbons) have lower boiling points and escape as vapor higher up. Larger molecules condense lower down.

example.problem: Why does petrol (C₅–C₁₀) condense in the middle of the fractionating column while bitumen (very long chains) condenses at the bottom?
example.solution: Boiling point increases with chain length (more intermolecular forces). Petrol (smaller) boils at ~170°C, condenses in the warm middle. Bitumen (very large) boils at >350°C, remains liquid until the coolest bottom section.

slides.inSimpleWords: Crude oil is separated into useful fractions by boiling point—longer hydrocarbons boil at higher temps and condense lower in the column.

image.alt: Worked Example: Oil Refining and Fractional Distillation — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Challenge: Predict Reactivity Based on Structure
slides.storyContext: Neha is given three unknowns—an alkane, an alkene, and an aromatic—and must predict their reactions with Br₂, H₂SO₄, and KMnO₄.

example.problem: Given: (A) hexane (C₆H₁₄), (B) hex-3-ene (C₆H₁₂), (C) benzene (C₆H₆). Predict reactions with Br₂, H₂SO₄, and KMnO₄.
example.solution: Hexane: No reaction with Br₂ (at room temp). No reaction with H₂SO₄ (dilute). Burns to CO₂ + H₂O in KMnO₄ (combustion only). Hex-3-ene: Decolorizes Br₂ (addition). No reaction with dilute H₂SO₄. Oxidized by KMnO₄ (double bond opens). Benzene: No reaction with Br₂ (at room temp, needs FeBr₃ catalyst). No reaction with dilute H₂SO₄. Very resistant to KMnO₄ (aromatic ring is stable).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes are inert; alkenes readily add halogens and are oxidized; aromatics resist addition and oxidation.

image.alt: Challenge: Predict Reactivity Based on Structure — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Sustainability & Alternative Fuels
slides.storyContext: Neha raises an important question: 'Crude oil is a fossil fuel—it will run out. What are we doing to find alternatives?' Ms. Verma explains: 'Biofuels from plants, hydrogen fuel cells, and electric vehicles powered by renewable energy. The chemistry remains hydrocarbon-based or hydrogen-based, but the source is shifting.'

points.text: Biofuels: ethanol from sugarcane, biodiesel from vegetable oil—renewable hydrocarbons
Hydrogen: can be produced from water via electrolysis; burns to H₂O with zero emissions
Electric vehicles: use rechargeable batteries instead of combustion (but storage is key)

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbon chemistry is driving innovation in sustainable fuels and energy storage.

image.alt: Sustainability & Alternative Fuels — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Cracking & Reforming: Industrial Hydrocarbon Processing

points.label: Cracking
points.text: Breaking long-chain alkanes into smaller ones by heating with a catalyst. Produces both alkanes and alkenes.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Crude oil refining produces too much heavy fuel oil and not enough petrol. Cracking converts heavy fractions into useful petrol-range hydrocarbons.

points.label: Reforming
points.text: Converting straight-chain alkanes into branched alkanes and aromatics to improve octane rating of petrol.

example.problem: What happens when dodecane (C₁₂H₂₆, too large for petrol) is cracked?
example.solution: C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ (octane, useful in petrol) + C₄H₈ (butene, useful in polymerization). Cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter, more useful products.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cracking and reforming transform crude oil fractions into more valuable products—this is how refineries maximize usable petrol from crude oil.

image.alt: Cracking & Reforming: Industrial Hydrocarbon Processing — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Substitution vs. Addition in Alkanes vs. Alkenes
slides.storyContext: Neha summarizes the key difference between alkane and alkene chemistry: how their C–C bonds determine their reactions.

example.problem: Compare: (1) Ethane + Cl₂ vs. (2) Ethene + Cl₂. Write the products and explain why they're different.
example.solution: (1) C₂H₆ + Cl₂ (UV light, 60°C) → C₂H₅Cl + HCl (SUBSTITUTION: H is replaced by Cl via free-radical mechanism). (2) C₂H₄ + Cl₂ (room temp) → ClCH₂–CH₂Cl (ADDITION: Cl₂ opens the double bond). Different mechanisms and products because ethane has only single bonds (stable); ethene has a reactive π bond.

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkanes undergo substitution (swap atoms); alkenes undergo addition (open the double bond). The difference stems from the C–C bond type.

image.alt: Substitution vs. Addition in Alkanes vs. Alkenes — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Structural Isomerism in Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Arun explores how different chain arrangements create isomers with identical formulas but different properties. 'Chain isomers have the same atoms but different boiling points and physical properties.'

points.label: Chain isomers
points.text: Same molecular formula, different carbon chain arrangement (e.g., butane vs. isobutane).

points.label: Position isomers
points.text: Functional group (double bond) at different positions (e.g., pent-1-ene vs. pent-2-ene).

points.label: Property differences
points.text: Isomers have same chemical formula but different bp, density, and reactivity.

example.problem: C₅H₁₀ can be pent-1-ene (CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃) or pent-2-ene (CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂–CH₃). Are they isomers?
example.solution: Yes. Both have C₅H₁₀. They're position isomers—the double bond is at different positions. They have different boiling points and different reactivities (pent-1-ene is terminal, pent-2-ene is internal).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons with the same formula can have different structures—chain isomers and position isomers.

image.alt: Structural Isomerism in Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Alkyne Reactions: Triple Bond Reactivity
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma demonstrates that alkynes are even more reactive than alkenes. 'The triple bond can add two molecules instead of one. This makes alkynes powerful synthetic intermediates.'

example.problem: Write the products when acetylene (HC≡CH) reacts with (1) H₂ (excess, catalyst) and (2) Br₂ (excess).
example.solution: (1) HC≡CH + 2H₂ (Ni catalyst) → CH₃–CH₃ (ethane, both pi bonds saturated). (2) HC≡CH + 2Br₂ → BrCH₂–CHBr₂ (1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane, both pi bonds opened and filled with Br).

slides.inSimpleWords: Alkynes can add two molecules (or equivalents) because they have two π bonds instead of one.

image.alt: Alkyne Reactions: Triple Bond Reactivity — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons: IUPAC Rules Applied

points.label: Alkane naming
points.text: Identify longest chain, number from nearest end, name substituents: e.g., 2-methylpropane.

points.label: Alkene naming
points.text: Longest chain including C=C, number from end nearest double bond, use suffix -ene: e.g., pent-2-ene.

points.label: Alkyne naming
points.text: Similar to alkenes but with suffix -yne and triple-bond number: e.g., pent-2-yne.

example.problem: Name: CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH=CH–CH₃
example.solution: Longest chain: 5 carbons. Double bond present: use -ene. Number from nearest end (C=C at positions 3–4, so number from left: C1-C2-C3=C4-C5). Methyl branch at C2. Name: 2-methylpent-3-ene.

slides.inSimpleWords: IUPAC nomenclature for hydrocarbons follows the same rules: longest chain, functional groups get priority, substituents alphabetically.

image.alt: Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons: IUPAC Rules Applied — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Combustion Analysis of Hydrocarbons
slides.storyContext: Arun learns that burning a hydrocarbon in oxygen tells you its exact composition. 'All the carbon becomes CO₂, all the hydrogen becomes H₂O. By weighing these products, we deduce the C:H ratio.'

example.problem: 0.1 g of a hydrocarbon (unknown CₓHᵧ) burns to give 0.22 g CO₂ and 0.09 g H₂O. Find x and y.
example.solution: Moles of CO₂ = 0.22/44 = 0.005; moles of C = 0.005. Moles of H₂O = 0.09/18 = 0.005; moles of H = 0.01. Ratio C:H = 0.005:0.01 = 1:2. Empirical formula: CH₂. Mass of empirical = 14. Sample mass = 0.1 g, so roughly CH₂ or (CH₂)ₙ for n ≈ 7 if molar mass ≈ 98.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combustion analysis: burn the hydrocarbon, weigh CO₂ and H₂O, deduce C:H ratio.

image.alt: Combustion Analysis of Hydrocarbons — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Predicting Products: Reaction Type Determines Outcome
slides.storyContext: Ms. Verma challenges the class: 'You have an alkane, an alkene, and an aromatic. Given the same reagent (e.g., KMnO₄), each reacts differently or not at all. Predict which reacts and what the product is.'

example.problem: Predict reactions with dilute KMnO₄: (1) butane, (2) but-2-ene, (3) benzene
example.solution: (1) Butane (C₄H₁₀): no reaction (saturated, stable alkane). (2) But-2-ene (C₄H₈): double bond is oxidatively cleaved; purple KMnO₄ turns brown as the C=C is broken. (3) Benzene: very resistant (aromatic); no reaction with dilute KMnO₄ unless heated and concentrated.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbon type determines reactivity: alkanes resist oxidation; alkenes are readily oxidized; aromatics are extremely stable.

image.alt: Predicting Products: Reaction Type Determines Outcome — Hydrocarbons

slides.title: Recap: Hydrocarbons Power the World
slides.storyContext: As the unit concludes, Arun, Neha, and Ms. Verma reflect on what they've learned. 'Hydrocarbons are everywhere,' Neha says. 'And understanding their structure and reactivity helps us use them wisely—for energy, for materials, and even for the medicines that save lives.'

points.text: Hydrocarbons are compounds of C and H only; classified by C–C bond type
Alkanes (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂): saturated, stable, react by combustion or substitution
Alkenes (CₙH₂ₙ): unsaturated, reactive, undergo addition reactions
Alkynes (CₙH₂ₙ₋₂): very reactive, triple bond, used in synthesis and welding
Aromatic hydrocarbons: resonance-stabilized rings, undergo substitution not addition
Reactions follow predictable rules (Markovnikov, free radical, electrophilic substitution)
Hydrocarbons are the foundation of fuels, plastics, medicines, and modern chemistry

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrocarbons come in different types—each with its own reactivity and uses. Learn to recognize them, predict their reactions, and harness their power.

image.alt: Recap: Hydrocarbons Power the World — Hydrocarbons

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices
title: Arjun's First Share: How the Stock Market Works
hook: When Arjun buys a tiny piece of a company, who sets the price? Let's follow the market.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: His cousin, a stock broker in Mumbai

slides.title: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

image.alt: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: The Tea Company Needs Money
slides.storyContext: Arjun's favourite tea brand in Bangalore wants to expand. The owner splits the company into 1 million tiny pieces called 'shares' and sells them to raise ₹50 crore. Arjun buys 10 shares for ₹5,000. Now he owns a small piece of the company. Every day, buyers and sellers meet on the stock exchange to trade these shares. The price moves based on how many people want to buy vs. how many want to sell. Priya, his cousin, shows him the BSE platform.

image.alt: The Tea Company Needs Money — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: What is a Share (Equity)?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A share is a unit of ownership in a company. If a company has 1,00,000 shares and you own 100, you own 0.1% of the company.

points.label: Rights
points.text: Shareholders get voting rights (choose the board of directors) and a claim on profits (dividends), though not guaranteed.

points.label: Liquidity
points.text: Shares can be bought and sold on stock exchanges (BSE, NSE) during trading hours. You can convert shares to cash quickly.

slides.inSimpleWords: A share is a certificate of partial ownership. Buy shares, become part-owner; the company's profits are partly yours.

example.problem: Maruti Suzuki has 2 crore shares issued. Arjun buys 50 shares. What % of the company does he own?
example.solution: Arjun's ownership = 50 / (2 crore) = 50 / 2,00,00,000 = 0.000025% = 1 in 40 lakh shareholders.

slides.title: Inside the Exchange: Buyers & Sellers Meet
slides.storyContext: One morning, Arjun logs into his broker's app. It's 9:15 AM, market open. He sees a screen with the tea company's shares: 'Buy at ₹98, Sell at ₹100.' He's confused. Priya explains: 'The person selling wants ₹100 minimum (that's the 'ask'). The person buying offers ₹98 max (that's the 'bid'). Right now they disagree. But within seconds, someone will accept ₹99, the trade happens, and thousands of people buy and sell at that price. It's like a marketplace, but digital and instant.'

slides.title: Supply & Demand Sets the Price

points.label: Price Discovery
points.text: On the stock exchange, buyers place 'bids' (offer price) and sellers place 'asks' (asking price). When bid matches ask, a trade happens at that price.

points.label: Demand ↑ = Price ↑
points.text: If 10,000 investors want to buy the tea stock but only 1,000 shares are for sale, the price rises. Scarcity increases value.

points.label: Supply ↑ = Price ↓
points.text: If a big shareholder dumps 50,000 shares on the market, prices often fall as supply floods demand.

slides.inSimpleWords: Price is decided by who wants to buy and who wants to sell. More buyers than sellers = higher price. More sellers than buyers = lower price.

example.problem: On Day 1, the tea stock opens at ₹100. By noon, 50,000 people want to buy but only 5,000 shares are on offer. By 2 PM it reaches ₹120. Why?
example.solution: Demand is 10x supply. Buyers are willing to pay higher prices to get shares. The price rises until enough buyers step back and enough sellers step forward to balance.

image.alt: Supply & Demand Sets the Price — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Why Did the Price Jump? (A Real-Life Story)
slides.storyContext: The tea company announces a ₹200 crore profit—double last year's earnings. Immediately, investors flood the market with buy orders. News spreads via financial media: 'Tea Company Q1 beats expectations.' Within 5 minutes, the stock jumps from ₹100 to ₹115. By evening, it settles at ₹112. Arjun calls Priya: 'Did something change about the company in 5 minutes?' She laughs: 'No. The company is the same. But NOW everyone knows it's profitable. Demand surged. Price rose to balance buyers and sellers.'

slides.title: The Stock Exchange: BSE & NSE

points.label: BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange)
points.text: India's oldest exchange (since 1875). Headquartered in Mumbai. Main index: Sensex (30 companies). Trading via licensed brokers.

points.label: NSE (National Stock Exchange)
points.text: Younger, electronic exchange (founded 1992). Main index: Nifty 50 (50 companies). More volumes, faster.

points.label: How It Works
points.text: You don't go to the exchange floor. You call a broker (online or human), place an order, and the broker matches you with a seller/buyer. The exchange records and settles the trade (T+1: trade day + 1, shares land in your account next day).

slides.inSimpleWords: BSE and NSE are electronic marketplaces. You use a broker to buy or sell. They find the other party, execute the trade, and settle it the next day.

image.alt: The Stock Exchange: BSE & NSE — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Priya Shows Arjun the Trading Terminal
slides.storyContext: Arjun sits in Priya's BSE office. She pulls up the terminal. 'See this? The bid column shows all offers to buy. The ask column shows all offers to sell. Most trades happen where they overlap. During India-US news or market-moving events, the spreads widen because people are uncertain. When sentiment is clear, trades cluster tightly around one price.'

slides.title: Types of Orders & Strategies

points.label: Market Order
points.text: Buy/sell immediately at whatever the current price is. Fast, but you don't control the exact price.

points.label: Limit Order
points.text: Set a price cap: 'Sell at ₹120 or higher, not lower.' It waits until that price is available or the order expires.

points.label: Stop-Loss Order
points.text: Protect yourself: 'If the price drops to ₹90, auto-sell.' Prevents big losses if the stock crashes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different order types give you different levels of control. Market order is fast. Limit order is precise. Stop-loss protects you from big drops.

example.problem: Arjun buys 100 shares at ₹100 = ₹10,000. He sets a stop-loss at ₹90. If the stock crashes to ₹85, what happens?
example.solution: The broker auto-sells the 100 shares at ₹90 (or the next best price), locking in a ₹10 loss per share = ₹1,000 total loss. Without the stop-loss, he might have lost ₹1,500 or more.

image.alt: Types of Orders & Strategies — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: When Arjun's Market Order Backfires
slides.storyContext: One afternoon, Arjun panics. The tea stock is sliding from ₹100 to ₹98. He hits 'Sell Market Order' without thinking. The order instantly matches at ₹97.50 (not ₹98). Mr. Desai shakes his head: 'You got 'slippage'—the price moved between your order and execution. Next time, use a limit order. Say 'sell at ₹98 or higher.' You'll wait a bit, but you get YOUR price, not the market's.'

slides.title: Bid-Ask Spread & Brokers

points.label: Bid-Ask Spread
points.text: At any moment, the highest bid (buy price) might be ₹100 and the lowest ask (sell price) ₹100.50. That ₹0.50 gap is the spread — profit for market makers.

points.label: Broker Commission
points.text: Your broker takes a small fee (e.g. 0.1% of trade value) for matching you with the other party. ₹10,000 trade = ₹10 commission.

points.label: Impact on Returns
points.text: A ₹10,000 investment at 0.2% fees costs ₹20 immediately. High-frequency traders can't profit from 0.1% moves; long-term investors ignore the spread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Brokers and market makers take a tiny cut. The bid-ask spread is usually small for popular shares (liquid) and bigger for unpopular ones (illiquid).

image.alt: Bid-Ask Spread & Brokers — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: T+1 Settlement: Why Your Shares Arrive Tomorrow
slides.storyContext: Arjun places a buy order on Monday at 10 AM. The trade is matched instantly. But he calls his broker on Monday afternoon asking, 'Where are my shares?' The broker says, 'T+1. T = Today (Monday). +1 = Tomorrow (Tuesday). Your shares land in your demat account by Tuesday 4 PM. The money leaves your bank account today, but the exchange needs time to clear and verify millions of trades.'

slides.title: Market Hours & Trading Rules

points.label: Regular Trading Hours
points.text: BSE & NSE open at 9:15 AM and close at 3:30 PM, Monday to Friday (except national holidays). Pre-open session starts at 9:00 AM (no actual trades, just order placement).

points.label: After-Hours Trading
points.text: No official after-hours trading in India, unlike US markets. But you can place orders anytime on your broker's app (they execute when market opens).

points.label: Weekly Holidays
points.text: Closed on Saturdays, Sundays, national holidays (26 Jan, 15 Aug, 2 Oct, Diwali, Holi, etc.). Plan your trades accordingly; don't place emergency orders on weekends.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock market is open 9:15 AM–3:30 PM on weekdays. You can't trade outside these hours in India. Place orders in advance for market open.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Arjun's First Trade
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees the tea company's Q1 results are strong. He decides to buy 100 shares. Priya walks him through the entire trade.

points.label: Step 1: Research
points.text: Current price ₹100. Market cap ₹1,000 crore. P/E ratio 15. Priya says: 'Fair value is ₹100–110. Good time to buy.'

points.label: Step 2: Place Order
points.text: Arjun places a limit order: 'Buy 100 shares at max ₹102.' Within 2 minutes, 100 shares at ₹101 are matched. Cost = ₹10,100.

points.label: Step 3: Brokerage & Settlement
points.text: Broker charges ₹20 (0.2% of ₹10,100). Arjun pays ₹10,120 total. Next day (T+1), 100 shares appear in his demat account.

points.label: Step 4: Ownership
points.text: Arjun now holds a certificate: 'You own 100 units of Tea Co. Ltd.' He can vote in AGM, receive dividends, or sell anytime the market is open.

slides.inSimpleWords: Buying shares is like buying a fractional ownership certificate. Research the price, place an order, pay the broker fee, and own it next day.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Arjun's First Trade — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Arjun Watches His Investment Volatility
slides.storyContext: Two weeks after buying, Arjun's 100 shares have swung wildly: Monday ₹101, Tuesday ₹104 (he's up ₹300!), Wednesday ₹99 (he's down ₹200), Thursday ₹106, Friday ₹102. He panics every day. Mr. Desai calls: 'This is normal. Short-term, stocks are random. Long-term, good companies trend upward. You're looking at minute-by-minute noise. Check back in 5 years, not 5 days.'

slides.title: Price Volatility: Short-term Noise vs. Long-term Trend

points.label: Intraday Volatility
points.text: A stock can swing 2–5% in a single day due to news, algorithms, and sentiment. This is noise for long-term investors.

points.label: Trends Over Time Horizons
points.text: 1-day move is random (~50% chance up or down). 1-month trend has some direction. 1-year trends correlate with company fundamentals. 5-year returns strongly reflect whether you picked a good company.

points.label: Dollar-Cost Averaging
points.text: Instead of buying 100 shares at once, buy 20 shares every month for 5 months. You average out the price swings and reduce timing risk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices jump around daily, but good companies trend upward over years. Don't panic-sell on daily drops. Hold for long-term, or buy gradually to reduce timing risk.

slides.title: Arjun Discovers Circuit Breakers
slides.storyContext: One day, panic selling causes the tea stock to plummet 20% in 30 minutes. Priya calls: 'The exchange just halted trading for 15 minutes�that's a circuit breaker. It's a safety mechanism to prevent crashes. Prices can't swing more than 10% in 5 minutes without a pause.'

slides.title: Market Safeguards: Circuit Breakers & Holidays
slides.inSimpleWords: Circuit breakers pause trading during extreme moves to prevent panic. Daily limits prevent a single stock from moving >20%. Plan trades around holidays.

points.text: When Sensex moves 10% or more in 5 min, trading halts for 15 min. This prevents panic cascades. Re-evaluated every 5 minutes.
points.label: Circuit Breakers

points.text: Individual stocks have daily limits. A stock can't rise >20% or fall >20% in a day (depends on category). Hits circuit = no trading until next day.
points.label: Upper & Lower Circuits

points.text: Markets close on national holidays (26 Jan, 15 Aug, 2 Oct, Diwali, Holi). No trading = no price discovery on those days.
points.label: Trading Holidays

slides.title: Case Study: How News Moves the Market
slides.storyContext: The tea company announces it's entering a new market (Japan). Within 1 second of the news release, algorithmic traders execute thousands of buy orders. Price jumps ₹2. Within 5 minutes, human traders read the news, evaluate the long-term impact, and adjust. Price settles at ₹1.50 above the pre-news level. By next day, analysts publish reports, and the market digests the strategy. Price stabilizes at ₹1.75 up.

points.label: Second 0–1 (Algo Traders)
points.text: Machines react to the keyword 'Japan' and keywords in the press release. Huge volume, price jumps ₹2.

points.label: Minute 1–5 (Human Traders)
points.text: Brokers and traders read the release, think about long-term effects ('Japan is a mature market, low growth'), and execute more measured trades.

points.label: Hours 1–24 (Market Digestion)
points.text: Analysts publish notes, other companies react, sector dynamics shift. Final price reflects the collective 'fair value' of this news.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices react instantly to news via algorithms, then adjust as humans analyze. The final price reflects the market's consensus view of what the news means for future earnings.

slides.title: Arjun Learns Emotion Control
slides.storyContext: After 6 months, Arjun's tea stock is up 15% (from ₹101 to ₹116). He's euphoric and wants to go all-in and buy more. Then a market correction happens, stock drops to ₹108. He panics and considers selling. Mr. Desai intervenes: 'This is FOMO buying and fear selling. Both are traps. Stick to your plan. Rebalance periodically, not emotionally. The investors who got rich didn't time peaks and troughs; they held winners and averaged their cost.'

slides.title: Challenge: Price Movements During Market Hours
slides.storyContext: It's 9:15 AM on a Monday. The tea stock opens at ₹100. By 10:30 AM, Arjun sees it's ₹105. He wonders: Should he still buy? His friend says the price might drop again by 3:30 PM.

points.label: The Scenario
points.text: Morning: stock at ₹105 (up 5%). Afternoon: slips to ₹102. End of day (3:30 PM): settles at ₹104. Q: What caused the intraday swings, and when is the 'best' time to buy?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Intraday price swings depend on news, sentiment, and volume. Morning surge might be profit-taking by overnight traders.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: No one can predict the best second to buy. But for long-term investors, the entry price within a 5% range doesn't matter much over 5 years.

example.problem: Arjun commits ₹10,000 to the tea stock. If he buys at ₹100 (100 shares) or ₹105 (95 shares), which is better if the stock reaches ₹200 in 5 years?
example.solution: At ₹100: 100 shares × ₹200 = ₹20,000 profit = 100% return. At ₹105: 95 shares × ₹200 = ₹19,000 profit = 90% return. Entry price matters for final returns, but both are good. Timing the exact low is impossible; dollar-cost averaging (buying in tranches) is smarter.

image.alt: Challenge: Price Movements During Market Hours — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Challenge: Market Crash vs. Opportunity
slides.storyContext: In 2020, COVID crashed the market. Sensex fell 40% in 3 weeks. Arjun watched his ₹50,000 portfolio drop to ₹30,000. Mr. Desai's advice: 'This is when brave investors buy.' But Arjun is scared. Should he buy now or wait for it to drop further?

points.label: The Dilemma
points.text: Stock prices are at 10-year lows. Companies haven't changed fundamentally (yet). Is this a buying opportunity or a trap?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Stock prices fall on FEAR, not facts. Companies' earnings might take 6–12 months to decline. Early buyers catch the rebound.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: No one times the market perfectly. But if you're buying for 5+ years, 30% downside vs. long-term 100%+ upside rarely matters.

example.problem: TCS stock crashed from ₹3,500 to ₹2,100 in one month (2020). Arjun wonders: Should he buy at ₹2,100 or wait for ₹1,500? (Today, TCS is ₹3,800.)
example.solution: No one can predict if it'll drop to ₹1,500. If he bought at ₹2,100 and held, 5-year return = (3,800 - 2,100) / 2,100 = 81% CAGR. Even if he bought at ₹3,500 (the peak), holding 5 years = 1.8% total loss (negligible vs. dividends). The key: time in market beats timing the market for long-term investors.

image.alt: Challenge: Market Crash vs. Opportunity — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Challenge: Avoiding Emotional Trading
slides.storyContext: Arjun's investment portfolio is up 20% in 3 months. He's euphoric and wants to go 'all-in' on tech stocks. But Priya warns: 'When everyone is greedy, markets often correct.' Mr. Desai says: 'You're feeling FOMO (Fear of Missing Out). This is the most dangerous emotion in investing.'

points.label: The Trap
points.text: When an investment is 'hot' (everyone talking about it, everyone buying), prices are often already inflated. You're buying at the peak, not the bottom.

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Markets go in cycles: fear → value buying → recovery → greed → correction → fear again. The best investors buy when others are fearful and sell when others are greedy.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: Stick to a plan. Rebalance periodically (e.g., every 6 months), not based on emotions. Sell winners to avoid concentration risk, not to lock in quick profits.

example.problem: Arjun's portfolio: 20% in tea stock (up 20%), 50% in FD (safe but boring), 30% in other stocks (up 10%). Should he move FD money to tea stock to 'ride the wave'?
example.solution: No. He'd be buying a stock at its peak on emotion. Instead: rebalance to original 20/50/30 by selling some tea stock (locking gains) and reinvesting in other opportunities. The rule: if a holding grows > plan, trim it. This forces you to sell high and buy low systematically.

slides.title: Arjun's Year-End Portfolio Review
slides.storyContext: It's December. Arjun reviews his ?50,000 portfolio: ?30,000 in stocks (100% return!), ?20,000 in bonds (12% return). Now stocks are 60% but should be 50%. He sells ?5,000 of stocks and buys bonds. 'This discipline keeps me safe and forces me to sell winners and buy losers,' he tells Mr. Desai. 'Exactly. Most investors do the opposite�they chase winners and avoid losers,' Mr. Desai replies.

slides.title: Systematic Investing: SIP & Rebalancing
slides.inSimpleWords: Use SIP to invest consistently every month. Rebalance annually. These simple habits outperform 90% of investors over 20 years.

points.text: Invest a fixed amount (e.g. ?5,000) monthly in mutual funds or stocks, regardless of price. Eliminates emotion, averages cost, builds discipline.
points.label: Systematic Investment Plan (SIP)

points.text: Review every 3�6 months. If any holding is >target+5%, trim it. If <target-5%, add to it. This forces a 'sell high, buy low' discipline.
points.label: Quarterly/Annual Rebalancing

points.text: SIP of ?10,000/month for 20 years at 12% returns = ?1+ crore. The power is in time, consistency, and letting gains compound.
points.label: Compounding Over Time

slides.title: Diversification & Risk Management

points.label: Why Diversify
points.text: No single stock is certain to outperform. By owning 10–20 different stocks across sectors, you reduce the risk that one company fails and wipes you out.

points.label: Portfolio Allocation
points.text: Young investors: 80% stocks, 20% bonds/FDs. Mid-career: 60% stocks, 40% bonds. Nearing retirement: 40% stocks, 60% bonds. Adjust based on risk tolerance and timeline.

points.label: Rebalancing
points.text: If stocks surge and become 90% of your portfolio, sell some and buy bonds back to 80/20. This forces you to sell high (winners) and buy low (losers).

slides.inSimpleWords: Don't put all money in one stock. Spread across 10–20 stocks and multiple asset classes. Rebalance yearly to maintain your target allocation.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Ownership & Shares
points.text: A share = fractional ownership. Buy shares on BSE/NSE via a broker.

points.label: Price Discovery
points.text: Price = where supply meets demand. More buyers (or fewer sellers) = higher price.

points.label: The Mechanism
points.text: Brokers match buyers & sellers. T+1 settlement. Bid-ask spread & fees apply.

points.label: Order Types
points.text: Market order (fast), Limit order (precise), Stop-loss (protection).

points.label: Long-term Investing
points.text: Exact entry price matters less than 5-year hold. Diversify, don't time the market, avoid emotional decisions.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stock market is a place where fractional ownership of companies changes hands based on supply and demand. Understand the mechanism, use a broker, set stop-losses, and invest for the long term with a plan.

image.alt: What We Learned — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices
title: Priya's Market Report: Reading Stock Prices & Indices
hook: The Sensex falls 200 points—what does it mean and who should care? Priya teaches Arjun to read the market.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Growing investor learning to read market data

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Stock broker and mentor from BSE Mumbai

characters.name: Mr. Desai
characters.role: Retired fund manager who explains indices

slides.title: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

image.alt: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: The Morning Market Report
slides.storyContext: Arjun opens the Economic Times on his phone. He reads: 'Sensex tumbles 200 points on profit-taking; Nifty holds 24,000 level.' He has no idea what it means. He calls Priya, who's at BSE watching the live tickers. She says, 'Sensex and Nifty are like the 'pulse' of the market. They tell you if India Inc. is healthy or anxious. Let me break it down for you step by step.'

image.alt: The Morning Market Report — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Stock Price vs. Market Capitalization

points.label: Stock Price (₹)
points.text: The price per share. A company might trade at ₹50/share or ₹2,000/share. The absolute price is not a measure of 'bigness.'

points.label: Market Cap = Price × Shares Outstanding
points.text: A better measure of company size. If TCS trades at ₹3,500 and has 350 crore shares, Market Cap = ₹12.25 lakh crore. Reliance at ₹2,500 with 180 crore shares = ₹4.5 lakh crore. TCS is bigger.

points.label: Why This Matters
points.text: You can't compare 'Is ₹50/share cheap vs. ₹2,000/share expensive?' without knowing the share count. Market cap is apples-to-apples.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock price alone is misleading. Market cap (price × total shares) tells you how big the company really is. A ₹50 stock with 1 billion shares is bigger than a ₹5,000 stock with 50 million shares.

example.problem: Stock A: ₹100/share, 10 crore shares. Stock B: ₹500/share, 1 crore shares. Which company is bigger?
example.solution: Stock A: Market Cap = ₹100 × 10 crore = ₹1,000 crore. Stock B: Market Cap = ₹500 × 1 crore = ₹500 crore. Stock A's company is 2x bigger, even though its per-share price is 1/5th.

image.alt: Stock Price vs. Market Capitalization — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Arjun's 'Price Trap': ₹20 vs. ₹2,000
slides.storyContext: Arjun finds two stocks: Company X at ₹20/share and Company Y at ₹2,000/share. He thinks, 'X is cheap, Y is expensive!' Priya laughs and pulls up the market caps. X has 100 crore shares = ₹2,000 crore market cap. Y has 1 crore shares = ₹2,000 crore market cap. They're THE SAME SIZE. The share price alone tells you NOTHING. 'This is the biggest trap retail investors fall into,' she warns.

image.alt: Arjun's 'Price Trap': ₹20 vs. ₹2,000 — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: What is a Stock Index?

points.label: Definition
points.text: An index is a weighted basket of leading company stocks. Think of it as the 'representative sample' of the whole market. If the index is up, the market is generally up.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Indices measure market health at a glance. You don't need to track all 5,000 listed companies; track the index instead.

points.label: Weighting
points.text: Indices are usually weighted by market cap. Bigger companies (higher market cap) have more influence on the index movement. TCS (₹12 lakh crore) moves Sensex more than a ₹1,000 crore micro-cap.

slides.inSimpleWords: An index is like the 'health report' of the stock market. It's a basket of top companies weighted by size. When Sensex goes up, it means the big companies are doing well.

image.alt: What is a Stock Index? — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Mr. Desai's Index Analogy
slides.storyContext: Mr. Desai explains: 'An index is like a school's average score. If Arjun (genius) scored 95 and 29 other students scored 50 each, the class average is ~50. But if Arjun scores 100, the class average jumps to 51. Arjun (TCS, top 10% weight in Sensex) moves the average more. Similarly, TCS rising 5% pushes Sensex up 0.5%. A ₹100 crore company rising 50% barely moves it.'

slides.title: Sensex: The 30-Company Pulse (BSE)

points.label: 30 Largest Companies
points.text: Sensex = Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index. It includes India's 30 largest companies (TCS, Reliance, HDFC Bank, Infosys, ITC, ICICI Bank, Bajaj, etc.).

points.label: Market-Cap Weighted
points.text: TCS (₹12+ lakh crore) has ~10% weight in Sensex. A ₹1,000 crore company has <0.1% weight. If TCS stock rises 5%, Sensex rises ~0.5%.

points.label: Historical Baseline
points.text: Jan 1, 1979 baseline = 100 points. Today, Sensex is 80,000+ points. It's gone up 800x in 45 years. A proxy for India's economic growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sensex = the top 30 Indian companies. If Sensex is up, India's best companies are making profits. If down, there's concern in the market.

example.problem: Sensex is 80,000 today. It was 70,000 a year ago. What's the annual return?
example.solution: Return = (80,000 - 70,000) / 70,000 = 10,000 / 70,000 = 14.3% annual appreciation (before dividends). This is the 'market return' for 2024.

image.alt: Sensex: The 30-Company Pulse (BSE) — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Priya Decodes a Sensex Announcement
slides.storyContext: The news says: 'Sensex closes at 82,500, up 450 points, +0.55%. Nifty 50 at 24,800, up 180 points, +0.73%. Advance-decline 21:9.' Arjun asks what it all means. Priya breaks it down: 'Sensex gained ₹450 = 0.55% gain. Nifty gained more (0.73%), so smaller companies outperformed. 21 stocks up, 9 down = broad market strength. Volume high? Then conviction is real. Volume low? Might reverse.'

slides.title: Nifty 50: The NSE's 50-Stock Index

points.label: NSE's Answer to Sensex
points.text: Nifty 50 = 50 largest companies on National Stock Exchange (NSE). Launched 1996. Includes Sensex stocks + 20 others (Bajaj Finance, Wipro, Maruti, NTPC, etc.).

points.label: Slightly Broader
points.text: 50 stocks vs. Sensex's 30 gives a wider view. But correlation is very high (~0.99). If Sensex up 2%, Nifty is usually up ~2%.

points.label: Mutual Fund Benchmark
points.text: Nifty 50 is the standard benchmark. 'Our fund returned 18% vs. Nifty's 16%' means it beat the market. If it returned 14% vs. Nifty 16%, it underperformed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nifty 50 = top 50 Indian companies. Similar to Sensex but slightly broader. Most mutual funds measure themselves against Nifty.

image.alt: Nifty 50: The NSE's 50-Stock Index — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: When All 30 Sensex Stocks Fell But Sensex Gained
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees a news headline: 'All 30 Sensex stocks down, but Sensex up 100 points.' He's confused. Priya explains: 'This happens when the market cap-weighted composition shifts. TCS might be up 2% while others drop 1% each. Since TCS has 10% weight and others average 0.3% weight, the net is positive. Or, Sensex got rebalanced—high-cap stocks replaced with mega-cap ones. The index itself is a rule, not a reflection of every stock.'

slides.title: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio & Valuation

points.label: P/E Ratio = Stock Price / Earnings Per Share (EPS)
points.text: TCS stock ₹3,500. Annual EPS ₹200. P/E = 3,500 / 200 = 17.5. Means: You're paying ₹17.50 for every ₹1 of annual earnings.

points.label: Market P/E vs. Stock P/E
points.text: Sensex's average P/E is ~20. If a stock's P/E is 15, it's undervalued (cheap). If 30, it's expensive (investors expect high future growth).

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: High P/E (>25) = expensive but high growth expected. Low P/E (<15) = cheap but may have risks or low growth. Average P/E (15–25) = fairly priced.

slides.inSimpleWords: P/E ratio shows how many rupees you pay per rupee of company earnings. Lower P/E = cheaper (potentially undervalued). Higher P/E = expensive (growth expected).

example.problem: Stock X: ₹1,000 price, ₹50 EPS. Stock Y: ₹2,000 price, ₹100 EPS. Which is cheaper?
example.solution: Stock X P/E = 1,000/50 = 20. Stock Y P/E = 2,000/100 = 20. Both have the same valuation! Per-share price alone is misleading.

image.alt: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio & Valuation — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: The Hidden Story in P/E Ratios
slides.storyContext: Company A has P/E 15. Company B has P/E 30. Arjun thinks A is cheap. But Priya adds context: 'A's earnings grew 5% last year. B's grew 50% last year. B is expensive NOW, but if growth continues, its earnings double in 2 years. Then P/E falls to 15. You're paying for future growth with B; buying current cheap assets with A. Different investors, different strategies.'

slides.title: Other Key Metrics: Dividend Yield & Price-to-Book

points.label: Dividend Yield = Annual Dividend / Stock Price
points.text: Reliance pays ₹60/share dividend, stock price ₹2,500. Yield = 60/2,500 = 2.4%. Higher-yielding stocks are favored by income investors (retirees). Growth stocks often have 0% yield.

points.label: Price-to-Book (P/B) Ratio
points.text: Market Cap / Book Value of Equity. P/B < 1 suggests undervaluation (stock trading below asset value). P/B > 2 suggests premium valuation or expectations of high future profits.

points.label: PEG Ratio = P/E Ratio / Earnings Growth Rate
points.text: Adjusts P/E for growth. A stock with P/E 30 and 30% growth has PEG 1.0 (fair). P/E 30 with 5% growth has PEG 6.0 (very expensive). Useful for comparing growth vs. value.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividend yield shows cash income from the stock. P/B shows if the stock is valued above or below its assets. PEG adjusts valuation for growth rate.

slides.title: Reading the Daily Market Report

points.label: Sensex 80,000, up 200 points (+0.25%)
points.text: The 30-stock index closed at 80,000. It gained 200 points from yesterday's close. That's a 0.25% daily move (200/80,000). Normal volatility.

points.label: Volume: 500 million shares traded
points.text: Total shares traded across all 30 stocks = 500 million. High volume = high interest, more conviction in the move. Low volume = uncertain, could reverse.

points.label: Advance/Decline Ratio: 18 up, 12 down
points.text: Of the 30 stocks, 18 ended in green (profit), 12 in red (loss). Ratio 60:40 (up:down). A healthy day. If it's 29:1, that's 'euphoria.' If 1:29, that's a 'crash.'

points.label: Sector Performance
points.text: IT stocks +2%, Finance +1%, Pharma -0.5%. You can see which part of the economy is favored today.

slides.inSimpleWords: A market report tells you the index level, the points gained/lost, the volume (intensity), and the advance-decline ratio (how many stocks went up vs. down). All tell you the 'mood' of the market.

image.alt: Reading the Daily Market Report — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Priya Explains Small-Cap vs. Large-Cap
slides.storyContext: Arjun discovers a small-cap stock trading at ?30 with a market cap of ?500 crore. The price seems 'cheap.' Priya warns: 'Don't confuse cheap price with cheap valuation. Small-caps are riskier: lower liquidity, more volatile, higher bankruptcy risk. A large-cap at ?3,000 could be safer than a small-cap at ?30.'

slides.title: Market Cap Categories: Large, Mid, Small Caps
slides.inSimpleWords: Large-caps are stable and liquid but lower returns. Mid-caps are balanced. Small-caps are risky but can deliver 30%+ returns. Match your risk tolerance and timeline.

points.text: TCS, Reliance, HDFC Bank. Stable, liquid, pay dividends. Returns ~10�12% CAGR. Suitable for conservative investors.
points.label: Large-Cap (Market Cap > ?20,000 crore)

points.text: Growing companies, higher risk than large-cap. Returns ~12�18% CAGR. More volatile, but potential for capital appreciation.
points.label: Mid-Cap (?5,000�?20,000 crore)

points.text: High risk, high reward. Returns can be 30%+ but also -50%. Low liquidity, high bankruptcy risk. Only for risk-tolerant, patient investors.
points.label: Small-Cap (< ?5,000 crore)

slides.title: Arjun Tracks Analyst Ratings
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees 15 analysts covering TCS: 12 say 'Buy,' 3 say 'Hold.' Average price target is ?4,200 vs. current ?3,680. Priya explains: 'If consensus is bullish but consensus target is ?4,200 (+14%), that's built-in upside. If the stock rises 30% before you buy, that upside shrinks. Analyst ratings matter less than valuations relative to price targets.'

slides.title: Analyst Ratings & Consensus Estimates
slides.inSimpleWords: Don't blindly follow 'Buy' ratings. Compare current price to analyst price targets. If upside is <10%, the opportunity is small. Look for 20%+ upside.

points.text: 12 'Buys' vs. 3 'Holds' = strong consensus. But 1 'Sell' during a bull market often means the stock is expensive.
points.label: Buy/Hold/Sell Ratings

points.text: If 15 analysts target ?4,200 and stock is at ?3,680, built-in upside = +14%. But if upside has already been realized (stock jumped to ?4,100), the opportunity is gone.
points.label: Price Targets

points.text: Ratings are clues, not directions. A 'Buy' at ?50 with target ?80 is great. A 'Buy' at ?75 with target ?80 is mediocre. Focus on risk-reward ratio, not ratings.
points.label: Using Ratings

slides.title: Reading a Stock Quote: Detailed Breakdown
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at TCS's live quote on his broker's app. Priya walks him through every number.

points.label: Current Price: ₹3,680
points.text: The last traded price. Real-time, updated every second during market hours (9:15 AM–3:30 PM, Monday–Friday).

points.label: 52-Week High: ₹4,100 | 52-Week Low: ₹2,800
points.text: TCS's highest and lowest price in the past 52 weeks. Currently trading near the high, suggesting optimism.

points.label: Market Cap: ₹12.85 lakh crore
points.text: The company's total value. TCS is India's largest IT company by market cap.

points.label: P/E Ratio: 18 | Industry Average: 22
points.text: TCS is cheaper than average IT stock. Might be undervalued or facing near-term headwinds.

points.label: Dividend Yield: 1.2%
points.text: TCS pays ₹44/share annual dividend. ₹44 / ₹3,680 = 1.2%. Plus capital appreciation, this is total return.

points.label: Volume (10M shares traded today)
points.text: High volume = liquid, easy to buy/sell. Low volume = illiquid, wider bid-ask spread, risk of slippage.

slides.inSimpleWords: A stock quote shows price, valuation, dividends, and trading activity. High 52-week high = stock doing well. Low P/E relative to peers = potentially undervalued. High volume = easy to exit.

image.alt: Reading a Stock Quote: Detailed Breakdown — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Challenge: Comparing Two Stocks
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to invest ₹50,000 in either Bank A or Bank B. He pulls up their quotes. Bank A: ₹500/share, Market Cap ₹5 lakh crore, P/E 12. Bank B: ₹2,000/share, Market Cap ₹8 lakh crore, P/E 18. He calls Mr. Desai for advice.

points.label: The Question
points.text: Based on price alone, Bank B (₹2,000) looks 'expensive' vs. Bank A (₹500). Is Bank B really expensive, or is it just higher-priced?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Don't compare per-share prices directly. Compare market caps and P/E ratios.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: A lower P/E means lower expectations for growth, or market is pessimistic. A higher P/E means growth is expected.

example.problem: Using the above data, which stock offers better value: Bank A (P/E 12) or Bank B (P/E 18)?
example.solution: Bank A has a lower P/E (12 vs. 18), so it's cheaper relative to earnings. You're paying ₹12 per ₹1 of earnings at Bank A vs. ₹18 at Bank B. Bank A looks undervalued unless Bank B is expected to grow faster. Check recent profit growth and guidance before deciding.

image.alt: Challenge: Comparing Two Stocks — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Challenge: Sector Rotation & Index Composition
slides.storyContext: Sensex is up 1%, but Arjun notices IT stocks are down 3%, Finance stocks up 5%. He asks: 'How can the overall index go up if half of it went down?' Priya explains sector rotation and weightage.

points.label: The Puzzle
points.text: Sensex = 60% IT + 40% Finance (simplified). IT down 3%, Finance up 5%. Expected Sensex move = (0.6 × -3%) + (0.4 × +5%) = -1.8% + 2% = +0.2%. Index can go up even if IT falls.

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Index movements are weighted. Big sectors (by market cap) dominate. Finance (HDFC Bank, ICICI, Axis) is 40% of Sensex value, not stock count.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: Sector rotation is normal. Sometimes tech booms (2010–2015). Sometimes banks boom (2015–2020). Watch where money flows.

example.problem: Sensex breakdown: TCS (10% weight) down 2%, HDFC Bank (12% weight) up 3%, others (78% weight) flat. What's Sensex's move?
example.solution: Move = (10% × -2%) + (12% × +3%) + (78% × 0%) = -0.2% + 0.36% + 0 = +0.16%. Despite TCS (biggest IT company) down, HDFC Bank's gain dominates because it's also huge.

image.alt: Challenge: Sector Rotation & Index Composition — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: When Priya's Mutual Fund Underperformed
slides.storyContext: Priya manages a large-cap mutual fund that returned 10% vs. Nifty's 14%. Investors left in droves. She explains the logic: 'I held 5% cash (defensive), missed a 20% rally in August, but that saved me during the October crash. Risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe ratio) beat the index, but absolute returns look worse.' The lesson: compare risk-adjusted returns, not just absolute returns.

slides.title: Risk-Adjusted Returns: Sharpe Ratio
slides.inSimpleWords: Higher returns with wild swings (high volatility) can be worse than steady returns with low swings. Use Sharpe ratio to compare funds fairly.

points.text: Measures return per unit of risk. A fund returning 12% with 15% volatility might have a better Sharpe ratio than a 14% return with 25% volatility.
points.label: Sharpe Ratio = (Return - Risk-Free Rate) / Volatility

points.text: A fund that returns 15% with 30% volatility can lose 30% in crashes. One that returns 12% with 10% volatility is smoother. Over 20 years, volatility compounds against you.
points.label: Why It Matters

points.text: Prefer funds with Sharpe > 1.0. Compare only within categories. A bond fund (Sharpe 0.8) shouldn't be compared to an equity fund (Sharpe 1.2).
points.label: Using Sharpe Ratio

slides.title: Priya Reviews Arjun's Portfolio Against Benchmarks
slides.storyContext: Arjun has ?1 lakh in stocks (50% allocation, up 15% YTD) and ?1 lakh in bonds (50% allocation, up 6% YTD). Portfolio return = 10.5%. Nifty returned 12%, Nifty PSU Bonds returned 5.5%. His blended benchmark return = 8.75%. Arjun beat the benchmark! Priya: 'This is over 1 year. Over 10 years, consistency matters more than 1-year outperformance.'

slides.title: Building a Personal Benchmark
slides.inSimpleWords: Create a weighted benchmark matching your portfolio (e.g., 50% Nifty + 50% bond index). Beat it consistently over 5+ years to prove skill.

points.text: If your portfolio is 50% stocks and 50% bonds, your benchmark = (50% � Nifty return) + (50% � bond index return). Beat this consistently = skilled investing.
points.label: Asset-Weighted Benchmark

points.text: 1-year outperformance = luck. 5-year outperformance = skill + luck. 20-year outperformance = skill (luck washes out).
points.label: Time Horizon Matters

points.text: If you beat your benchmark with 2x the volatility, you underperformed on risk-adjusted basis. Use Sharpe ratio to compare fairly.
points.label: Risk-Adjusted Comparison

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Market Cap, Not Price
points.text: Use market cap to compare company size, not per-share price.

points.label: Sensex & Nifty
points.text: Sensex (30 stocks, BSE) and Nifty (50 stocks, NSE) are benchmarks for market health. Both move together.

points.label: P/E Ratio
points.text: P/E = Price / Earnings. Low P/E = cheap (but risky). High P/E = expensive (but growth expected).

points.label: Daily Report
points.text: Read index points, volume, advance-decline, and sector moves. They tell the market's mood.

points.label: Stock Quote
points.text: Price, 52-week range, P/E, market cap, dividend yield, volume — all are clues to value and liquidity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use market cap and P/E ratios to compare stocks fairly. Watch Sensex/Nifty for market trend. Read the daily report to understand which sectors are in favor. A lower P/E isn't always 'cheap'—it depends on growth prospects.
