subject: Mathematics
title: Pairing Students with Subjects: Relations and Functions
hook: When does a pairing rule become a true function? Arjun and Priya explore the rules.

slides.title: Subject Assignment at School
slides.storyContext: At Class 11A, Priya is assigned students to elective subjects. She tracks: 'Arjun takes Math, Karan takes Physics, Priya takes Math, Deepak takes Chemistry.' Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Is every student taking exactly one subject? Can one student take two subjects?' Priya realizes she needs to formalize this relationship.

image.alt: Subject Assignment at School — Relations and Functions

slides.title: The Pairing Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya writes on the board: 'Arjun → Math, Karan → Physics, Priya → Math.' Mrs. Sharma asks: 'Can Arjun take both Math and Physics?' Priya: 'No, each student takes one main elective.' Mrs. Sharma: 'Good. That's important. Let me show you how to formalize pairings.'

image.alt: The Pairing Problem — Relations and Functions

slides.title: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs
slides.storyContext: Priya writes all possible (student, subject) pairs on the board: (Arjun, Math), (Arjun, Physics), (Karan, Math), ...

points.label: Ordered pair
points.text: (a, b) is different from (b, a) — order matters.

points.label: Cartesian product
points.text: A × B = {(a, b) | a ∈ A and b ∈ B} — all possible ordered pairs from A and B.

example.problem: If A = {Ram, Priya} and B = {Math, Physics}, list A × B.
example.solution: A × B = {(Ram, Math), (Ram, Physics), (Priya, Math), (Priya, Physics)}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A Cartesian product pairs every element from the first set with every element from the second.

image.alt: Cartesian Product and Ordered Pairs — Relations and Functions

slides.title: Example: All Possible Subject Assignments
slides.storyContext: Priya lists all possible (student, subject) pairs: A = {Arjun, Karan}, B = {Math, Physics, Chemistry}.

example.problem: List A × B.
example.solution: A × B = {(Arjun, Math), (Arjun, Physics), (Arjun, Chemistry), (Karan, Math), (Karan, Physics), (Karan, Chemistry)}. Total: 2 × 3 = 6 pairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Cartesian product lists every possible combination, even ones that won't actually happen.

image.alt: Example: All Possible Subject Assignments — Relations and Functions

slides.title: What is a Relation?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma says: 'A relation is simply a subset of the Cartesian product — some (but not all) pairs from A × B satisfy a rule.'

points.label: Relation definition
points.text: R ⊆ A × B is a relation from A to B.

points.label: Domain
points.text: The set of all first elements in R — the 'input' set.

points.label: Codomain
points.text: The set B (the intended 'output' set).

points.label: Range
points.text: The set of all second elements actually appearing in R — subset of codomain.

example.problem: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and R = {(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6), (4, 8)} (the 'double' relation). Find domain, codomain, range.
example.solution: Domain = {1, 2, 3, 4}. Codomain = ℕ (all natural numbers, assumed). Range = {2, 4, 6, 8}.

slides.inSimpleWords: A relation picks some pairs from a Cartesian product according to a rule.

slides.title: Arjun's Subject Relation
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma says: 'Priya, you have a relation: {(Arjun, Math), (Karan, Physics), (Priya, Math), (Deepak, Chemistry)}. This is a subset of A × B. But notice: Arjun and Priya both map to Math. That's allowed in a relation.'

slides.title: What is a Function?
slides.storyContext: Priya says: 'Wait — can one student take two subjects at the same time?' Mrs. Sharma: 'If we're assigning ELECTIVES, each student takes exactly one. That's a function.'

points.label: Function definition
points.text: f: A → B is a relation where EVERY element of A maps to EXACTLY ONE element of B.

points.label: Notation
points.text: f(x) = y means the element x maps to y.

points.label: Test
points.text: A relation R is a function if no element of domain appears twice in the pairs.

example.solution: No — 1 maps to both 2 and 4. Each input must have exactly one output.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function gives each input exactly one output — no input can have two answers.

slides.title: Example: Valid Elective Assignment
slides.storyContext: Priya checks: 'Is 'each student assigned exactly one elective' a function?'

example.problem: f: {Arjun, Karan, Priya, Deepak} → {Math, Physics, Chemistry} with f(Arjun) = Math, f(Karan) = Physics, f(Priya) = Math, f(Deepak) = Chemistry. Is f a function?
example.solution: Yes. Every student (input) is assigned exactly one subject (output). Two students (Arjun, Priya) can have the same output (Math), and that's fine.

slides.inSimpleWords: A function ensures each input has one output, but multiple inputs can share the same output.

slides.title: Types of Functions: Injective, Surjective, Bijective
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Can two students take the same subject? Can a subject have no student?' Mrs. Sharma introduces three types.

points.label: Injective (one-to-one)
points.text: If f(a) = f(b), then a = b. Different inputs → different outputs.

points.label: Surjective (onto)
points.text: Every element of B is the image of some element in A (range = codomain).

points.label: Bijective
points.text: Both injective and surjective — a perfect one-to-one matching.

example.problem: f: {1, 2, 3} → {a, b, c} with f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c. Is f bijective?
example.solution: Yes — f is injective (each input maps to a different output) and surjective (every element in codomain is hit). So f is bijective.

slides.inSimpleWords: Injective = no sharing outputs; surjective = all outputs are used; bijective = both.

slides.title: Three Types of Subject Assignments
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma explains: 'Suppose we have 3 students and 3 subjects. If each student gets a different subject AND each subject has exactly one student, that's a bijection. If two students can take Math, it's not injective. If Chemistry has no student, it's not surjective.'

slides.title: Composition of Functions
slides.storyContext: Arjun takes subject Math (function f), which has a difficulty level: Math → Level 3 (function g). Priya asks: 'What if I combine the two assignments?'

points.label: Composition
points.text: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) — apply f first, then g to the result.

points.label: Condition
points.text: f: A → B and g: B → C, then g ∘ f: A → C.

points.label: Order matters
points.text: f ∘ g is usually different from g ∘ f (not commutative).

example.problem: f(x) = 2x and g(x) = x + 3. Find (g ∘ f)(5) and (f ∘ g)(5).

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition chains functions — output of the first becomes input of the second.

slides.title: Example: Subject to Difficulty Composition
slides.storyContext: Let f: student → subject, and g: subject → difficulty. Then g ∘ f: student → difficulty.

example.problem: f(Arjun) = Math, g(Math) = 7. Find (g ∘ f)(Arjun).
example.solution: (g ∘ f)(Arjun) = g(f(Arjun)) = g(Math) = 7. So Arjun has difficulty level 7 (through Math).

slides.inSimpleWords: Composition lets you chain mappings: student → subject → difficulty in one step.

slides.title: Inverse Functions
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma: 'If Arjun's Math assignment is f, can we reverse it? If we know his subject is Math, can we get Arjun back?'

points.label: Inverse function
points.text: f⁻¹: B → A exists only if f is bijective.

points.label: Property
points.text: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(y)) = y.

points.label: Finding inverse
points.text: Set y = f(x), solve for x in terms of y, swap variables.

example.problem: If f(x) = 2x + 3, find f⁻¹.
example.solution: Set y = 2x + 3. Solve: x = (y − 3)/2. Swap: f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: An inverse function 'undoes' the original — if f sends x to y, f⁻¹ sends y back to x.

slides.title: Reversing the Assignment
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Can we reverse the subject assignment? If I know Arjun took Math, can I go backwards to find which student took it?' Mrs. Sharma: 'Only if each subject has exactly one student—a bijection. Then yes, we can invert.'

slides.title: Full Problem: Verifying Bijection and Finding Inverse
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma defines f: {1, 2, 3} → {5, 7, 9} by f(x) = 2x + 3. She asks: 'Is f bijective? Find f⁻¹.'

example.problem: Check if f is injective and surjective, then find f⁻¹.
example.solution: f(1) = 5, f(2) = 7, f(3) = 9. All different (injective). All elements {5, 7, 9} are hit (surjective). So f is bijective. f⁻¹(5) = 1, f⁻¹(7) = 2, f⁻¹(9) = 3, or f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify bijection, check that every input has one output and every output comes from one input.

slides.title: Challenge: Composition and Injectivity
slides.storyContext: Given f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = 2x, find (f ∘ g) and (g ∘ f). Verify that both are injective.

example.problem: Compute (f ∘ g)(x) and (g ∘ f)(x). Are both injective?
example.solution: (f ∘ g)(x) = f(2x) = 2x + 1. (g ∘ f)(x) = g(x + 1) = 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2. Both are injective because if 2x₁ + 1 = 2x₂ + 1, then x₁ = x₂.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check injectivity by assuming f(a) = f(b) and proving a = b.

slides.title: Challenge: Three Functions Chain
slides.storyContext: Let f: students → subjects, g: subjects → difficulty, h: difficulty → time-needed. Find (h ∘ g ∘ f).

example.problem: If f(Arjun) = Math, g(Math) = 7, h(7) = 14 hours, find (h ∘ g ∘ f)(Arjun).
example.solution: (h ∘ g ∘ f)(Arjun) = h(g(f(Arjun))) = h(g(Math)) = h(7) = 14 hours. Arjun needs 14 hours to master Math.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chaining three functions: apply the innermost first, then work outward.

slides.title: Identity Function
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma introduces: 'There's a special function: the identity function, I(x) = x. It maps every element to itself. (I ∘ f)(x) = f(x) — composing with identity doesn't change anything.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The identity function maps x → x. Composing with it doesn't change the original function.

slides.title: Example: Verifying an Inverse
slides.storyContext: If f(x) = 3x − 2, verify that f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3 by showing f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

example.problem: Show that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for f(x) = 3x − 2.
example.solution: f(f⁻¹(x)) = f((x + 2)/3) = 3((x + 2)/3) − 2 = (x + 2) − 2 = x. Yes, the inverse works!

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify an inverse, compute f(f⁻¹(x)) and check that it equals x.

slides.title: Transformations via Functions
slides.storyContext: Functions can model transformations. If f: students → scores, then f is assigning scores. If g: scores → grades, then g assigns grades. Together, they 'transform' students into grades.

points.label: Transformation
points.text: A function transforms inputs into outputs via a rule.

points.label: Linear transformation
points.text: f(x) = mx + b transforms x by scaling and shifting.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: In coordinates, (x, y) → (x, mx + b) shifts and stretches the plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions transform inputs: scale them, shift them, reverse them—any rule that maps one set to another.

slides.title: Functions in the Real World
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes: 'Functions are everywhere. Temperature changes over time (time → temp). Marks map to grades (marks → grade). Prices depend on demand (demand → price). Every real-world relationship can be modeled as a function.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world relationships—temperature, grades, prices, distance—are all functions.

slides.title: Challenge: Modeling with Functions
slides.storyContext: A taxi charges: ₹50 base fare + ₹15 per km. Model this as a function and find the fare for 20 km.

example.problem: Let f(x) = 50 + 15x, where x = distance in km. Find f(20).

slides.inSimpleWords: Model real costs/prices as functions to predict outcomes instantly.

slides.title: Challenge: Composite Real Scenario
slides.storyContext: A laptop costs $100. Tax adds 10% (₹1 USD = ₹83). Find the final INR cost.

example.problem: f(x) = 1.1x (tax), g(x) = 83x (conversion). Cost = (g ∘ f)(100).

slides.inSimpleWords: Chaining real-world functions (tax, currency) compounds costs step by step.

slides.title: Functions: The Language of Relationships
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma concludes: 'Relations and functions are how we describe the world. Science, economics, engineering—all use functions to model how one thing depends on another. You've just learned the language of causality and dependence.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Functions describe all relationships: cause-and-effect, input-to-output, question-to-answer.

slides.title: Identity Function
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma introduces: 'There's a special function: the identity function, I(x) = x. It maps every element to itself. (I ∘ f)(x) = f(x) — composing with identity doesn't change anything.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The identity function maps x → x. Composing with it doesn't change the original function.

slides.title: Example: Verifying an Inverse
slides.storyContext: If f(x) = 3x − 2, verify that f⁻¹(x) = (x + 2)/3 by showing f(f⁻¹(x)) = x.

example.problem: Show that f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for f(x) = 3x − 2.
example.solution: f(f⁻¹(x)) = f((x + 2)/3) = 3((x + 2)/3) − 2 = (x + 2) − 2 = x. Yes, the inverse works!

slides.inSimpleWords: To verify an inverse, compute f(f⁻¹(x)) and check that it equals x.

slides.title: Transformations via Functions
slides.storyContext: Functions can model transformations. If f: students → scores, then f is assigning scores. If g: scores → grades, then g assigns grades. Together, they 'transform' students into grades.

points.label: Transformation
points.text: A function transforms inputs into outputs via a rule.

points.label: Linear transformation
points.text: f(x) = mx + b transforms x by scaling and shifting.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: In coordinates, (x, y) → (x, mx + b) shifts and stretches the plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions transform inputs: scale them, shift them, reverse them—any rule that maps one set to another.

slides.title: Functions in the Real World
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes: 'Functions are everywhere. Temperature changes over time (time → temp). Marks map to grades (marks → grade). Prices depend on demand (demand → price). Every real-world relationship can be modeled as a function.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world relationships—temperature, grades, prices, distance—are all functions.

slides.title: Challenge: Modeling with Functions
slides.storyContext: A taxi charges: ₹50 base fare + ₹15 per km. Model this as a function and find the fare for 20 km.

example.problem: Let f(x) = 50 + 15x, where x = distance in km. Find f(20).

slides.inSimpleWords: Model real costs/prices as functions to predict outcomes instantly.

slides.title: Challenge: Composite Real Scenario
slides.storyContext: A laptop costs $100. Tax adds 10% (₹1 USD = ₹83). Find the final INR cost.

example.problem: f(x) = 1.1x (tax), g(x) = 83x (conversion). Cost = (g ∘ f)(100).

slides.inSimpleWords: Chaining real-world functions (tax, currency) compounds costs step by step.

slides.title: Functions: The Language of Relationships
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Sharma concludes: 'Relations and functions are how we describe the world. Science, economics, engineering—all use functions to model how one thing depends on another. You've just learned the language of causality and dependence.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Functions describe all relationships: cause-and-effect, input-to-output, question-to-answer.

slides.title: Relations and Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: A Cartesian product A × B is all ordered pairs (a, b) with a ∈ A, b ∈ B.
A relation is any subset of a Cartesian product.
A function f: A → B is a relation where every element of A maps to exactly one element of B.
Domain = inputs; codomain = intended outputs; range = actual outputs.
Injective = different inputs → different outputs. Surjective = all codomain elements are hit.
Bijective functions have inverses; composition chains functions (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Functions map each input to exactly one output; special types (injective, surjective, bijective) impose stronger conditions.

image.alt: Relations and Functions: Key Takeaways — Relations and Functions

subject: Mathematics
title: Angles and Shadows: Trigonometry in Daily Life
hook: From measuring temple heights to tracking the sun's angle — trigonometric functions are everywhere.

image.alt: Trigonometric Functions: Angles and Ratios

slides.title: Measuring the School Temple Height
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 meters from a temple and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 45°. Priya says: 'We can find the height without climbing!' Mr. Kapoor, a surveyor, explains: 'This is trigonometry.'

slides.title: Why Trigonometry Matters
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor tells Arjun and Priya: 'Trigonometry built the pyramids. It guides ships across oceans. Architects use it to design buildings. Astronomers use it to measure stars.'

slides.title: Angle Measurement: Degrees and Radians
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor teaches: 'Angles can be measured two ways — degrees (protractor) and radians (mathematical standard).'

points.label: Degree
points.text: 1° = 1/360 of a full rotation. Straight angle = 180°.

points.label: Radian
points.text: 1 radian = angle when arc length = radius. π radians = 180°.

points.label: Conversion
points.text: Degrees = (radians) × (180/π). Radians = (degrees) × (π/180).

example.problem: Convert 90° and π/3 radians.

slides.inSimpleWords: Degrees divide a circle into 360 parts; radians use radius length as the natural unit.

slides.title: Degree vs. Radian: Key Anchors
slides.storyContext: Priya practices conversions using key anchors.

example.problem: Convert 180° and 2π radians.
example.solution: 180° = π radians. 2π radians = 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Key fact: 180° = π and 360° = 2π. Use these anchors to convert any angle.

slides.title: Right Triangles: The Foundation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor draws a right triangle. 'This 90° angle is the key. All trig ratios start here.'

points.label: Right angle
points.text: One angle = 90°. The opposite side is the hypotenuse.

points.label: Opposite side
points.text: The side across from the angle you're studying.

points.label: Adjacent side
points.text: The side next to your angle (not the hypotenuse).

points.label: Hypotenuse
points.text: The longest side, opposite the right angle.

example.problem: In a right triangle with angle θ, identify opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.
example.solution: Label the angle θ. Opposite is across from θ. Adjacent touches θ. Hypotenuse is longest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every trig ratio compares pairs of sides in a right triangle.

slides.title: Sine, Cosine, and Tangent: The Big Three
slides.storyContext: Arjun draws a right triangle. Mr. Kapoor labels the sides. 'These ratios between sides are the trig functions.'

points.label: sine θ
points.text: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.

points.label: cosine θ
points.text: cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.

points.label: tangent θ
points.text: tan θ = opposite / adjacent = sin θ / cos θ.

points.label: Reciprocals
points.text: csc θ = 1/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ.

example.problem: In a right triangle with opposite = 3, adjacent = 4, hypotenuse = 5. Find sin, cos, tan.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sine, cosine, tangent are ratios of triangle sides.

image.alt: Sine, Cosine, Tangent

slides.title: SOH-CAH-TOA: Memory Trick
slides.storyContext: Priya struggles to remember which ratio is which. Arjun teaches: 'SOH-CAH-TOA. SOH = Sine is Opposite/Hypotenuse. CAH = Cosine is Adjacent/Hypotenuse. TOA = Tangent is Opposite/Adjacent.'

slides.title: Applying SOH-CAH-TOA
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor says: 'Use this trick to solve any right triangle problem.'

example.problem: Adjacent side = 5, hypotenuse = 13. Find sin, cos, tan.

slides.inSimpleWords: SOH-CAH-TOA is your map. Pick the ratio you need, then calculate.

slides.title: Unit Circle and Trig for Any Angle
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'What if the angle is 120° or 270°? No right triangle exists.' Mr. Kapoor draws a unit circle. 'The sine and cosine are simply the coordinates of the point.'

points.label: Unit circle
points.text: Circle of radius 1. Point on circle: (cos θ, sin θ).

points.label: For any angle
points.text: cos θ = x-coordinate, sin θ = y-coordinate.

points.label: Ranges
points.text: −1 ≤ sin θ ≤ 1 and −1 ≤ cos θ ≤ 1.

points.label: Identity
points.text: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 (Pythagorean identity).

example.problem: Find sin 90°, cos 90°, sin 180°, cos 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: The unit circle extends trig functions to all angles using point coordinates.

slides.title: Quadrants and Sign Rules
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor divides the unit circle into four quadrants. 'Q1: all positive. Q2: sin positive. Q3: tan positive. Q4: cos positive. Acronym: ASTC — All Students Take Calculus.'

slides.title: Special Angles: 30°, 45°, 60°
slides.storyContext: Arjun memorizes: '0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° are special. Their trig values come up constantly.'

points.label: Memorization
points.text: Use hand trick or table — values repeat in all quadrants with sign changes.

example.solution: sin 135° = sin 45° = 1/√2 (sine is positive in Q1 and Q2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize 30°, 45°, 60° — they appear constantly in problems.

image.alt: Special Angles

slides.title: The Hand Trick for Special Angles
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor shows his hand: 'Curl fingers for 0° to 90°. Fingers represent 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° from pinky to thumb. For sin, count fingers below (√count/2). For cos, count above.'

slides.title: Periodicity and Graphs
slides.storyContext: Priya plots sin θ. 'It repeats every 360°!' Mr. Kapoor: 'That's periodicity — sin(θ + 360°) = sin θ.'

points.label: Period of sine
points.text: sin(θ + 2π) = sin θ. Period = 360° or 2π.

points.label: Period of cosine
points.text: cos(θ + 2π) = cos θ. Period = 360° or 2π.

points.label: Period of tangent
points.text: tan(θ + π) = tan θ. Period = 180° or π.

points.label: Amplitude
points.text: Max/min of sine/cosine are ±1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions repeat periodically.

image.alt: Periodicity

slides.title: Temple Height Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands 20 m from temple, angle of elevation is 45°.

example.problem: Find height. tan 45° = height / 20.
example.solution: 1 = height / 20. height = 20 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up right triangle, identify known angle and side, use correct ratio, solve.

slides.title: Angles of Elevation and Depression
slides.storyContext: Arjun is on a 30 m bridge looking down at Priya. Angle of depression (looking down) and angle of elevation (looking up) are equal.

points.label: Angle of elevation
points.text: Angle above horizontal when looking UP.

points.label: Angle of depression
points.text: Angle below horizontal when looking DOWN.

points.label: Key insight
points.text: Elevation from A = Depression from B (alternate interior angles).

example.problem: From 30 m bridge, angle of depression to boat is 60°. Distance from base?
example.solution: tan 60° = 30/distance. √3 = 30/distance. distance = 10√3 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Elevation is looking up; depression is looking down.

image.alt: Elevation and Depression

slides.title: Real Applications: Navigation and Astronomy
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor: 'Pilots calculate angle of elevation from ground to sky. Astronomers measure star positions. These angles matter in the real world every single day.'

slides.title: Trigonometric Identities
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor writes key identities: 'These hold for all angles and shortcut harder problems.'

points.label: Pythagorean identity
points.text: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.

points.label: Reciprocal identity
points.text: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

points.label: Sum/difference
points.text: sin(A+B) = sinA cosB + cosA sinB.

example.problem: Verify sin²30° + cos²30° = 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identities relate trig functions; they simplify expressions and solve equations.

slides.title: Simplifying with Identities
slides.storyContext: Priya simplifies tan θ using cos and sin.

example.problem: Simplify tan θ / sin θ.
example.solution: = (sin θ / cos θ) / sin θ = 1 / cos θ = sec θ.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rewrite in terms of sin/cos, cancel, apply identities.

slides.title: Two-Angle Building Height
slides.storyContext: From 100 m away, angle of elevation = 30°. Move 50 m closer, angle = 45°. Find height.

example.problem: tan 30° = h/100. tan 45° = h/50. Verify.
example.solution: h₁ = 100/√3 ≈ 57.7 m. h₂ = 50 m. Inconsistent — problem setup wrong. Real problems will match.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up equations from each angle, solve simultaneously.

image.alt: Building Problem

slides.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
slides.storyContext: Priya knows opposite = 7, hypotenuse = 10. Find angle θ using inverse sine.

example.problem: Find θ such that sin θ = 7/10.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inverse trig functions find the angle when you know the ratio.

slides.title: Inverse Functions in Navigation
slides.storyContext: Mr. Kapoor: 'In navigation, you know horizontal and vertical distances. You need the angle. Inverse trig functions shine here.'

slides.title: Complementary and Supplementary Angles
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: 'If θ + φ = 90°, then sin θ = cos φ.' Mr. Kapoor shows this via the unit circle.

points.label: Complementary
points.text: θ + φ = 90°. sin θ = cos φ, cos θ = sin φ.

points.label: Supplementary
points.text: θ + φ = 180°. sin θ = sin φ, cos θ = −cos φ.

example.problem: If sin 30° = 1/2, find cos 60°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Complements swap sine and cosine; supplements share sine, flip cosine.

slides.title: Using Complementary Angles
slides.storyContext: Priya uses complementary angle relationships to solve problems faster.

example.problem: Find tan 75° using tan 15°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rewrite large angles as 90° − small angle, then use complements.

slides.title: Ladder Against Wall Problem
slides.storyContext: A 10m ladder leans on a wall. The angle between ladder and ground is 60°. How high on the wall?

example.problem: If angle with ground is 60°, height = 10 sin 60°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify angle, pick correct trig ratio, solve.

slides.title: Trigonometric Functions: Key Takeaways

points.text: sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj.
180° = π radians. Convert using π/180.
Unit circle: (cos θ, sin θ); sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
Special angles: 30°, 45°, 60° with exact values.
sin/cos repeat every 360°; tan every 180°.
Elevation = up, depression = down.
Inverse trig finds angle; identities simplify expressions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Trig functions relate angles to side ratios; solve real-world height/distance problems.

image.alt: Key Takeaways

subject: Mathematics
title: Imaginary Treasures: Complex Numbers Unlock Solutions
hook: Not all quadratic equations have real solutions — complex numbers complete the picture.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Student puzzled by negative square roots

image.alt: Complex Numbers

slides.title: The Unsolvable Quadratic
slides.storyContext: Arjun tries x² + 1 = 0, getting x² = −1. He says: 'Square roots of negatives don't exist!' Dr. Patel smiles: 'What if we invent i where i² = −1?'

image.alt: Unsolvable

slides.title: History of the Imaginary Unit
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel: 'For centuries, mathematicians dismissed square roots of negatives. Then Cardano, Euler, Gauss realized: if we invent i where i² = −1, all polynomial equations have solutions.'

slides.title: The Imaginary Unit i
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel defines: 'i satisfies i² = −1. Any number a + bi is a complex number.'

points.label: Complex number
points.text: z = a + bi where a, b ∈ ℝ.

points.label: Real part
points.text: a is the real component.

points.label: Imaginary part
points.text: b is the coefficient of i.

example.problem: Identify parts of 3 + 4i.
example.solution: Real part = 3, imaginary part = 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complex number is 'real part + imaginary part' using i.

slides.title: Powers of i: A Pattern
slides.storyContext: Arjun calculates: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, i⁵ = i... 'It repeats every 4!' Priya uses this: i⁹⁹ = i³ = −i since 99 = 4(24) + 3.

slides.title: Computing Powers of i
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel teaches: 'Always reduce the exponent modulo 4.'

points.label: i¹
points.text: i.

points.label: i⁴
points.text: 1. Then repeat.

example.problem: Find i⁴³.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide exponent by 4; remainder tells you the answer.

slides.title: Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Can we add/subtract complex numbers like real numbers?' Dr. Patel: 'Yes, term by term.'

points.label: Addition
points.text: (a + bi) + (c + di) = (a+c) + (b+d)i.

points.label: Subtraction
points.text: (a + bi) − (c + di) = (a−c) + (b−d)i.

example.problem: Compute (2 + 3i) + (1 − 2i).

slides.inSimpleWords: Add real to real, imaginary to imaginary.

slides.title: Multiplication of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'How do we multiply?' Dr. Patel: 'FOIL, but remember i² = −1.'

points.label: Multiplication
points.text: (a + bi)(c + di) = ac + adi + bci + bdi² = (ac−bd) + (ad+bc)i.

example.problem: Compute (2 + 3i)(1 − 2i).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply like binomials, use i² = −1 to simplify.

image.alt: Multiplication

slides.title: Why Multiply Complex Numbers?
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'When would we multiply complex numbers?' Dr. Patel: 'In electrical engineering, alternating currents are modeled by complex numbers. Multiplying impedances requires complex multiplication.'

slides.title: Complex Conjugate
slides.storyContext: To divide, Dr. Patel multiplies by the conjugate: if z = a + bi, the conjugate z̄ = a − bi.

points.label: Conjugate
points.text: z = a + bi → z̄ = a − bi.

points.label: Property
points.text: z · z̄ = a² + b² (always real).

example.problem: Find conjugate of 3 + 4i.

slides.inSimpleWords: Flip the sign of the imaginary part.

slides.title: Division of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: To divide z₁/z₂, multiply by z̄₂/z̄₂.

points.label: Division
points.text: z₁/z₂ = (z₁ · z̄₂)/(z₂ · z̄₂).

example.problem: Compute (2+i)/(1+i).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply by conjugate of denominator to rationalize.

image.alt: Division

slides.title: Modulus and Argument
slides.storyContext: Priya visualizes complex numbers on a plane: real axis horizontal, imaginary axis vertical.

points.label: Argument
points.text: arg(z) = angle θ from positive real axis.

points.label: Polar form
points.text: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r e^(iθ).

example.problem: Modulus and argument of 3 + 4i.

slides.inSimpleWords: Modulus is distance from origin; argument is the angle.

image.alt: Modulus

slides.title: The Complex Plane
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel draws axes. 'Horizontal is real; vertical is imaginary. Every complex number is a point. Addition becomes vector addition!'

slides.title: Discriminant and Root Types
slides.storyContext: Before solving, Dr. Patel teaches: 'Calculate Δ = b² − 4ac. This tells root types.'

points.label: Δ > 0
points.text: Two distinct real roots.

points.label: Δ = 0
points.text: One repeated real root.

points.label: Δ < 0
points.text: Two complex conjugate roots.

example.problem: Find Δ for x² + 2x + 5 = 0.
example.solution: Δ = 4 − 20 = −16 < 0. Complex roots.

slides.inSimpleWords: The discriminant predicts root type before solving.

slides.title: Quadratic Formula with Complex Roots
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves x² + 2x + 5 = 0. Δ = −16 < 0, so complex solutions exist.

example.problem: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: When Δ < 0, roots are complex conjugates.

image.alt: Quadratic

slides.title: Solving 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0
slides.storyContext: Solve and verify solutions.

example.problem: Use quadratic formula.

slides.inSimpleWords: Substitute, simplify radicals, express as a + bi.

image.alt: Solving

slides.title: Vieta's Formulas
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel: 'For ax² + bx + c = 0 with roots r and s, sum = −b/a and product = c/a.'

points.label: Sum
points.text: r + s = −b/a.

points.label: Product
points.text: r × s = c/a.

points.label: Use case
points.text: Verify roots or find equations from root conditions.

example.problem: If roots sum to 3 and product to 2, find the equation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sum and product of roots relate to coefficients; useful shortcut.

slides.title: De Moivre's Theorem
slides.storyContext: Priya raises 1 + i to the 10th power. Using polar form is easier: (r e^(iθ))^n = r^n e^(iθn).

points.label: De Moivre's Theorem
points.text: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

points.label: nth roots
points.text: nth roots of z: r^(1/n) e^(i(θ+2πk)/n), k=0,1,...,n−1.

example.problem: Find (1+i)⁴.

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert to polar, apply theorem, convert back.

image.alt: De Moivre

slides.title: Complex Numbers in 3D Graphics
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: 'Video games use complex numbers to rotate objects. Multiplying by e^(iθ) rotates by angle θ. Complex multiplication = rotation + scaling!'

slides.title: Cubic: x³ − 1 = 0
slides.storyContext: One root is x = 1; the other two are complex.

example.problem: Factor and find all three roots.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor, solve each factor — some yield complex roots.

image.alt: Cubic

slides.title: Complex Cube Roots of 8
slides.storyContext: Priya: 'How many cube roots does 8 have?' Dr. Patel: 'In reals, one (2). In complex, three.'

example.problem: Find all cube roots of 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every non-zero complex number has n distinct nth roots.

slides.title: Finding Square Roots of Complex Numbers
slides.storyContext: Priya finds the square roots of 3 + 4i.

example.problem: If (a+bi)² = 3 + 4i, find a and b.
example.solution: a² − b² = 3, 2ab = 4. Solving: a = 2, b = 1. Roots: ±(2+i).

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up system of equations from real and imaginary parts.

slides.title: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel concludes: 'Every degree-n polynomial has exactly n roots in the complex numbers. Real numbers alone weren't enough. Complex numbers complete the picture.'

slides.title: Converting Between Rectangular and Polar Forms
slides.storyContext: Arjun learns: 'Rectangular form z = a + bi is convenient for addition. Polar z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) is better for multiplication and powers.'

points.label: Rectangular to polar
points.text: r = √(a²+b²), θ = arctan(b/a).

points.label: Polar to rectangular
points.text: a = r cos θ, b = r sin θ.

example.problem: Convert 1 + i to polar form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance and angle ↔ horizontal and vertical components.

slides.title: Multiplying in Polar Form
slides.storyContext: Multiplying in polar is simpler: multiply radii, add angles.

example.problem: Multiply z₁ = 2e^(iπ/4) and z₂ = 3e^(iπ/6).

slides.inSimpleWords: Polar: |z₁z₂| = r₁r₂, arg(z₁z₂) = θ₁ + θ₂.

slides.title: Complex Quadratic with Geometric Interpretation
slides.storyContext: Arjun solves z² − 2z + 2 = 0 and interprets roots on complex plane.

example.problem: Solve and find modulus and argument of each root.

slides.inSimpleWords: Roots are complex conjugates (symmetric across real axis).

slides.title: Complex Numbers: Key Takeaways

points.text: i² = −1; z = a + bi.
Add/subtract term-by-term. Multiply using FOIL + i² = −1.
Divide by multiplying by conjugate.
Modulus |z| = √(a²+b²); argument θ from real axis.
Convert rectangular ↔ polar using r, θ.
Δ < 0 → complex conjugate roots.
De Moivre: [r(cos θ + i sin θ)]^n = r^n(cos nθ + i sin nθ).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex numbers extend reals; solve all quadratics.

image.alt: Recap

subject: Mathematics
chapterAliases: Linear Inequalities in One and Two Variables
title: Dividing the Market: Linear Inequalities in Budgets and Boundaries
hook: When resources are limited, inequalities define what's possible — not just exact answers.

image.alt: Inequalities

slides.title: Budgeting for the Festival Stall
slides.storyContext: Arjun runs a fruit stall. He has ₹500 for apples (₹40) and oranges (₹30). Priya: 'How many of each?' Mr. Gupta: 'That's a range of possibilities, not one answer.'

image.alt: Stall

slides.title: Why Inequalities Matter
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'In life, you rarely have exact values. At least ₹500, not exactly. At least 10 kilos. These inequalities define real constraints.'

slides.title: Inequality Symbols
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta writes: x > 5, y ≤ 10. 'Each symbol defines a relationship.'

points.text: strictly greater than.
greater than or equal.
strictly less than.
less than or equal.

example.problem: Is x = 5 a solution to x > 3 AND x ≤ 10?
example.solution: Yes to both: 5 > 3 (true) and 5 ≤ 10 (true).

slides.inSimpleWords: An inequality shows a relationship; solve by finding all values making it true.

image.alt: Symbols

slides.title: Solving One-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants apples to cost < ₹300: 40x < 300. Priya solves: x < 7.5, so max 7 apples.

points.label: Add/Subtract
points.text: Add or subtract same from both sides; sign stays same.

points.label: Multiply/Divide positive
points.text: Multiply/divide by positive; sign stays same.

points.label: Multiply/Divide negative
points.text: Multiply/divide by negative; FLIP the sign.

example.problem: Solve −2x + 5 > 9.
example.solution: −2x > 4. Divide by −2 (flip): x < −2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Solve like equations; flip sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.

image.alt: Solving

slides.title: The Critical Rule: Negative Flip
slides.storyContext: Arjun forgets and gets it wrong. Priya reminds: 'Multiply by negative? Flip the sign. Example: 5 > 3, but −5 < −3. Negating reverses order!'

slides.title: Multi-Step Solving
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 7.'

example.problem: Solve 2x − 3 ≤ 7.
example.solution: Add 3: 2x ≤ 10. Divide by 2: x ≤ 5. Solution: (−∞, 5].

slides.inSimpleWords: Step-by-step: isolate variable, apply operations, remember flip rule.

slides.title: Compound Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun: 'I want between 5 and 10 apples' (5 ≤ x ≤ 10). Mr. Gupta: 'Two conditions at once.'

points.label: AND
points.text: Both true. 2 < x < 5.

points.label: OR
points.text: At least one true. x < 0 OR x > 10.

points.label: Interval notation
points.text: (a,b) open; [a,b] closed; [a,b) half-open.

example.problem: Write 3 < x ≤ 7 in interval notation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compound: two ranges; intervals use parentheses (open) and brackets (closed).

slides.title: Number Line Visualization
slides.storyContext: Priya draws: 'For x ∈ [5, 10], mark 5 with a closed dot (included) and 10 closed. Shade between. For 5 < x < 10, use open dots.'

slides.title: Absolute Value Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: '|x − 3| < 2 means the distance from 3 is less than 2. Rewrite as −2 < x − 3 < 2.'

points.label: |x| < a
points.text: −a < x < a.

points.label: |x| > a
points.text: x < −a OR x > a.

points.label: |x| ≤ a
points.text: −a ≤ x ≤ a.

points.label: |x| ≥ a
points.text: x ≤ −a OR x ≥ a.

example.problem: Solve |x − 3| < 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Absolute value measures distance; expand using compound inequalities.

slides.title: Two-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Arjun's budget: 40x + 30y ≤ 500. Priya graphs: 'The solution is a region, not a line.'

points.label: Boundary line
points.text: 40x + 30y = 500 is the border.

points.label: Solution region
points.text: All (x,y) where 40x + 30y ≤ 500.

points.label: Test point
points.text: Test (0,0): 0 ≤ 500? Yes, so shade that region.

points.label: Solid vs Dashed
points.text: Solid for ≤, ≥; dashed for <, >.

example.problem: Graph 2x + y > 4.
example.solution: Dashed line 2x + y = 4. Test (0,0): false, shade NOT containing (0,0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plot boundary; test point to decide which side; solid or dashed based on symbol.

image.alt: Two-Variable

slides.title: Budget Constraint Graph
slides.storyContext: Arjun has ₹500, wants ≥5 apples, ≥3 oranges. Graph feasible region, find valid point.

example.solution: Boundaries: 40x + 30y = 500, x = 5, y = 3. Valid point: (5, 8) costs ₹440 ≤ ₹500.

slides.inSimpleWords: All constraints as inequalities, plot lines, shade overlap, pick point inside.

slides.title: Systems of Two-Variable Inequalities
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta adds x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 (non-negative). Priya: 'Solution is intersection of all regions.'

points.label: System
points.text: Multiple inequalities simultaneously.

points.label: Solution region
points.text: Intersection (overlap) of all regions.

points.label: Vertices
points.text: Boundary line intersections — often optimal.

example.problem: Solve: x + y ≤ 5, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 0.
example.solution: Graph all three. Vertices: (1, 0), (1, 4), (5, 0).

slides.inSimpleWords: Graph all; solution is where all shading overlaps.

slides.title: Vertices and Optimization
slides.storyContext: Priya notes: 'Vertices matter because the best solution is always at a corner. To maximize profit, check every vertex.'

slides.title: Linear Programming: Objective Function
slides.storyContext: Arjun profits ₹10/apple, ₹8/orange. Maximize P = 10x + 8y subject to constraints.

points.label: Objective function
points.text: Maximize/minimize: P = 10x + 8y.

points.label: Constraints
points.text: Subject to: 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3.

points.label: Optimal solution
points.text: Usually at a vertex.

example.problem: Maximize P = 10x + 8y.
example.solution: Check vertices: (5,10) → P = 130, (12.5,0) → P = 125. Max at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Find vertex giving max/min value of objective.

slides.title: Real-World Linear Programming
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'Airlines maximize profit. Factories minimize cost. Hospitals optimize schedules. It's one of math's most powerful tools.'

slides.title: Finding Vertices by Solving Systems
slides.storyContext: To find vertices, solve systems of boundary equations.

example.problem: Find intersection of 40x + 30y = 500 and x = 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Boundary lines meet at vertices; solve equations to find coordinates.

slides.title: Maximize Profit
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to maximize P = 10x + 8y subject to 40x + 30y ≤ 500, x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3.

example.problem: List all feasible vertices and evaluate P at each.
example.solution: Valid vertices: (5,3)→P=74, (5,10.67)→P=135, (11.67,3)→P=140. Optimal: buy ~12 apples, 3 oranges.

slides.inSimpleWords: Evaluate objective at every vertex; best vertex is optimal.

slides.title: Minimize Cost
slides.storyContext: Priya: minimize C = 40x + 30y with x ≥ 5, y ≥ 3. Cheapest way to meet minimums?

example.problem: Minimize C = 40x + 30y.
example.solution: Feasible region unbounded. Minimum at closest corner: (5,3). C = ₹290.

slides.inSimpleWords: In minimization, optimal is the corner with smallest objective value.

slides.title: The Simplex Method
slides.storyContext: Mr. Gupta: 'With 2 variables, we graphed. Real problems have 100s. The Simplex Method finds optimal vertices automatically. It's how the world optimizes.'

slides.title: Graphing Half-Planes
slides.storyContext: Priya: 'For 2x − y ≥ 4, I draw the boundary line 2x − y = 4, then test a point to shade the correct half-plane.'

points.label: Boundary line
points.text: Equation with = sign.

points.label: Half-plane
points.text: Region on one side of boundary.

points.label: Test point (0,0)
points.text: Easy point; usually on one side of boundary.

points.label: Shade
points.text: Side containing (or not) the test point.

example.problem: Graph 2x − y ≥ 4.
example.solution: Solid line 2x − y = 4. Test (0,0): −0 ≥ 4? No. Shade opposite side.

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw boundary, test any point, shade the region making inequality true.

slides.title: Inequality Word Problem: Production Limits
slides.storyContext: A factory makes chairs and tables. Chairs need 2 hours, tables 3 hours. Total 24 hours available. Profit: ₹500/chair, ₹600/table. Maximize profit.

example.problem: Constraints: 2x + 3y ≤ 24, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Maximize P = 500x + 600y.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify variables, constraints (inequalities), objective. Graph, find vertices, evaluate.

slides.title: Feasible Region with 3+ Constraints
slides.storyContext: Graph the region where x + y ≤ 6, x ≥ 1, y ≥ 1, 2x − y ≥ 0.

example.problem: List all vertices of feasible region.
example.solution: Vertices: (1,1), (1,5), (2,4), (3,3) [approximated]. Check intersections of each pair.

slides.inSimpleWords: Draw each constraint; find region where all shade overlaps; list corner points.

slides.title: Unbounded Optimization
slides.storyContext: Minimize C = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≥ 5, 2x + y ≥ 8, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.

example.problem: Find optimal vertex.
example.solution: Feasible region unbounded (extends to ∞). Minimum occurs at vertex: (3, 2) → C = 13.

slides.inSimpleWords: Unbounded regions still have optimal vertex (at boundary intersection).

slides.title: Integer Solutions and Rounding
slides.storyContext: Priya: 'We can't buy 0.67 apples! If optimal vertex is (5.5, 3.2), check nearby integers (5,3), (6,3), (5,4), (6,4) — one is the real answer.'

slides.title: Linear Inequalities: Key Takeaways

points.text: One-variable: solve like equations; flip sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.
Compound: combine ranges (AND/OR); write in interval notation.
Absolute value: |x − a| < b means −b < x − a < b.
Two-variable: graph boundary line, shade region, use solid/dashed based on symbol.
Systems: graph all, solution is intersection.
Linear programming: maximize/minimize objective over feasible region; optimal is a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inequalities describe ranges/regions; systems combine constraints; LP optimizes objectives.

subject: Mathematics
title: Arranging Friends and Choosing Teams: Counting Principles
hook: How many ways can you arrange or select? Permutations and combinations count it all.

slides.title: Permutations and Combinations: Counting Arrangements and Selections
Planning the School Talent Show
slides.storyContext: Arjun is organizing the talent show. 'In how many orders can 3 singers perform?' Priya asks: 'Or if we're picking 2 dancers from 5, how many ways?' Prof. Sharma: 'One counts arrangements (order matters), the other counts selections (order doesn't). Both use factorials and formulas.'

slides.title: Factorial Notation
slides.storyContext: Prof. Sharma writes: 5! = 5 Ã— 4 Ã— 3 Ã— 2 Ã— 1 = 120. 'Factorial is the foundation of counting.'

points.label: Special cases
points.text: 0! = 1 (by definition). 1! = 1.

points.label: Growth
points.text: n! grows very quickly: 5! = 120, 10! = 3,628,800.

example.problem: Calculate 4! and 6!.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factorial n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n.

slides.title: Permutations: Order Matters
slides.storyContext: Arjun has 5 singers but only 3 performance slots. 'How many different orderings are there?' Prof. Sharma: 'That's a permutation: P(5, 3).'

points.label: Permutation definition
points.text: An arrangement of objects where ORDER MATTERS.

points.label: Formula
points.text: P(n, r) = n! / (nâˆ’r)! â€” number of ways to arrange r objects from n.

points.label: Meaning
points.text: P(n, r) counts ordered selections of r items from n items.

points.label: All together
points.text: P(n, n) = n! (arranging all n objects).

example.problem: How many ways can 3 singers perform in order from 5 singers?

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutation P(n, r) counts ordered arrangements; the first position has n choices, second has nâˆ’1, etc.

slides.title: Why Order Matters in Performances
slides.storyContext: Arjun realizes that (Raja sings first, then Asha, then Meera) is DIFFERENT from (Meera sings first, then Raja, then Asha). The audience experience changes! That's why permutations care about order.
slides.inSimpleWords: In permutations, the sequence/order creates different outcomes.

slides.title: Permutation Example: Podium Rankings
slides.storyContext: Three runnersâ€”Anil, Bina, and Chitraâ€”finish a 100m race. How many different podium orderings (1st, 2nd, 3rd place)?

example.problem: How many ways can 3 runners finish in 1st, 2nd, 3rd place?
example.solution: P(3, 3) = 3! = 6 orderings: (A,B,C), (A,C,B), (B,A,C), (B,C,A), (C,A,B), (C,B,A).

slides.inSimpleWords: When position/rank matters, use permutations.

slides.title: Combinations: Order Doesn't Matter
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'I need to pick 2 dancers for a duet from 5 dancers. How many ways can I choose them? The order doesn't matter â€” (Raj, Karan) is the same team as (Karan, Raj).'

points.label: Combination definition
points.text: A selection of objects where ORDER DOES NOT MATTER.

points.label: Formula
points.text: C(n, r) = n! / [r! Ã— (nâˆ’r)!] â€” number of ways to choose r objects from n.

points.label: Notation
points.text: Also written as â¿Cáµ£ or (â¿_áµ£).

points.label: Relationship
points.text: C(n, r) = P(n, r) / r! (divide out the ordering of r items).

example.problem: How many ways can we choose 2 dancers from 5?

slides.inSimpleWords: Combination C(n, r) counts unordered selections; divide permutations by r! to remove the importance of order.

slides.title: Why Order Doesn't Matter in Team Selection
slides.storyContext: Priya notices that picking dancers {Raja, Meera} is the SAME team as {Meera, Raja}. They dance together, so order is irrelevant. This is why combinations divide out the r! arrangements of the selected items.
slides.inSimpleWords: In combinations, the group/team is what counts, not the order within it.

slides.title: Combination Example: Choosing Committee Members
slides.storyContext: A school needs to pick 3 students from a class of 8 for a cleanup committee. How many different committees can be formed?

example.problem: How many ways can we choose 3 students from 8?

slides.inSimpleWords: When you just need to pick a group without caring about roles or positions, use combinations.

slides.title: Fundamental Counting Principle
slides.storyContext: Arjun designs event programs. 'There are 3 venues, 4 time slots, and 2 themes. How many programs are possible?' Prof. Sharma: 'Multiply: 3 Ã— 4 Ã— 2 = 24.'

points.label: Principle
points.text: If task 1 has m ways and task 2 has n ways, together they have m Ã— n ways.

points.label: Generalization
points.text: For k tasks with nâ‚, nâ‚‚, ..., nâ‚– ways: total = nâ‚ Ã— nâ‚‚ Ã— ... Ã— nâ‚–.

points.label: Without replacement
points.text: If one choice affects the next, update the count for each step.

example.problem: A password has 2 digits (0â€“9), then 3 letters (Aâ€“Z). How many passwords?
example.solution: First digit: 10 choices. Second digit: 10 choices. First letter: 26 choices. Second letter: 26 choices. Third letter: 26 choices. Total: 10 Ã— 10 Ã— 26 Ã— 26 Ã— 26 = 17,576,000.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply the number of ways for each step to get the total number of ways for all steps combined.

slides.title: Building Choices Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Priya plans outfits: 3 shirts, 2 pants, 4 scarves. Prof. Sharma: 'For each shirt, pick any pants (6 combos). For each combo, pick any scarf (24 total). Multiply at each step: 3 Ã— 2 Ã— 4 = 24.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Fundamental counting: when tasks are independent, multiply the number of choices.

slides.title: Full Problem: Seating Arrangement at a Dinner
slides.storyContext: A school dinner has 8 teachers and 10 students. Seats are arranged as: 1 head teacher, then 4 teachers on the left, 4 students on the right. How many seating arrangements?

example.problem: Count arrangements: pick 1 head teacher from 8, arrange 4 teachers from remaining 7, arrange 4 students from 10.
example.solution: Head teacher: 8 choices. Remaining 4 teachers from 7: P(7, 4) = 7 Ã— 6 Ã— 5 Ã— 4 = 840. 4 students from 10: P(10, 4) = 10 Ã— 9 Ã— 8 Ã— 7 = 5,040. Total: 8 Ã— 840 Ã— 5,040 = 33,868,800.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break into sub-problems; use permutation for ordered positions; multiply the counts.

slides.title: Permutations with Repetition
slides.storyContext: Arjun assigns 5 students to 3 subjects, allowing each student to take multiple subjects. 'How many assignments?' Prof. Sharma: 'Each student has 3 choices independently, so 3âµ.'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Number of arrangements of n objects chosen from k types (with repetition): kâ¿.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: Each of n positions has k independent choices.

points.label: Example
points.text: 3-letter codes from alphabet: 26 Ã— 26 Ã— 26 = 26Â³.

example.problem: How many 4-letter sequences can be formed from {A, B, C}?
example.solution: Each position has 3 choices: 3â´ = 81.

slides.inSimpleWords: With repetition allowed, each position has the full set of choices; multiply for each position.

slides.title: Why Repetition Changes the Count
slides.storyContext: Priya realizes: if we assign 2 dancers to 3 dance styles with repetition allowed, dancer 1 has 3 choices, dancer 2 has 3 choices (can be the same style). That's 3 Ã— 3 = 9 ways, not C(3,2) = 3.
slides.inSimpleWords: Allowing repetition means objects/items can be reused across selections.

slides.title: Repetition Example: Phone PIN Codes
slides.storyContext: An ATM PIN has 4 digits (0â€“9) and digits can repeat. How many PINs are possible?

example.problem: How many 4-digit PINs using digits 0â€“9 with repetition?
example.solution: Each digit position has 10 choices: 10â´ = 10,000 possible PINs.

slides.inSimpleWords: When items repeat freely, use exponential counting (base choices)^(number of positions).

slides.title: Permutations with Identical Objects
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges 5 flags: 2 red, 2 blue, 1 green. 'How many distinct arrangements?' Prof. Sharma: 'Divide by factorials of repetitions: 5! / (2! Ã— 2! Ã— 1!).'

points.label: Formula
points.text: Arrangements of n objects where nâ‚ are identical, nâ‚‚ are identical, ...: n! / (nâ‚! Ã— nâ‚‚! Ã— ...).

points.label: Intuition
points.text: Start with n!, then divide out overcounting due to swaps of identical items.

example.problem: Arrange the letters in BOOK.
example.solution: 4 letters, but O appears twice. Arrangements = 4! / 2! = 24 / 2 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count total permutations, then divide by factorials of the multiplicities of identical objects.

slides.title: Dividing Out Identical Items
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges 3 balls: 1 red, 2 blue. If the blues were distinct (Bâ‚, Bâ‚‚), there'd be 3! = 6 orderings. But since both blues are identical, (Red, Blueâ‚, Blueâ‚‚) and (Red, Blueâ‚‚, Blueâ‚) look the same. So divide 3! by 2! = 3 distinct arrangements.
slides.inSimpleWords: Identical objects reduce the count because swapping them doesn't create new arrangements.

slides.title: Identical Objects Example: Necklace Beads
slides.storyContext: Arrange 7 beads on a necklace: 3 red, 2 green, 2 yellow. How many distinct necklaces?

example.problem: How many ways to arrange 7 beads with 3 identical red, 2 identical green, 2 identical yellow?

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide by the factorial of each group's count to eliminate redundant orderings.

slides.title: Permutation vs Combination Quick Decision Tree
slides.storyContext: Prof. Sharma teaches: Ask yourself these questions: (1) Does order/position/rank matter? (2) Are we arranging or selecting?

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Is order/sequence important in the problem?

points.label: If YES
points.text: Use permutation P(n,r). Examples: arrange books, order of runners, seating positions.

points.label: If NO
points.text: Use combination C(n,r). Examples: select committee, choose items, form teams.

example.problem: Are these permutation or combination? (a) Arranging 4 friends in a photo. (b) Picking 3 fruits from 7.
example.solution: (a) Permutation-order matters (positions). (b) Combination-we just pick, order doesn't matter.

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutation = order matters; Combination = order doesn't matter.

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Counting Problem
slides.storyContext: A school committee has 8 people. They must elect a president (1 person), then choose a 3-person subcommittee from the remaining 7. How many ways?

example.problem: Find the number of ways to elect president and then select a subcommittee.
example.solution: President: 8 choices. Subcommittee from remaining 7: C(7, 3) = 7! / (3! Ã— 4!) = 35. Total: 8 Ã— 35 = 280.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use multiplication for sequential tasks; use P or C based on whether order matters within each task.

slides.title: Challenge: Permutation vs. Combination
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'If I arrange 5 books on a shelf, is that P or C? What if I just pick 3 books for a gift box without caring about order?'

example.problem: Arrange 5 books on a shelf vs. choose 3 books from 8 for a box.
example.solution: Shelf (order matters): P(5,5) = 5! = 120. Gift box (order doesn't matter): C(8,3) = 56. Memorize: permutation = position-specific; combination = group-only.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ask: does the order/position/arrangement matter? YES â†’ permutation; NO â†’ combination.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Multi-Step Problem
slides.storyContext: A movie theater has 5 rows with 8 seats each. A group wants: row 1 seat for lead actor, row 2 seats for supporting actors (2 people, order matters), row 3 a group of 3 friends (order doesn't matter). Count all arrangements.

example.problem: Lead: C(8,1)=8. Supporting: P(8,2)=56. Friends: C(8,3)=56. Total: 8 Ã— 56 Ã— 56.
example.solution: 8 Ã— 56 Ã— 56 = 25,088 seating arrangements.

slides.inSimpleWords: Decompose complex problems into independent sub-tasks and multiply.

slides.title: Arranging Objects with Some Restrictions
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges performers: 'Of 5 singers, which 3 must perform together (in any order) and 2 must NOT perform adjacent?' Prof. Sharma: 'Break into cases: first pick the 3 (C(5,3)), then apply restriction rules.'

points.label: Restriction strategy
points.text: Identify constraints. Use complementary counting: total arrangements minus restricted ones.

points.label: Common patterns
points.text: Certain objects must be adjacent (treat as one block). Certain objects must NOT be adjacent (subtract their count).

example.problem: Arrange 4 books where 2 specific books must be adjacent.
example.solution: Treat the 2 books as one block. Now arrange 3 units: 3! = 6. But within the block, 2 books can swap: 2! = 2. Total: 6 Ã— 2 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: For restricted arrangements, use blocks or complementary counting.

slides.title: Grouping and Constraints in Real Problems
slides.storyContext: Priya selects a dance team: 'The lead pair must dance together always. The remaining 3 dancers can go anywhere.' Arjun realizes: 'That's C(4,1) for selecting the position of the pair-block, then P(3,3) for the others.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When some objects must stay together, treat them as a single unit and adjust your formula.

slides.title: Restrictions Example: Seating with Conditions
slides.storyContext: Seat 5 people at a round table where person A and person B must sit next to each other.

example.problem: Fix A and B as one unit. Arrange A-B block + 3 others in a circle: (4-1)! = 3! = 6 rotations. Within block: 2! = 2. Total: 6 Ã— 2 = 12.
example.solution: 12 valid seating arrangements where A and B are adjacent.

slides.inSimpleWords: For circular arrangements with restrictions, fix the position and use the block method.

slides.title: Circular Permutations
slides.storyContext: Arjun arranges people in a circle: 'On a line, 4 people have 4! = 24 orderings. In a circle, we ignore rotationsâ€”(A,B,C,D) rotating is the same. So it's (4-1)! = 3! = 6.'

points.label: Circular permutation
points.text: For n objects in a circle: (n-1)! arrangements (fix one position, arrange the rest).

points.label: Necklace/bracelet (reflections also identical)
points.text: If reflections count as same: (n-1)! / 2.

example.problem: Arrange 5 people at a circular table.
example.solution: (5-1)! = 4! = 24 circular arrangements.

slides.inSimpleWords: In circular arrangements, fix one object and permute the restâ€”rotations don't count as different.

slides.title: From Linear to Circular Counting
slides.storyContext: Arjun notices: 'On a line, (A,B,C,D), (B,C,D,A), (C,D,A,B), and (D,A,B,C) look different. But in a circle, they're all the same rotation! So divide by 4.' Prof. Sharma: 'Exactly. That's why circular is (n-1)!/1 instead of n!/n.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Circular arrangements divide out rotational equivalence by fixing one object's position.

slides.title: Permutations and Combinations: Key Takeaways

points.text: Factorial n! = n Ã— (nâˆ’1) Ã— ... Ã— 2 Ã— 1; 0! = 1.
Permutation P(n, r) = n! / (nâˆ’r)! â€” arrangements where ORDER MATTERS.
Combination C(n, r) = n! / [r! Ã— (nâˆ’r)!] â€” selections where ORDER DOES NOT MATTER.
Fundamental counting principle: multiply the choices for each step.
With repetition: k^n arrangements of n items from k types.
With identical objects: divide by factorials of multiplicities.
Circular permutations: (n-1)! arrangements to account for rotational equivalence.
For restrictions, use block grouping or complementary counting.

slides.inSimpleWords: Permutations count ordered arrangements; combinations count unordered selections; use the counting principle for multi-step problems. Adapt formulas for repetition, identical objects, circles, and restrictions.

slides.title: The Binomial Theorem: Statement and Formula
slides.storyContext: Dr. Verma writes the theorem: (a + b)â¿ = Î£ â¿Cáµ£ aâ¿â»Ê³ bÊ³, r = 0 to n.

points.label: Binomial theorem

slides.title: What is a Sequence?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A sequence is a set of numbers arranged in a definite order, following a rule. Denoted aâ‚, aâ‚‚, aâ‚ƒ, ..., aâ‚™.

points.label: Arithmetic Sequence (AP)
points.text: Each term differs from the previous by a constant d (common difference). Example: 5, 10, 15, 20, ... has d = 5.

points.label: General Term (AP)
points.text: aâ‚™ = aâ‚ + (n-1)d, where aâ‚ is the first term and d is the common difference.

example.solution: This is an AP: aâ‚ = 12, d = 2. Using aâ‚™ = aâ‚ + (n-1)d, aâ‚â‚€ = 12 + (10-1)Ã—2 = 12 + 18 = 30 chairs.

slides.inSimpleWords: In arithmetic sequences, you add the same number every time.

slides.title: Geometric Sequencesâ€”The Doubling Rule

points.text: Each term is multiplied by a constant r (common ratio). Example: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 has r = 2.

points.label: General Term (GP)
points.text: aâ‚™ = aâ‚ Ã— r^(n-1), where aâ‚ is the first term and r is the common ratio.

points.label: Priya's Savings

points.label: Sum Formula (AP)

slides.title: Arithmetic Mean and Harmonic Mean
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If I have 3 and 9, what's in the middle?' Grandfather: 'The arithmetic mean is (3+9)/2 = 6. But there's also the harmonic mean, used for rates.'

points.label: Arithmetic Mean (AM)
points.text: For two numbers a and b: AM = (a+b)/2. For n numbers: AM = (sum of all)/n.

points.label: Geometric Mean (GM)
points.text: For two numbers a and b: GM = âˆš(ab). Always: AM â‰¥ GM (with equality iff a=b).

points.label: Harmonic Mean (HM)
points.text: For two numbers a and b: HM = 2ab/(a+b). Used for average rates.

example.problem: If a car goes 60 km/h for the first 100 km and 40 km/h for the next 100 km, what is the average speed?
example.solution: Average speed â‰  (60+40)/2 = 50 km/h. Use harmonic mean: HM = 2Ã—60Ã—40/(60+40) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h.

slides.inSimpleWords: AM averages quantities; GM is the geometric average; HM averages rates.

slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'I ran at 10 m/s for the first 50 meters, then 5 m/s for the next 50 meters. My average speed isn't (10+5)/2.' Grandfather: 'Exactly! Use harmonic mean for speeds/rates: 2Ã—10Ã—5/(10+5) = 100/15 â‰ˆ 6.67 m/s.'

example.problem: Let the three numbers be (a-d), a, (a+d). Sum: (a-d)+a+(a+d)=27, so 3a=27, a=9. Product: (a-d)Ã—aÃ—(a+d)=a(aÂ²-dÂ²)=9(81-dÂ²)=504.
example.solution: 81-dÂ²=56, so dÂ²=25, d=5. The three numbers are 4, 9, 14.

slides.title: Harmonic Sequences and Their Sums
slides.storyContext: Grandfather introduces: 'If 1/aâ‚, 1/aâ‚‚, 1/aâ‚ƒ form an AP, then aâ‚, aâ‚‚, aâ‚ƒ form a harmonic sequence.' Priya: 'Wait, so if the reciprocals are in AP, the originals are harmonic?'

points.label: Harmonic Sequence
points.text: A sequence whose reciprocals form an AP. Example: 1, 1/2, 1/3 (reciprocals 1, 2, 3 are in AP).

points.label: Properties
points.text: Harmonic sequences don't have a simple closed-form sum formula like AP and GP.

points.label: Partial sums
points.text: Must compute term-by-term. Example: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n is the nth harmonic number Hâ‚™, which diverges as nâ†’âˆž.

example.solution: Reciprocals: 1/2, 1/3, 1/6. Common difference: 1/3 - 1/2 = -1/6; 1/6 - 1/3 = -1/6. Yes, they form an AP, so 2, 3, 6 is harmonic.

slides.inSimpleWords: Harmonic sequences are defined by reciprocals in AP; they lack simple sum formulas.

slides.inSimpleWords: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... diverges despite terms approaching zeroâ€”a famous counterexample.

slides.title: Three Classical Means and Their Uses

points.label: Arithmetic Mean (AM)
points.text: AM = (a+b)/2, used for averaging quantities (heights, weights, scores).

points.label: Geometric Mean (GM)
points.text: GM = √(ab), used for ratios, growth rates, proportional changes.

points.label: Harmonic Mean (HM)
points.text: HM = 2ab/(a+b), used for averaging rates, speeds, or reciprocal quantities.

example.problem: Car travels 100 km at 60 km/h, then 100 km at 40 km/h. Average speed?
example.solution: NOT arithmetic mean 50 km/h. Use HM: 2×60×40/(60+40) = 4800/100 = 48 km/h, because speed = distance/time and time depends on distance inversely.

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose the right mean: AM for quantities, GM for proportions, HM for rates.

slides.title: Why Harmonic Mean for Speeds
slides.inSimpleWords: Rates (distance/time) average differently than quantities because of reciprocal relationships.

slides.title: Using Means in Algebraic Sequences

example.problem: Find three numbers in AP where sum = 27 and product = 504.
example.solution: Let the numbers be (a-d), a, (a+d). Sum: 3a = 27 → a = 9. Product: 9(81-d²) = 504 → 81-d² = 56 → d² = 25 → d = 5. Numbers: 4, 9, 14. Check: 4+9+14=27 ✓, 4×9×14=504 ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean arithmetic simplifies solving systems involving sequences.

slides.title: Harmonic Sequences

points.label: Definition
points.text: A sequence is harmonic if its reciprocals form an arithmetic progression. Example: 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... (reciprocals 1, 2, 3 are AP with d=1).

example.problem: Verify that 2, 3, 6 form a harmonic sequence.
example.solution: Reciprocals: 1/2, 1/3, 1/6. Differences: 1/3 - 1/2 = -1/6, 1/6 - 1/3 = -1/6. Common difference = -1/6, so reciprocals are AP. Therefore 2, 3, 6 is harmonic. ✓

slides.inSimpleWords: Harmonic sequences lack simple closed-form sum formulas, unlike AP and GP.

slides.title: The Divergent Harmonic Series
slides.inSimpleWords: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... diverges to infinity despite terms shrinking toward zero—a famous paradox.

slides.title: Harmonic Numbers and Growth Rates

example.problem: Compute H_6 (6th harmonic number) = 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + 1/5 + 1/6.
example.solution: 1 + 0.5 + 0.333... + 0.25 + 0.2 + 0.167... ≈ 2.45. Harmonic numbers grow like ln(n), very slowly.

slides.inSimpleWords: Partial sums of harmonic series (harmonic numbers) grow logarithmically, not linearly.

slides.title: Sequences & Series Summary

points.text: Sequence: ordered list of numbers following a rule (aâ‚, aâ‚‚, aâ‚ƒ, ...).
Arithmetic Sequence: constant difference d; aâ‚™ = aâ‚ + (n-1)d; Sâ‚™ = n/2 Ã— (aâ‚ + aâ‚™).
Geometric Sequence: constant ratio r; aâ‚™ = aâ‚ Ã— r^(n-1); Sâ‚™ = aâ‚(r^n-1)/(r-1).
Infinite GP with |r|<1 converges: S = aâ‚/(1-r).
Use AP for linear growth (stairs, rows, daily increases). Use GP for exponential growth (doubling, viral spread).
Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic means serve different purposesâ€”use AM for quantities, GM for ratios, HM for rates.
Harmonic sequences have reciprocals in AP; their sums lack simple formulas.
Master all to solve real problems: harvests, savings, cricket scores, crowd sizes, average speeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sequences organize data; series sum them up. Both are tools for predicting and planning. Choose formulas based on the patternâ€”linear or exponential, and whether order or totals matter.

image.alt: Sequences & Series Summary â€” Sequences and Series

subject: Mathematics
title: The Village Path Blueprint
hook: A surveyor maps village paths—learn the math behind straight lines and angles.

characters.name: Meena
characters.role: Local farmer interested in land division

slides.title: Straight Lines: Mapping the Village Path
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must map new paths between the village well (at 2,3) and the temple (at 8,9) on a coordinate grid. Arjun asks: how do we describe this path mathematically?
slides.inSimpleWords: A straight line on a coordinate plane can be described with equations and slopes.

slides.title: The Well and the Temple
slides.storyContext: Arjun holds the surveyor's chain as Surveyor Sharma plots coordinates. 'The well is at grid (2,3). The temple is at (8,9),' Sharma explains. 'To find the path, we need to know the direction—how steep is the climb? And where does the path cross the well's baseline?' Arjun sketches on paper. 'Is there a formula?' Sharma nods. 'Yes—we call it the slope-intercept form.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Every straight line has a slope (steepness) and a y-intercept (where it crosses the y-axis).

slides.title: Slope of a Line

points.label: Definition
points.text: Slope m = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). It measures how steep a line is.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: m > 0: line rises (northeast). m < 0: line falls (southeast). m = 0: horizontal. m undefined: vertical.

points.label: Well to Temple
points.text: Points (2,3) and (8,9). Slope m = (9-3)/(8-2) = 6/6 = 1. The path rises at a 45° angle.

example.problem: A farmer walks from point (1,2) to point (4,8). What is the slope of the path?
example.solution: m = (8-2)/(4-1) = 6/3 = 2. The path rises 2 units for every 1 unit walked horizontally.

slides.inSimpleWords: Slope tells you how fast a line rises or falls—steeper slope means a sharper climb.

slides.title: Slope in Four Directions
slides.storyContext: Meena asks, 'Can slopes be negative?' Surveyor Sharma nods. 'Absolutely. A path going uphill to the northeast has positive slope. But if it goes downhill to the southeast, slope is negative. Horizontal paths have zero slope. Vertical cliffs have undefined slope.' Meena draws four paths: one rising, one falling, one flat, one vertical.
slides.inSimpleWords: Slopes can be positive (uphill), negative (downhill), zero (flat), or undefined (vertical).

slides.title: Worked Example: Slope Through Practice
slides.storyContext: Meena's farmland runs from point A(0,1) to point B(5,11). What slope describes the farm's boundary line?

points.label: Apply Slope Formula
points.text: m = (11-1)/(5-0) = 10/5 = 2. For every 1 meter east, the boundary rises 2 meters north.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: A slope of 2 means a fairly steep climb. This boundary line tilts significantly upward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice calculating slopes with real farm coordinates—always subtract in the same order.

slides.title: Equation of a Line: Slope-Intercept Form

points.label: Form
points.text: y = mx + c, where m is slope and c is the y-intercept (where line crosses y-axis).

points.label: Finding c
points.text: Using the well-temple line: slope m = 1, point (2,3). Substitute: 3 = 1(2) + c → c = 1.

points.label: Final Equation
points.text: The path line is y = x + 1. Any point (x,y) on this path satisfies this equation.

example.problem: A road passes through (3,5) with slope 2. Find its equation.
example.solution: y = mx + c. Using (3,5): 5 = 2(3) + c → c = -1. Equation: y = 2x - 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: The equation y = mx + c is the universal formula for any straight line.

slides.title: Building the Line Step by Step
slides.storyContext: Arjun sketches while Surveyor Sharma explains: 'First, calculate slope from two points. Then substitute one point into y = mx + c to find c. Finally, write the complete equation. This equation lets us find any point on the line, predict where the line goes, or draw it on any scale.' Meena draws three different lines and writes their equations.
slides.inSimpleWords: The process is always the same: slope first, then intercept, then equation.

slides.title: Worked Example: Building the Line Equation
slides.storyContext: Arjun records that Surveyor Sharma's mapping line passes through (1,4) with slope 3. What's the equation of this survey line?

points.label: Use Point-Slope
points.text: Given: point (1,4), slope m = 3. Formula y = mx + c becomes 4 = 3(1) + c.

points.label: Solve for c
points.text: 4 = 3 + c → c = 1. The y-intercept is 1.

points.label: Final Equation
points.text: y = 3x + 1. Any coordinate on this survey line satisfies this equation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Once you know slope and one point, you can write the complete line equation.

slides.title: Two-Point Form and General Form

points.label: Two-Point Form
points.text: (y - y₁)/(x - x₁) = (y₂ - y₁)/(x₂ - x₁). Use this when you have two points.

points.label: General Form
points.text: Ax + By + C = 0. Example: x - y + 1 = 0 is the well-temple line rearranged.

points.label: Intercept Form
points.text: x/a + y/b = 1, where a is x-intercept and b is y-intercept. Useful for axes crossings.

example.problem: Write the equation of the line through (0,4) and (2,0).
example.solution: Intercept form: x/2 + y/4 = 1, or 2x + y = 4. General form: 2x + y - 4 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different forms of line equations serve different situations—pick the form that fits your data.

slides.title: Worked Example: General Form from Two Points
slides.storyContext: Meena needs to write the boundary line through villages at (1,3) and (4,9) in general form Ax + By + C = 0.

points.label: Convert to General Form
points.text: y = 2x + 1 → 2x - y + 1 = 0. This is the general form Ax + By + C = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start with slope-intercept, then rearrange to general form when needed for calculations.

slides.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

points.label: Parallel Lines
points.text: Two lines are parallel if they have the same slope: m₁ = m₂. They never meet.

points.label: Perpendicular Lines
points.text: Two lines are perpendicular if m₁ × m₂ = -1. Example: if m₁ = 2, then m₂ = -1/2.

points.label: Village Application
points.text: The path y = x + 1 is perpendicular to y = -x + 5 (slopes: 1 and -1, product = -1).

example.problem: Find a line parallel to y = 3x + 2 passing through (1,5).
example.solution: Parallel means same slope m = 3. Using y = 3x + c: 5 = 3(1) + c → c = 2. Answer: y = 3x + 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel lines have same slope; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1.

slides.title: Water Channel Design
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma explains to Meena: 'When we build water channels perpendicular to main paths, we use this slope rule. If the main path has slope 2, the channel must have slope -1/2. This ensures they meet at 90 degrees.' Meena nods, understanding how mathematics ensures proper water flow through the fields.
slides.inSimpleWords: Perpendicular structures like water channels need slopes that are negative reciprocals.

slides.title: Worked Example: Perpendicular Lines in Practice
slides.storyContext: A water channel must be perpendicular to the main path y = 2x + 1 and pass through the well at (2,3). Find the channel's equation.

points.label: Find Perpendicular Slope
points.text: Main path slope m₁ = 2. Perpendicular slope m₂ satisfies 2 × m₂ = -1 → m₂ = -1/2.

points.label: Use Point and Slope
points.text: Channel passes through (2,3) with m = -1/2. So 3 = (-1/2)(2) + c → 3 = -1 + c → c = 4.

points.label: Channel Equation
points.text: y = -x/2 + 4 or x + 2y - 8 = 0. Water flows at 90° to the main path.

slides.inSimpleWords: To build perpendicular structures, multiply slopes by -1 and divide: one gives you the other.

slides.title: Distance from a Point to a Line

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance from point (x₀,y₀) to line Ax + By + C = 0 is d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).

points.label: Use Case
points.text: How far is Meena's farm at (5,7) from the path-line x - y + 1 = 0?

example.problem: Find the distance from (2,3) to the line 3x + 4y - 5 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distance formula helps measure shortest separation between a point and a line.

slides.title: Worked Example: Measuring Distance to Survey Line
slides.storyContext: Arjun checks how far the well at (1,2) is from the surveyor's main line 2x - 3y + 4 = 0.

points.label: Identify Values
points.text: Point: (x₀,y₀) = (1,2). Line: A=2, B=-3, C=4.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The well lies exactly ON the survey line (distance = 0), so it's perfectly aligned with the surveyor's path.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if a point is on a line: if distance = 0, the point is exactly on the line.

slides.title: Intersection Points and Angle Between Lines
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma points to where two paths cross in the village. 'Two lines intersect at exactly one point—unless they're parallel,' he explains. 'And we can measure the angle between them using their slopes.' Meena sketches: 'So slopes tell us not just direction, but also the angle of intersection?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Where two lines cross is their intersection point; the angle between them depends on their slopes.

slides.title: Full Problem: Mapping Two Farm Boundaries
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma must find where two farm boundaries meet. Farm A's edge: y = 2x + 3. Farm B's edge: y = -x + 9. Where do they intersect?

points.label: Set Equal
points.text: At intersection, y values are equal: 2x + 3 = -x + 9.

points.label: Find y
points.text: y = 2(2) + 3 = 7. Intersection at (2,7).

slides.inSimpleWords: To find where two lines meet, solve their equations simultaneously.

slides.title: Angle Between Two Lines

points.label: Formula
points.text: tan(θ) = |(m₁ - m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, where m₁ and m₂ are the slopes.

points.label: Special Cases
points.text: If 1 + m₁m₂ = 0, then m₁m₂ = -1 (perpendicular, θ = 90°). If m₁ = m₂, then θ = 0° (parallel).

example.problem: Find the angle between y = x + 2 and y = 2x + 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: The angle between two lines is determined entirely by their slopes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Angle Between Farm Boundaries
slides.storyContext: At the intersection point (2,7), what angle do the two farm boundaries make? (A: y = 2x+3, B: y = -x+9)

points.label: Identify Slopes
points.text: Farm A: m₁ = 2. Farm B: m₂ = -1.

points.label: Find Angle
points.text: θ = arctan(3) ≈ 71.57°. The boundaries meet at approximately 71.6 degrees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Verify perpendicularity: if the product of slopes is -1, the angle is always 90°.

slides.title: A Complete Land Survey
slides.storyContext: Surveyor Sharma gathers Arjun and Meena for a final lesson. 'We've learned slopes, equations, parallel and perpendicular lines, distances, intersections, and angles. Together, these let us survey any piece of land, design any path, and solve any positioning problem.'
