They review a complex village map with multiple property boundaries, paths, and water channels—all described by straight line equations.
slides.inSimpleWords: All the tools of straight line mathematics work together to solve real surveying problems.

slides.title: Why Lines Matter
slides.storyContext: Arjun reflects: 'Lines seem simple, but they're everywhere. Roads, rivers, property borders, building edges—they're all straight lines or parts of straight lines. Understanding line equations lets us design cities, predict paths, and make precise measurements.' Meena adds, 'And once you master lines, circles and curves become easier to understand too.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Straight lines are the building blocks of coordinate geometry—master them and unlock 2D mathematics.

slides.title: Challenge: Parallel Farm Paths
slides.storyContext: Meena wants a new boundary line parallel to y = (1/2)x + 3 passing through her barn at (6,2). Write the equation and convert it to general form.

example.problem: Find a line parallel to y = (1/2)x + 3 through (6,2), then write in general form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice finding parallel lines—they have identical slopes but different y-intercepts.

slides.title: Challenge: Distance to Boundary
slides.storyContext: Calculate how far Meena's house at (3,4) is from the boundary line 3x + 4y - 12 = 0.

example.problem: Find distance from (3,4) to line 3x + 4y - 12 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always use absolute value in the numerator to get a positive distance.

slides.title: Challenge: Finding Intersection Points
slides.storyContext: Two village paths are y = 3x - 2 and y = -2x + 8. Find their intersection and the angle between them.

example.problem: Find intersection and angle for y = 3x - 2 and y = -2x + 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine intersection and angle concepts: solve for x-y, then use slope formula for angle.

slides.title: Challenge: Intercept Form Application
slides.storyContext: A village boundary line crosses the x-axis at (4,0) and the y-axis at (0,6). Write its equation in intercept form and convert to general form.

example.problem: Line through (4,0) and (0,6)—write in intercept and general form.
example.solution: Intercept form: x/4 + y/6 = 1. General form: 3x + 2y - 12 = 0. (Multiply by 6 to clear fractions.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Intercept form is fastest when you know where a line crosses the axes.

slides.title: Straight Lines Summary

points.text: Slope m = Δy/Δx. It measures line steepness and direction.
Equations: y = mx + c (slope-intercept), Ax + By + C = 0 (general), x/a + y/b = 1 (intercept).
Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes with product -1.
Distance from point to line: d = |Ax₀ + By₀ + C|/√(A² + B²).
Angle between lines: tan(θ) = |(m₁ - m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| at their intersection.
Applications: surveying lands, designing roads, planning buildings, farm boundaries, navigation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Straight line equations are the foundation of coordinate geometry—used in architecture, surveying, and engineering.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Mirror and the Curve
hook: A satellite dish, a bridge arch, and a planet's orbit—all follow conic section curves.

slides.title: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas
slides.storyContext: When light rays are cut by a cone at different angles, they create curves used everywhere: satellite dishes, bridge arches, planets' orbits, and water fountains.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are curves made by slicing a cone—each has unique properties and equations.

image.alt: Conic Sections: Circles, Ellipses, Parabolas, Hyperbolas — Conic Sections

slides.title: The Fountain Challenge
slides.storyContext: Govind is designing a water fountain for the village square. The water jets must follow a perfect arch—not too steep, not too flat. Ravi says, 'That's a parabola!' Govind nods: 'Yes, and I need its equation to calculate flow rates.' Diya adds, 'Parabolas appear in satellites too—they focus signals to a receiver.' All three realize conics are everywhere.
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections model real-world curves from engineering to astronomy.

slides.title: What are Conic Sections?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Conic sections are curves formed when a plane intersects a cone at different angles.

points.label: Four Types
points.text: Circle (horizontal slice), Ellipse (angled slice), Parabola (parallel to edge), Hyperbola (steep angled slice through both nappes).

points.label: Eccentricity
points.text: A parameter e determines the type: circle (e=0), ellipse (0<e<1), parabola (e=1), hyperbola (e>1).

example.problem: Name the conic section with eccentricity 0.7.
example.solution: Since 0 < 0.7 < 1, this is an ellipse. Ellipses have eccentricity between 0 and 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: All conic sections come from slicing a cone—the angle of slice determines the curve shape.

slides.title: Circle: The Perfect Curve

points.label: Definition
points.text: A circle is the set of all points equidistant from a center. Distance = radius r.

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r², where (h,k) is center and r is radius.

points.label: General Equation
points.text: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0. Center = (-g, -f), radius = √(g² + f² - c).

example.problem: A circular well has center at (2,3) and radius 5. Write its equation.
example.solution: (x - 2)² + (y - 3)² = 25. Expanding: x² + y² - 4x - 6y - 12 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: A circle is defined by one center point and a radius—the simplest conic section.

slides.title: Orbits and Water Wheels
slides.storyContext: Diya sketches a circular orbit for a satellite. 'Every point on this circle is the same distance from Earth's center,' she explains. Govind points to his fountain design. 'My water wheel is circular—it rotates around a fixed center. Both need the circle equation.' Ravi adds, 'Circular motion appears everywhere—atoms, planets, machines.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Circles model wheels, orbits, and any system rotating around a fixed center.

slides.title: Worked Example: Circle from General Form
slides.storyContext: Ravi records a circular orbit described by x² + y² - 6x - 8y = 0. Find the center and radius.

points.label: Group Terms
points.text: (x² - 6x) + (y² - 8y) = 0. Complete the square for each variable.

points.label: Extract Info
points.text: Center (3,4), radius = 5 units. This circular orbit has its center 3 units east and 4 units north.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find center and radius from general form, complete the square and compare to standard form.

slides.title: Parabola: The Arch of Motion

points.label: Definition
points.text: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a focus F and a directrix line.

points.label: Standard Equation (Vertex at origin)
points.text: y² = 4ax (opens right) or x² = 4ay (opens up). Here a is distance from vertex to focus.

points.label: Fountain Example
points.text: Water jet equation x² = 4(1.25)y = 5y. Focus at (0, 1.25), directrix at y = -1.25.

example.problem: A water fountain parabola is x² = 8y. Find focus and directrix.
example.solution: 4a = 8 → a = 2. Focus at (0, 2). Directrix: y = -2. Water rises symmetrically from the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolas are perfect arches used in water fountains, bridge cables, and satellite dishes.

slides.title: Focus and Reflection Properties
slides.storyContext: Diya holds up a parabolic mirror. 'Light rays parallel to the axis reflect to the focus. This is why satellite dishes work—they collect weak signals and concentrate them at the receiver.' Govind nods. 'My fountain works the same way, but in reverse. The water shoots from the focus and spreads along the parabola.' Ravi sketches the reflection paths.
slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolas have a special focus point where parallel rays or signals concentrate.

slides.title: Worked Example: Finding Focus of Parabola
slides.storyContext: Govind's fountain design follows y² = 12x. Where is the receiver at the focus?

points.label: Identify Form
points.text: This is y² = 4ax form, opening rightward (horizontal).

points.label: Locate Focus
points.text: Focus at (a, 0) = (3, 0). Directrix is the line x = -3. The receiver is 3 units to the right of the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: For parabola y² = 4ax, the focus is always at distance a from the vertex along the axis.

slides.title: Ellipse: The Stretched Circle

points.label: Definition
points.text: An ellipse is the set of points where sum of distances to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a ≥ b). Semi-major axis = a, semi-minor axis = b.

points.label: Foci and Eccentricity
points.text: Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² - b². Eccentricity e = c/a (0 < e < 1).

example.problem: A planet's orbit is x²/100 + y²/64 = 1 (in million km). Find semi-major axis, semi-minor axis, and foci.
example.solution: a = 10, b = 8. c² = 100 - 64 = 36 → c = 6. Foci at (±6, 0). Semi-major = 10, semi-minor = 8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ellipses describe planetary orbits and stretched circular paths—essential to astronomy.

slides.title: Planetary Orbits and Whispering Galleries
slides.storyContext: Diya explains Kepler's First Law: 'Planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus.' She draws an ellipse with the Sun marked. Ravi asks, 'What's special about the two foci?' Govind replies, 'In a whispering gallery—an elliptical room—sound from one focus echoes perfectly to the other focus!' All three see the power of ellipse geometry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Ellipses have two foci; the sum of distances from any point to both foci is constant.

slides.title: Worked Example: Ellipse Eccentricity
slides.storyContext: Diya studies an asteroid orbit: x²/49 + y²/24 = 1. How stretched is this ellipse?

points.label: Identify Parameters
points.text: a² = 49 → a = 7 (semi-major). b² = 24 → b ≈ 4.9 (semi-minor).

points.label: Find Eccentricity
points.text: e = c/a = 5/7 ≈ 0.714. This ellipse is fairly stretched (close to 1 means very elongated).

slides.inSimpleWords: Eccentricity measures how much an ellipse stretches: e=0 is a circle, e close to 1 is very elongated.

slides.title: Hyperbola: The Twin Curves

points.label: Definition
points.text: A hyperbola is the set of points where |difference of distances| to two foci = constant (2a).

points.label: Standard Equation
points.text: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1 (opens left-right). Foci at (±c, 0) where c² = a² + b².

points.label: Asymptotes
points.text: Lines y = ±(b/a)x. Hyperbola approaches these lines but never crosses.

example.problem: Write the equation of a hyperbola with foci at (±5, 0) and difference of distances = 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hyperbolas are two mirrored curves that approach asymptotes—used in radar and navigation.

slides.title: GPS and Hyperbolic Navigation
slides.storyContext: Ravi explains to Diya: 'GPS works using hyperbolas! When a signal arrives from satellite A before satellite B, the difference in signal times defines a hyperbola. The receiver is somewhere on that hyperbola. Signals from multiple satellites create multiple hyperbolas—their intersection is your exact location.' Diya sketches overlapping hyperbolas with their solution point.
slides.inSimpleWords: Hyperbolas help locate objects using signal time differences—the basis of modern navigation.

slides.title: Worked Example: Hyperbola Asymptotes
slides.storyContext: A navigation system uses the hyperbola x²/25 - y²/16 = 1. What are its asymptotes?

points.label: Identify Hyperbola Type
points.text: This opens left-right (x² positive first). So a² = 25 → a = 5, b² = 16 → b = 4.

points.label: Asymptote Formula
points.text: For x²/a² - y²/b² = 1, asymptotes are y = ±(b/a)x = ±(4/5)x.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The hyperbola gets closer and closer to lines y = 0.8x and y = -0.8x as x increases.

slides.inSimpleWords: Asymptotes guide the shape of hyperbolas—they're the 'rails' the curves follow at infinity.

slides.title: Real-World Applications of Conics

points.label: Parabola
points.text: Satellite dishes, water fountains, bridge arches, projectile motion (cricket ball trajectory).

points.label: Ellipse
points.text: Planetary orbits (Kepler's 1st law), whispering galleries (sound focuses), swimming pools.

points.label: Hyperbola
points.text: Radio towers (hyperbolic reflectors), GPS systems, nuclear cooling towers.

points.label: Circle
points.text: Wheels, orbits (special case of ellipse), architectural designs, wheels on carts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every conic section solves real problems—from designing buildings to tracking satellites.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Bridge Arch
slides.storyContext: An engineer designs a bridge with a parabolic arch. The arch spans 40 meters horizontally and rises 10 meters at the center. Write the equation.

points.label: Set up coordinates
points.text: Vertex at origin (0,0). Left end at (-20,-10), right end at (20,-10). Opening downward: x² = -4ay.

points.label: Equation
points.text: x² = -40y or y = -x²/40. This describes the bridge's perfect arch.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real bridge arches are parabolas—calculated to support weight evenly across the span.

image.alt: Full Problem: The Bridge Arch — Conic Sections

slides.title: A Journey Through Conics
slides.storyContext: Govind, Ravi, and Diya review their learning. 'Circles are simple and perfect. Ellipses stretch circles into planetary orbits. Parabolas catch signals and water. Hyperbolas navigate us across the Earth.' Ravi says, 'They're all from slicing the same cone, yet each solves completely different problems.' Diya nods: 'Mathematics is elegant—one family of curves, infinite applications.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All conics come from one source—a cone—yet each has unique geometry and real-world power.

slides.title: The Power of Conic Geometry
slides.storyContext: Diya marvels: 'Without conic sections, we couldn't predict planetary paths, design efficient antennas, or locate anything with GPS. One mathematical family unlocks the universe—from atoms to galaxies.' Govind adds: 'And engineers use conics to build everything—fountains, bridges, buildings. Mathematics isn't abstract—it's the language of creation.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections connect mathematics to the natural world and modern technology.

slides.title: Challenge: Satellite Dish Focus
slides.storyContext: A satellite receiver is designed as a parabolic mirror y² = 16x. A signal receiver sits at the focus. Find the focus coordinates.

example.problem: For the parabola y² = 16x, find the focus.
example.solution: Form y² = 4ax. Here 4a = 16 → a = 4. Focus at (4, 0). All signals parallel to the axis reflect to this point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parabolic mirrors focus parallel rays to a single point—the key to powerful receivers.

slides.title: Challenge: Elliptical Pool Design
slides.storyContext: A swimming pool has elliptical shape x²/100 + y²/64 = 1 (in meters). Find the major and minor axis lengths.

example.problem: For ellipse x²/100 + y²/64 = 1, find major and minor axis lengths.
example.solution: a² = 100 → a = 10 (semi-major). b² = 64 → b = 8 (semi-minor). Major axis = 2a = 20 m, Minor axis = 2b = 16 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pool designers use ellipses for elegant curves—the major and minor axes determine overall dimensions.

slides.title: Challenge: Hyperbola Focus Location
slides.storyContext: A navigation hyperbola is x²/36 - y²/64 = 1. Find the foci locations for this GPS system.

example.problem: For hyperbola x²/36 - y²/64 = 1, find the foci.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hyperbola foci are the signal sources in GPS systems—their location defines the navigation network.

slides.title: Challenge: Conic Identification by Eccentricity
slides.storyContext: Ravi identifies curves by eccentricity. If he measures e = 0.85 for an orbit, what conic section is it?

example.problem: Identify the conic with eccentricity e = 0.85.
example.solution: Since 0 < 0.85 < 1, this is an ellipse. The close-to-1 value means it's a very elongated, almost parabolic ellipse.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eccentricity uniquely determines the conic type—it's nature's way of classifying curves.

slides.title: Challenge: Circle Tangent Line
slides.storyContext: Find the equation of a line tangent to the circle (x-2)² + (y-3)² = 25 at the point (5, 7).

example.problem: Tangent line to circle (x-2)² + (y-3)² = 25 at point (5,7).
example.solution: Radius from center (2,3) to point (5,7) has slope (7-3)/(5-2) = 4/3. Tangent is perpendicular: slope = -3/4. Equation: y - 7 = -3/4(x - 5) → 3x + 4y - 43 = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Tangent lines are perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.

slides.title: Challenge: Parabola Vertex Form
slides.storyContext: A parabola has vertex at (2, 3) and opens upward with focus 2 units above the vertex. Write its equation.

example.problem: Parabola with vertex (2,3), opens up, focus 2 units above.
example.solution: a = 2 (distance from vertex to focus). Vertex form: (x - h)² = 4a(y - k) → (x - 2)² = 8(y - 3). Focus at (2, 5), directrix y = 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertex form (x-h)² = 4a(y-k) is convenient when vertex is not at origin.

slides.title: Conic Sections Summary

points.text: Circle: (x-h)² + (y-k)² = r². All points equidistant from center.
Parabola: y² = 4ax or x² = 4ay. Equidistant from focus and directrix. Used in dishes, fountains, arches.
Ellipse: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1. Sum of distances to foci is constant. Describes planetary orbits.
Hyperbola: x²/a² - y²/b² = 1. Difference of distances to foci is constant. Used in navigation.
Every conic has eccentricity e: circle (e=0), ellipse (0<e<1), parabola (e=1), hyperbola (e>1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Conic sections are the foundation of orbital mechanics, optics, and architectural design.

subject: Mathematics
title: Building in Three Dimensions
hook: From flat paper to real buildings—learn to navigate and measure in 3D space.

slides.title: 3D Geometry: Building in Three Dimensions
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel must design a new school building. The design requires coordinates in 3D: length, width, and height. Ankit asks, 'How do we describe positions in 3D space?'
slides.inSimpleWords: In 3D space, every point needs three coordinates (x, y, z)—length, width, and height.

image.alt: 3D Geometry: Building in Three Dimensions — Introduction to Three Dimensional Geometry

slides.title: From 2D Drawings to 3D Reality
slides.storyContext: Ankit holds the architect's blueprint. 'On the drawing, the door is at (2,3)—that's flat,' says Patel. 'But in the real building, we must say (2,3,0) for ground level, or (2,3,1.5) if it's on the wall. We need a third coordinate for height.' Priya sketches: 'So (x,y,z) describes any point in the building?' Patel nods. 'Exactly. Let's master 3D coordinates.'
slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system extends 2D coordinates by adding height as the z-axis.

slides.title: The 3D Coordinate System

points.label: Three Axes
points.text: x-axis (length), y-axis (width), z-axis (height). They meet at origin O(0,0,0).

points.label: Octants
points.text: 3D space divides into 8 octants, like quadrants in 2D but in 3D.

points.label: Point Representation
points.text: Any point P in 3D is (x, y, z). Example: a door handle at (2, 3, 1.8) meters.

example.problem: Locate the corner of a room at (4, 6, 0). What is its position relative to the origin?
example.solution: 4 meters along x-axis, 6 meters along y-axis, ground level (z=0). This is where a wall meets another wall on the floor.

slides.inSimpleWords: The 3D coordinate system uses three perpendicular axes to locate any point in space.

slides.title: Visualizing 3D Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Priya closes her eyes to picture the system. 'The origin is at the corner where three walls meet the floor. The x-axis runs east along the floor. The y-axis runs north along the floor. The z-axis points up toward the roof. Any room position is a combination of these three directions.' Ankit and Patel sketch along with her.
slides.inSimpleWords: Imagine three perpendicular rulers meeting at a corner—that's the 3D coordinate system.

slides.title: Worked Example: Identifying 3D Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Ankit points out three key building points: (0,0,0) at the entrance, (5,0,0) at the far wall, and (5,5,3) at the roof corner. Plot them mentally.

points.label: Entrance Point
points.text: (0,0,0) is the origin—right at the corner where two walls meet at ground level.

points.label: Far Wall Point
points.text: (5,0,0) is 5 meters along the x-axis, ground level—on the far wall.

points.label: Roof Corner Point
points.text: (5,5,3) is 5 meters along x, 5 meters along y, and 3 meters high—this is a corner of the roof.

slides.inSimpleWords: Picture each coordinate: the x-value steps right, y-value steps forward, z-value steps up.

slides.title: Distance Between Two Points in 3D

points.label: Distance Formula
points.text: Distance AB = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²)

points.label: Building Application
points.text: From ground door (2,3,0) to roof corner (5,8,10), distance = √((5-2)² + (8-3)² + (10-0)²) = √(9+25+100) = √134 ≈ 11.6 meters.

points.label: Pythagoras in 3D
points.text: The formula extends Pythagorean theorem to three dimensions.

example.problem: Find the distance from room corner (1,2,3) to ceiling point (4,6,5).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance formula is like the 2D Pythagorean theorem, but with a third dimension added.

slides.title: Measuring Through Space
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel explains: 'When we measure distances through buildings—not just along walls—we use the 3D distance formula. A cable from one roof corner to another corner spans 3D space, not just flat ground. The formula accounts for all three dimensions.' Priya nods, understanding how real measurements work.
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world distances through buildings need 3D calculations, not just 2D floor plans.

slides.title: Worked Example: Calculating Diagonal Distance
slides.storyContext: Priya measures the diagonal through a room from corner (0,0,0) to opposite corner (6,8,3). What's the room's diagonal length?

points.label: Calculate Result
points.text: √109 ≈ 10.44 meters. The room's body diagonal is about 10.44 meters long.

points.label: Verification
points.text: This is longer than any single side (6, 8, or 3) because it's a diagonal through 3D space.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always square each coordinate difference, sum them, then take the square root.

slides.title: Direction Cosines and Direction Ratios

points.label: Direction Ratios
points.text: For vector from A(x₁,y₁,z₁) to B(x₂,y₂,z₂): direction ratios are (a,b,c) = (x₂-x₁, y₂-y₁, z₂-z₁).

points.label: Direction Cosines
points.text: l = a/d, m = b/d, n = c/d, where d = √(a²+b²+c²) is the distance. Note: l² + m² + n² = 1.

points.label: Building Example
points.text: From (2,3,0) to (5,8,10), ratios are (3,5,10). Distance d = √134. Cosines: l≈0.26, m≈0.43, n≈0.87.

example.problem: Find direction cosines from A(0,0,0) to B(1,1,1).
example.solution: Ratios: (1,1,1). Distance: √3. Cosines: l = 1/√3, m = 1/√3, n = 1/√3. Each ≈ 0.577.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines describe how a line is oriented in 3D space—useful for architectural slopes.

slides.title: Slope and Direction in Buildings
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel explains drainage: 'Water must flow downhill. I calculate direction cosines for each gutter and pipe. The cosines tell me the slope in each dimension—how much the pipe drops east, north, and down. Combined, they define the water flow.' Ankit sketches the gutter system with direction vectors marked.
slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines help design slopes and flows in 3D building systems.

slides.title: Worked Example: Direction Cosines Calculation
slides.storyContext: A support beam runs from (1,2,2) to (4,6,5). What are its direction cosines?
slides.inSimpleWords: Direction cosines always sum to 1 (when squared)—a useful check on calculations.

slides.title: Section Formula: Dividing a Line Segment

points.label: Internal Division
points.text: Point P divides line AB in ratio m:n. Then P = ((m·x₂ + n·x₁)/(m+n), (m·y₂ + n·y₁)/(m+n), (m·z₂ + n·z₁)/(m+n)).

points.label: Midpoint (1:1 ratio)
points.text: Midpoint M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2, (z₁+z₂)/2).

points.label: Application
points.text: Architects use this to locate structural supports: if a beam runs from (0,0,0) to (10,10,10), support at 2:1 point is at (20/3, 20/3, 20/3) ≈ (6.67, 6.67, 6.67).

example.problem: Find point P dividing segment from A(1,2,3) to B(7,8,9) in ratio 2:1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula helps locate structural points along beams and construction lines.

slides.title: Support Point Placement
slides.storyContext: Priya asks, 'Why not always put supports at the midpoint?' Architect Patel explains: 'Sometimes the load distribution isn't equal. A beam might support more weight at one end. We use the section formula to place supports at points where the ratio matches the load distribution. This ensures efficient, safe designs.' Ankit draws a beam with multiple support points.
slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula places supports exactly where structural forces demand them.

slides.title: Worked Example: Midpoint in 3D
slides.storyContext: A building's main diagonal runs from (0,0,0) to (12,10,8). Find the center point of this diagonal.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The building's center is at (6, 5, 4) meters—exactly halfway through the diagonal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Midpoint is the simplest case of section formula—dividing a segment into two equal parts.

slides.title: Equation of a Line in 3D

points.label: Parametric Form
points.text: Line through point A(a,b,c) with direction (l,m,n): x = a + lt, y = b + mt, z = c + nt, where t is parameter.

points.label: Wall Edge Example
points.text: Wall edge from (0,0,0) to (0,5,3) has parametric: x=0, y=5t, z=3t. At t=0: (0,0,0); at t=1: (0,5,3).

example.problem: Write parametric equations for a line through (2,3,4) with direction (1,2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D line equations use parameters (t) to describe every point along the line.

slides.title: Cables and Conduits
slides.storyContext: Ankit watches electricians run cables through the building. 'Each cable follows a specific path—parametric equations describe that path perfectly. At any parameter value t, we know exactly where the cable is located in 3D space. Architects use this to avoid collisions between cables, pipes, and ducts.' Priya sketches multiple parametric paths weaving through the building.
slides.inSimpleWords: Parametric equations trace cables, pipes, and conduits through 3D buildings.

slides.title: Worked Example: Parametric Line from Two Points
slides.storyContext: A cable runs between two building points: (1,1,2) and (5,7,8). Write the parametric equations.

points.label: Write Parametric Equations
points.text: Using point (1,1,2): x = 1 + 4t, y = 1 + 6t, z = 2 + 6t.

points.label: Verify
points.text: At t=0: (1,1,2). At t=1: (5,7,8). The cable is traced as t goes from 0 to 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Start at a point, then add direction components scaled by parameter t—this traces the entire line.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Diagonal Beam
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel designs a diagonal support beam from corner A(0,0,0) to opposite corner B(10,8,6) of a building. Find the beam's length and the point exactly halfway along.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: The beam is 14.14 meters long. The midpoint (5,4,3) is where the architect plans a structural support.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D distance and section formulas are essential for structural engineering and construction planning.

slides.title: A Complete Building Design
slides.storyContext: Architect Patel reviews the entire building with Ankit and Priya. 'We've used 3D coordinates to locate every point, 3D distance to measure spans, direction cosines to slope systems correctly, section formulas to place supports, and parametric equations to route utilities. Together, these tools create a safe, efficient building.' They examine a complete 3D building model.
slides.inSimpleWords: All 3D geometry tools work together to design real buildings that stand and function.

slides.title: 3D Geometry in the Real World
slides.storyContext: Ankit looks at the finished school building under construction. 'Every beam, pipe, and cable was calculated using 3D geometry. Nothing is guessed—everything follows mathematical precision.' Priya adds: '3D coordinate geometry is how computers model space too. Video games, virtual reality, medical imaging—they all use these same formulas.' Architect Patel smiles: 'Mathematics is the blueprint of reality.'
slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry is the foundation of architecture, construction, computer graphics, and navigation systems.

slides.title: Challenge: Rooftop Antenna Length
slides.storyContext: An antenna is placed at (5, 4, 12)—on the roof corner at height 12m. The base of the antenna pole is at (5, 4, 0). Find the antenna's length and direction cosines.

example.problem: From (5,4,0) to (5,4,12), find length and direction cosines.
example.solution: Length: √((5-5)² + (4-4)² + (12-0)²) = √144 = 12 meters. Direction ratios: (0,0,12). Direction cosines: l=0, m=0, n=1 (points straight up).

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertical structures like antennas have simple direction cosines—all the cosine goes to n.

slides.title: Challenge: Support Point Location
slides.storyContext: A cable runs from (2,2,1) to (8,10,7). Find the point that divides this cable in the ratio 1:2 (closer to the first point).

example.problem: Divide segment from A(2,2,1) to B(8,10,7) in ratio 1:2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Section formula divides lines unequally—useful for placing supports not at the midpoint.

slides.title: Challenge: Parametric Path Verification
slides.storyContext: An air duct follows the path x = 1 + 2t, y = 2 + 3t, z = 1 + t. Find the coordinates at t = 2 and verify the direction vector.

example.problem: For path x = 1 + 2t, y = 2 + 3t, z = 1 + t, find coordinates at t = 2.
example.solution: At t=2: x = 1 + 2(2) = 5, y = 2 + 3(2) = 8, z = 1 + 1(2) = 3. Point is (5, 8, 3). Direction vector from coefficients: (2, 3, 1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Parametric equations let you find any point along a path—essential for routing building systems.

slides.title: Challenge: Octant Identification
slides.storyContext: Priya marks several points in the building. For point (3, -4, 5), which octant does it occupy and why?

example.problem: Identify the octant for point (3, -4, 5).
example.solution: x=3 (positive), y=-4 (negative), z=5 (positive). This is octant IV (using typical octant numbering). Negative y means the point is behind the reference plane.

slides.inSimpleWords: Octants in 3D are like quadrants in 2D—determined by the signs of the three coordinates.

slides.title: Challenge: Foot of Perpendicular
slides.storyContext: From a point P(2, 3, 4), find the foot of perpendicular to the line x = 1 + t, y = 2 + 2t, z = 1 + 3t.

example.problem: Find foot of perpendicular from P(2,3,4) to line x = 1+t, y = 2+2t, z = 1+3t.

slides.inSimpleWords: The foot of perpendicular is found by making the connecting vector perpendicular to the line.

slides.title: 3D Geometry Summary

points.text: 3D coordinates (x,y,z) locate points in space using three perpendicular axes.
Distance: d = √((x₂-x₁)² + (y₂-y₁)² + (z₂-z₁)²).
Direction cosines (l,m,n) describe line orientation; l² + m² + n² = 1.
Section formula divides a segment in any ratio; midpoint is the 1:1 case.
Line in 3D: parametric form (x,y,z) = (a,b,c) + t(l,m,n) or symmetric form.
Applications: architecture, construction, surveying, navigation, computer graphics.

slides.inSimpleWords: 3D geometry extends 2D coordinate ideas to the real world—essential for building and design.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Instantaneous Speed
hook: How fast is a cricket ball moving at one instant? Limits and derivatives unlock the secret.

slides.title: Limits and Derivatives: The Math of Instant Change
slides.storyContext: Rohan watches the cricket match. A bowler delivers at 140 km/h—but how do we define speed at ONE instant, not over a distance?
slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives measure instantaneous rates of change—how fast something is changing at this very moment.

slides.title: The Bowler's Speed
slides.storyContext: Coach Kumar explains to Rohan: 'Average speed is distance/time over a distance. But a radar gun measures speed at ONE instant—the ball's velocity now. That's where calculus comes in.' Aisha adds, 'We use limits to shrink the time interval to zero, then we get the derivative.' Coach nods: 'Exactly. Let me teach you both.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Average speed over time versus instantaneous speed at a single moment—derivatives bridge the gap.

slides.title: Limits: Approaching a Value

points.label: Definition
points.text: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means as x gets closer to a, f(x) gets closer to L.

points.label: Ball Distance
points.text: Distance traveled: s(t) = 5t². As time t → 1, what is s(t)? s(1) = 5, s(0.9) = 4.05, s(0.99) = 4.9005. Limit is 5.

points.label: Left and Right Limits
points.text: lim(x→a⁻) = left limit, lim(x→a⁺) = right limit. If both equal L, the limit exists.

example.problem: Find lim(x→2) (x² + 3x - 1).
example.solution: Direct substitution: 2² + 3(2) - 1 = 4 + 6 - 1 = 9. Limit = 9.

slides.inSimpleWords: A limit is the value a function approaches as the input gets closer to a specific number.

slides.title: Rohan's Limit Problem
slides.storyContext: Rohan throws a ball upward. Its height h(t) = 20t - 5t² meters. At t=2, it reaches h(2) = 40 - 20 = 20 meters. But what if we want to know the height at almost-2? Aisha says: 'As t gets closer to 2, h(t) approaches 20. That's a limit!' Coach laughs: 'The ball knows calculus without studying it!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Limits help us find values at critical points even when the function might be undefined there.

slides.title: Example: Computing Limits
slides.storyContext: Aisha calculates lim(x→3) (x² - 9)/(x - 3). Direct substitution gives 0/0, which is undefined.

points.label: Key Insight
points.text: The limit exists even though the function is undefined at x=3. This 'hole' is called a removable discontinuity.

slides.inSimpleWords: When direct substitution gives 0/0, factor and simplify to find the limit.

slides.title: Challenge: Left and Right Limits
slides.storyContext: Rohan explores: what if a function behaves differently from the left and right?

example.problem: Find lim(x→2⁻) and lim(x→2⁺) for f(x) = (x-2)/|x-2|.
example.solution: From left (x<2): |x-2| = -(x-2), so f(x) = (x-2)/[-(x-2)] = -1. lim(x→2⁻) = -1. From right (x>2): |x-2| = (x-2), so f(x) = (x-2)/(x-2) = 1. lim(x→2⁺) = 1. Limits differ, so lim(x→2) does NOT exist.

slides.inSimpleWords: When left and right limits differ, the overall limit does not exist.

slides.title: Continuity at a Point

points.label: Definition
points.text: f is continuous at x = a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).

points.label: Three Conditions
points.text: (1) f(a) exists, (2) lim(x→a) f(x) exists, (3) both are equal.

points.label: Real Example
points.text: A cricket ball's height as it flies—continuous unless it gets caught. A function with a hole or jump is discontinuous.

example.problem: Is f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x - 2) continuous at x = 2?
example.solution: f(2) is undefined (0/0). But lim(x→2) (x² - 4)/(x - 2) = lim(x→2) (x + 2) = 4. The function has a removable discontinuity at x = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous functions have no breaks, holes, or jumps—they graph as smooth, unbroken curves.

image.alt: Continuity at a Point — Limits and Derivatives

slides.title: Breaking Continuity
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks Coach Kumar: 'What if the ball teleports? It's at height 10m, then instantly at 5m?' Coach says: 'That's a jump discontinuity—not smooth. In physics, continuous motion means no teleportation.' Aisha sketches two graphs: one smooth (continuous), one with a jump (discontinuous).
slides.inSimpleWords: Discontinuities are breaks in a function's graph—jumps, holes, or vertical asymptotes.

slides.title: Example: Continuity Check
slides.storyContext: Check if f(x) = 2x + 3 is continuous at x = 1.

points.label: Are they equal?
points.text: Yes: f(1) = 5 = limit. So f is continuous at x=1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear functions are continuous everywhere—no breaks, jumps, or holes.

slides.title: The Derivative: Instantaneous Rate of Change

points.label: Definition
points.text: Derivative f'(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a+h) - f(a)]/h. It is the slope of the tangent at x = a.

points.label: Geometric Meaning
points.text: The slope of the tangent line to the curve at a point. For straight lines, it is the slope m.

points.label: Ball Velocity
points.text: Distance s(t) = 5t². Velocity = ds/dt = lim(h→0) [5(t+h)² - 5t²]/h = 10t. At t=1, velocity = 10 m/s.

example.problem: Find the derivative of f(x) = x² at x = 3 using the definition.

slides.inSimpleWords: The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line—it tells how fast the function is changing.

slides.title: Rohan Finds Instantaneous Speed
slides.storyContext: Rohan measures a cricket ball's position over time: s(t) = 4t². At t=2, position is 16 meters. But what's the speed exactly at t=2? Coach says: 'Use the derivative formula. Let h shrink to zero.' Aisha calculates: as h→0, the secant line becomes a tangent. That slope is the instantaneous speed!
slides.inSimpleWords: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change—as the interval shrinks to zero.

slides.title: Example: Derivative from Definition
slides.storyContext: Find f'(2) for f(x) = 3x² - 2.
slides.inSimpleWords: The derivative definition requires algebra to expand, simplify, and take the limit.

slides.title: Challenge: Derivative Definition
slides.storyContext: Find f'(1) for f(x) = x³.

example.problem: Use the definition: f'(1) = lim(h→0) [f(1+h) - f(1)]/h for f(x) = x³.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice the definition to build intuition—later, rules make it faster.

slides.title: Derivative Rules: Power, Product, Chain

points.label: Power Rule
points.text: If f(x) = xⁿ, then f'(x) = n·x^(n-1). Example: f(x) = x³ → f'(x) = 3x².

points.label: Chain Rule
points.text: [f(g(x))]' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Used for composite functions.

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = 3x⁴ - 2x² + 5.
example.solution: Using power rule: f'(x) = 12x³ - 4x.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative rules let you find rates of change quickly without using limits every time.

slides.title: Rules Save Time
slides.storyContext: Rohan says: 'Using the definition takes forever!' Coach smiles: 'True. Mathematicians found shortcuts—the power rule, product rule, chain rule. They're all derived from the definition, but we apply them directly now.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once you understand the definition, rules make derivatives easy.

slides.title: Example: Power Rule
slides.storyContext: Differentiate f(x) = 7x⁵.

points.label: Verify at x=1
points.text: f'(1) = 35(1)⁴ = 35. Slope of tangent at x=1 is 35.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: differentiate xⁿ by bringing down n and reducing the exponent by 1.

slides.title: Example: Chain Rule
slides.storyContext: Find the derivative of f(x) = (2x + 3)⁵.

points.label: Identify Composition
points.text: f(x) = g(h(x)) where h(x) = 2x + 3 (inner), g(u) = u⁵ (outer).

slides.inSimpleWords: Chain rule: differentiate the outer function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

slides.title: Challenge: Product Rule
slides.storyContext: Find f'(x) for f(x) = x² · sin(x).

example.problem: Differentiate f(x) = x² · sin(x).
example.solution: Using product rule: f'(x) = (x²)' · sin(x) + x² · (sin(x))' = 2x · sin(x) + x² · cos(x) = 2x sin(x) + x² cos(x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Useful for multiplied functions.

slides.title: Physical Interpretation: Velocity and Acceleration

points.label: Velocity
points.text: v(t) = ds/dt, where s is position. It is the first derivative of position.

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: a(t) = dv/dt, where v is velocity. It is the second derivative of position.

points.label: Cricket Ball
points.text: If s(t) = 5t² (position in meters), then v(t) = 10t (velocity), a(t) = 10 (constant acceleration = 10 m/s²).

example.problem: A car's position is s(t) = 2t³ + t². Find velocity and acceleration at t = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Velocity is the rate of position change; acceleration is the rate of velocity change—both are derivatives.

image.alt: Physical Interpretation: Velocity and Acceleration — Limits and Derivatives

slides.title: Coach Explains Motion
slides.storyContext: Coach Kumar tells Rohan: 'When the ball leaves my hand, its position changes. The rate of change is velocity—that's what the radar gun shows. If velocity itself changes, that's acceleration—my arm is still pushing!' Aisha draws the graphs: position (parabola), velocity (line), acceleration (constant).
slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives connect position → velocity → acceleration. Each is the rate of change of the previous.

slides.title: Example: Position, Velocity, Acceleration
slides.storyContext: A projectile's height is h(t) = 20t - 5t² meters. Find v(t) and a(t).

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: a(t) = dv/dt = -10 m/s² (gravity pulling down).

slides.inSimpleWords: Gravity creates constant negative acceleration of -10 m/s² (on Earth).

slides.title: Full Problem: The Bowler's Delivery
slides.storyContext: A fast bowler's hand (with ball) position during delivery is s(t) = 10t² - 2t + 1 meters. What is the ball's velocity and acceleration at t = 0.5 seconds?

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: a(t) = dv/dt = 20 m/s² (constant).

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: At release (t=0.5s), the ball moves at 8 m/s and accelerates at constant 20 m/s² due to the bowler's arm motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives of position give velocity; derivatives of velocity give acceleration—the chain of motion.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Pendulum Swing
slides.storyContext: A pendulum's angle is θ(t) = 0.5 sin(2t) radians. Find its angular velocity at t = π/4.

example.problem: Find dθ/dt for θ(t) = 0.5 sin(2t), then evaluate at t = π/4.
example.solution: dθ/dt = 0.5 × cos(2t) × 2 = cos(2t). At t = π/4: dθ/dt = cos(π/2) = 0 rad/s. (The pendulum momentarily stops at the highest point.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives of trigonometric functions describe oscillating motion—useful for pendulums, waves, and vibrations.

slides.title: Why Limits Matter
slides.storyContext: Aisha reflects: 'Limits started with a puzzle—how do we define speed at an instant? Now I see: by shrinking the time interval until it's zero. That's beautiful!' Coach nods: 'Limits bridge the gap between the everyday (average speed) and the ideal (instantaneous speed).'
slides.inSimpleWords: Limits connect discrete ideas (average) to continuous ones (instantaneous).

slides.title: Applications Beyond Cricket
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'What else use derivatives?' Aisha lists: 'Medicine—drug concentration changes in blood. Economics—marginal cost. Weather—temperature rate of change. Biology—population growth rates. Everywhere something changes, derivatives apply!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives model change in physics, economics, biology, medicine—any field where rates matter.

slides.title: Limits and Derivatives Summary

points.text: Limit: lim(x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) approaches L as x approaches a.
Continuity: f is continuous at a if lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
Derivative: f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h. Slope of tangent line at x.
Power Rule: d/dx[xⁿ] = n·x^(n-1). Chain Rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x))·g'(x).
Velocity = ds/dt (first derivative). Acceleration = d²s/dt² (second derivative).
Derivatives are the foundation of calculus—used in physics, engineering, economics, and motion analysis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives measure how fast things change instantaneously—the core concept of differential calculus.

image.alt: Limits and Derivatives Summary — Limits and Derivatives

subject: Mathematics
title: Understanding Data: The Village Health Survey
hook: A health worker surveys the village—learn to organize, analyze, and interpret data.

characters.name: Vikram
characters.role: Farmer providing data on crops and health

slides.title: Statistics: Understanding Data from the Village
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma conducts a health survey of 100 villagers. Neha helps record heights, weights, and ages. Can they find patterns and predict health trends?
slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data to find patterns.

slides.title: The Health Survey Begins
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma measures heights of 100 children: 120, 125, 130, 128, ... Neha writes them down. 'How do we find the typical height? How spread out are the heights?' she asks. Dr. Sharma smiles: 'That's statistics. We calculate mean, median, and standard deviation.' Vikram joins: 'How do we show this data clearly?' Neha says, 'With histograms and frequency tables!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Organize raw data into tables and graphs to reveal patterns and averages.

image.alt: The Health Survey Begins — Statistics

slides.title: Measures of Central Tendency: Mean, Median, Mode

points.label: Mean (Average)
points.text: Mean = Σx / n, where Σx is sum of all values and n is count. Heights: 120, 125, 130, 128, 132 → Mean = (120+125+130+128+132)/5 = 635/5 = 127 cm.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle value when data is sorted. For 5 values: 120, 125, 128, 130, 132 → Median = 128 (3rd value).

points.label: Mode
points.text: Most frequent value. If heights 128, 130, 128, 128 appear most, Mode = 128.

example.problem: 10 students' test scores: 65, 78, 82, 78, 90, 78, 85, 92, 88, 95. Find mean, median, and mode.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is the average, median is the middle value, mode is the most common value.

slides.title: Dr. Sharma Compares Measures
slides.storyContext: Neha asks: 'Why three different measures? When do we use each?' Dr. Sharma explains: 'Mean is pulled by outliers—if one very tall child joins, mean shifts. Median is stable. Mode shows the most common height. Use mean for balanced data, median when outliers exist, mode to find most frequent values.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Choose the right average: mean for balanced data, median for skewed data with outliers, mode for frequency.

slides.title: Example: When Median Beats Mean
slides.storyContext: Village wealth in rupees: 50,000, 55,000, 60,000, 65,000, 100,00,000 (one rich person).

points.label: Mean
points.text: (50k + 55k + 60k + 65k + 1Cr) / 5 = 1.23Cr / 5 = 24.6L. Pulled high by outlier!

points.label: Median
points.text: Sorted: 50k, 55k, 60k, 65k, 1Cr. Median = 60k (middle value). More representative of typical wealth.

points.label: Lesson
points.text: For skewed data (like income), median is more meaningful than mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Outliers can distort the mean; use median for data with extreme values.

slides.title: Challenge: Find All Three

example.problem: Calculate mean, median, and mode.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always sort data first to find median correctly.

slides.title: Measures of Dispersion: Range, Variance, Standard Deviation

points.label: Range
points.text: Range = Maximum - Minimum. Heights: 120 to 132 → Range = 132 - 120 = 12 cm.

points.label: Variance
points.text: Variance σ² = Σ(x - mean)² / n. Measures how spread out data is from the mean.

points.label: Standard Deviation
points.text: σ = √(variance). It is the 'average deviation' from the mean. Lower σ = data is tightly clustered; higher σ = data is spread out.

example.problem: Heights 120, 125, 130, 128, 132. Mean = 127. Find variance and standard deviation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Variance and standard deviation measure how spread out data is—useful for assessing consistency.

image.alt: Measures of Dispersion: Range, Variance, Standard Deviation — Statistics

slides.title: Spread Matters
slides.storyContext: Neha observes: 'Two villages both have mean height 128 cm. But Village A heights range 120-136, Village B heights range 125-131. Are they the same?' Dr. Sharma says: 'No! Village B is more consistent. Standard deviation captures this spread.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Two datasets with same mean can have very different spreads—measure variance to compare consistency.

slides.title: Example: Calculate Standard Deviation
slides.storyContext: Test scores: 70, 75, 80, 85, 90. Mean = 80.

points.label: Standard Deviation
points.text: √50 ≈ 7.07. Typical score deviates about 7 points from mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: SD step-by-step: find mean, compute deviations, square them, average, take square root.

slides.title: Challenge: Compare Dispersions
slides.storyContext: Dataset A: 10, 20, 30. Dataset B: 15, 20, 25. Both have mean 20. Which has larger SD?

example.problem: Calculate SD for both.
example.solution: Dataset A deviations: -10, 0, 10 → squared: 100, 0, 100 → variance = 200/3 ≈ 66.7 → SD ≈ 8.16. Dataset B deviations: -5, 0, 5 → squared: 25, 0, 25 → variance = 50/3 ≈ 16.7 → SD ≈ 4.08. Dataset A is more spread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Larger standard deviation means data is more spread out from the mean.

slides.title: Frequency Distribution and Histograms

points.label: Frequency Table
points.text: Organize data into classes. Heights 120-125: 5 children, 125-130: 12 children, 130-135: 8 children.

points.label: Histogram
points.text: Bar graph where height of bar = frequency. Width = class width (constant). Used for continuous data.

points.label: Frequency Polygon
points.text: Line graph connecting midpoints of histogram bars. Shows trend in data.

example.problem: 100 children's heights grouped: 120-125 (15), 125-130 (35), 130-135 (30), 135-140 (20). Sketch the histogram.
example.solution: x-axis: height ranges. y-axis: frequency. Bars at heights 15, 35, 30, 20 respectively. Tallest bar is 125-130 range (35 children).

slides.inSimpleWords: Frequency tables and histograms organize large datasets into visual patterns.

image.alt: Frequency Distribution and Histograms — Statistics

slides.title: Grouping Raw Data
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma has 100 exact heights. Listing all would be overwhelming. Neha suggests: 'Let's group them into classes.' They create intervals of 5 cm and count frequencies. This 'frequency table' reveals the shape: most children cluster around 128 cm.
slides.inSimpleWords: Grouping data reveals distribution patterns—normal, skewed, bimodal, etc.

slides.title: Example: Build a Frequency Table

points.label: Visualize
points.text: Bar graph shows most students scored 90-100 or 80-90 (high performers).

slides.inSimpleWords: Class width depends on data range; choose width so you have 5-10 classes.

slides.title: Challenge: Histogram Interpretation
slides.storyContext: Looking at a histogram of house prices (in lakhs): 20-30 (5 homes), 30-40 (15), 40-50 (20), 50-60 (12), 60-70 (3).

example.problem: What can you infer about the housing market?
example.solution: Most homes cost 40-50L (peak). Market skews toward 30-50L range. Few expensive homes (60-70L). Supply is concentrated in mid-range; luxury homes are rare.

slides.inSimpleWords: Histograms reveal market concentrations and trends at a glance.

slides.title: Cumulative Frequency and Quartiles

points.label: Cumulative Frequency
points.text: Running total of frequencies. Heights: 120-125 (5), then 125-130 (5+12=17), then 130-135 (17+8=25), etc.

points.label: Quartiles
points.text: Q₁ (25th percentile), Q₂ (median, 50th), Q₃ (75th). Divide sorted data into 4 equal parts.

points.label: Interquartile Range
points.text: IQR = Q₃ - Q₁. Measures middle 50% spread of data.

example.problem: For 100 children sorted by height, find Q₁ and Q₃. Q₁ is at position 25.5, Q₃ at 75.5.
example.solution: If sorted heights at position 25.5 is 127 cm, then Q₁ = 127. If at position 75.5 is 135 cm, then Q₃ = 135. IQR = 135 - 127 = 8 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Quartiles divide data into quarters—useful for understanding how data is distributed.

image.alt: Cumulative Frequency and Quartiles — Statistics

slides.title: From Frequency to Quartiles
slides.storyContext: Neha draws cumulative frequencies: running totals showing how many children have height ≤ each value. 'Where's the median?' she asks. Dr. Sharma: 'At 50 cumulative frequency—halfway. That's Q₂. Q₁ and Q₃ are at 25 and 75.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Cumulative frequency curves show percentiles visually—useful for finding quartiles.

slides.title: Example: Find Quartiles from Sorted Data

points.label: Median (Q₂)
points.text: Position (n+1)/2 = 6.5. Average of 6th and 7th values: (66 + 70)/2 = 68.

slides.inSimpleWords: Split data at median; quartiles of those halves give Q₁ and Q₃.

slides.title: Challenge: Box Plot
slides.storyContext: Using the above data (Q₁=54, median=68, Q₃=80, min=35, max=95), sketch a box plot.

example.problem: Draw a box plot and interpret it.
example.solution: Horizontal line from 35 to 95 (range). Box from Q₁=54 to Q₃=80. Line at median=68 inside box. Whiskers extend to min/max. The plot shows 50% of students scored 54-80, with median at 68—balanced distribution.

slides.inSimpleWords: Box plots visualize spread, median, and outliers compactly.

slides.title: Correlation and Regression (Introduction)

points.label: Correlation
points.text: Measures strength of linear relationship between two variables. Correlation coefficient r ranges from -1 to +1.

points.label: r = +1
points.text: Perfect positive correlation: as one increases, other increases.

points.label: r = -1
points.text: Perfect negative correlation: as one increases, other decreases.

points.label: r = 0
points.text: No linear correlation. Example: child height vs. test score (weak).

example.problem: A study shows age vs. income for 50 workers. Calculate correlation to see relationship strength.
example.solution: Using formula or tools, if r = 0.75, there is strong positive correlation (older workers tend to earn more).

slides.inSimpleWords: Correlation measures how two variables change together—positive (both up), negative (opposite), or zero (no link).

slides.title: Vikram's Curiosity
slides.storyContext: Vikram asks: 'Does rainfall predict crop yield? Does more fertilizer mean bigger harvest?' Neha says: 'We can check with correlation! If rainfall and yield move together, r is high. If they're unrelated, r is near zero.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Correlation quantifies whether two measurements move together—essential for predicting outcomes.

slides.title: Example: Correlation Patterns
slides.storyContext: Three scenarios: (1) Height vs. weight (tall people often heavier), (2) Height vs. IQ (unrelated), (3) Temperature vs. Ice cream sales (hotter days → more sales).

points.label: Positive Correlation
points.text: Height vs. weight (r ≈ 0.7). Taller people tend to weigh more.

points.label: No Correlation
points.text: Height vs. IQ (r ≈ 0). Height tells nothing about intelligence.

points.label: Negative Correlation
points.text: Price vs. demand (r ≈ -0.6). Higher prices → fewer buyers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Scatter plots reveal correlation visually: tight cluster (strong r), cloud (weak r), no pattern (r≈0).

slides.title: Full Problem: Analyzing Crop Yields
slides.storyContext: Vikram records maize yields (in quintals) from 10 farms: 15, 18, 20, 22, 17, 21, 19, 23, 20, 18. Analyze the data.

points.label: Mean
points.text: Sum = 193. Mean = 193/10 = 19.3 quintals.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle values are 19 and 20. Median = (19+20)/2 = 19.5 quintals.

points.label: Range
points.text: 23 - 15 = 8 quintals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Statistical analysis reveals farm yield patterns—useful for predicting future harvests and planning.

slides.title: Data Drives Decisions
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma tells Neha: 'Statistics isn't just numbers. It's stories. This data tells us which children are malnourished, which villages need health clinics, which crops thrive here. Numbers with context save lives and livelihoods.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics translates data into actionable insights—health, agriculture, policy, business.

slides.title: Your Challenge: Class Test Analysis
slides.storyContext: Class test scores: 45, 67, 78, 82, 55, 90, 73, 88, 60, 95. Find mean, median, standard deviation, and identify outliers.

example.problem: Analyze class test scores. Calculate mean, median, SD. Is 95 an outlier?
example.solution: Mean = 73.3. Sorted: 45,55,60,67,73,78,82,88,90,95. Median = 75.5. Using SD formula: σ ≈ 14.3. Using 3-sigma rule, 95 is within 3σ (73.3 + 3×14.3 = 116.2), so NOT a statistical outlier, but it's the highest score.

slides.inSimpleWords: Outliers are data points far from the mean—identify them using standard deviation.

slides.title: Neha's Insight: From Numbers to Action
slides.storyContext: Neha presents the findings to the village council: 'Dr. Sharma's data shows 25% of children are malnourished. The correlation between family income and child weight is 0.68—clear link. We need to improve nutrition programs.' Vikram adds: 'Can we predict next year?' Neha: 'Yes! Trends and patterns let us forecast.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics isn't an end—it's the start of informed action and real-world problem-solving.

slides.title: Statistics Summary

points.text: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most frequent) are central tendencies.
Range, Variance, Standard Deviation measure data spread—lower SD = tighter clustering.
Frequency tables and histograms organize and visualize grouped data.
Cumulative frequency and quartiles divide data into parts; IQR measures middle 50%.
Correlation (r) measures relationship strength between two variables.
Statistics powers real decisions: health surveys, crop planning, quality control, market research.

slides.inSimpleWords: Statistics transforms raw numbers into insights—mean, median, spread, and patterns reveal the story in data.

image.alt: Statistics Summary — Statistics

subject: Mathematics
title: The Game of Chance
hook: Rolling dice, drawing cards, cricket match predictions—probability measures the likelihood of outcomes.

characters.name: Aunt Savita
characters.role: Mathematics teacher with a knack for games

characters.name: Zara
characters.role: Younger cousin exploring probability through card games

slides.title: Probability: Measuring Chance and Likelihood
slides.storyContext: Arjun commentates a cricket match. 'The batsman has a 60% chance of hitting a six on this ball,' he says. How do we calculate such odds?
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability measures how likely an event is to happen—from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).

image.alt: Probability: Measuring Chance and Likelihood — Probability

slides.title: The Card Game Night
slides.storyContext: Aunt Savita gathers Arjun and Zara for a game. 'Here's a standard deck of 52 cards. If I draw one card, what's the chance it's a heart?' Zara thinks: 'There are 13 hearts, so 13/52 = 1/4 = 25%.' Aunt nods. 'Exactly! The probability is 0.25. Now let's explore the rules of probability.' Arjun adds: 'Can we predict cricket match outcomes?' Aunt smiles: 'We'll get there. First, master the basics.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability = (favorable outcomes) / (total possible outcomes).

slides.title: Sample Space and Events

points.label: Sample Space (S)
points.text: Set of all possible outcomes. For a die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. |S| = 6.

points.label: Event
points.text: Subset of sample space. Getting an even number: E = {2, 4, 6}. |E| = 3.

points.label: Probability of Event
points.text: P(E) = |E| / |S| = 3/6 = 0.5. Probability ranges from 0 to 1.

example.problem: A spinner has 8 equal sections: 4 red, 2 blue, 2 green. Find P(red) and P(not red).

slides.inSimpleWords: Sample space lists all outcomes; an event is a subset. Probability is favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

slides.title: Aunt Savita's Die Game
slides.storyContext: Aunt rolls a fair die. 'Sample space is all faces: {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Event A: rolling odd = {1,3,5}. Event B: rolling >3 = {4,5,6}.' Arjun asks: 'Can events overlap?' Aunt smiles: 'Yes! {5} is in both. That's why we need rules for combining events.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Events can overlap; use logic to count outcomes without double-counting.

slides.title: Example: Compound Events
slides.storyContext: Flip a coin twice. What's P(at least one head)?

points.label: Sample Space
points.text: S = {HH, HT, TH, TT}. |S| = 4.

points.label: Event (at least 1 H)
points.text: E = {HH, HT, TH}. |E| = 3.

points.label: Probability
points.text: P(at least 1 H) = 3/4 = 0.75.

slides.inSimpleWords: For 'at least one', count all outcomes with one or more of the desired result.

slides.title: Challenge: Sample Space
slides.storyContext: Aunt draws 2 cards from a 52-card deck without replacement. How many total outcomes? How many ways to draw 2 hearts?

example.problem: Find total outcomes and favorable outcomes for drawing 2 hearts.
example.solution: Total outcomes: 52 × 51 = 2652 (first card: 52 choices, second: 51). Favorable (2 hearts): 13 × 12 = 156.

slides.inSimpleWords: Without replacement changes the second outcome—subtract 1 from the total for each draw.

slides.title: Classical and Empirical Probability

points.label: Classical Probability
points.text: Used when outcomes are equally likely. P(E) = (# favorable) / (# possible).

points.label: Empirical Probability
points.text: Based on experiments: P(E) = (# times event occurred) / (# total trials). Used when classical method is hard.

points.label: Example
points.text: Toss a coin 100 times: heads appear 52 times. Empirical P(heads) = 52/100 = 0.52 (close to theoretical 0.5).

example.problem: A cricket batsman hits 40 sixes in 200 balls. Estimate P(six on next ball).
example.solution: Empirical P(six) = 40/200 = 0.2 or 20%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Classical probability uses logic; empirical probability uses real data from experiments.

image.alt: Classical and Empirical Probability — Probability

slides.title: Theory vs. Reality
slides.storyContext: Zara asks: 'A coin should have 50-50 odds. But when I flip it 10 times, I get 7 heads!' Aunt explains: 'That's empirical probability—real experiments vary. With 1000 flips, you'll approach 50-50. That's the law of large numbers.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Theory predicts long-run frequencies; individual experiments show variation.

slides.title: Example: Comparing Probabilities
slides.storyContext: A die is rolled 600 times. Count of each face: 1→95, 2→102, 3→98, 4→105, 5→100, 6→100.

points.label: Classical
points.text: Each face should have P = 1/6 ≈ 0.167 or 100 times in 600 rolls.

points.label: Empirical
points.text: Face 4 appeared 105 times → empirical P(4) = 105/600 = 0.175.

points.label: Close Match
points.text: Empirical ≈ Classical, confirming the die is fair.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fair objects have empirical probabilities close to classical predictions.

slides.title: Rules of Probability: Addition and Multiplication

points.label: Addition Rule (OR)
points.text: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). For mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B).

points.label: Multiplication Rule (AND)
points.text: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A), where P(B|A) is conditional probability of B given A.

points.label: Independent Events
points.text: If A and B are independent: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

example.problem: Draw a card, note it, put it back (draw with replacement). What's P(both hearts)?
example.solution: P(1st heart) = 13/52 = 1/4. P(2nd heart | 1st heart) = 13/52 = 1/4 (independent). P(both hearts) = 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition for 'or' (combine probabilities); multiplication for 'and' (successive events).

slides.title: OR vs. AND
slides.storyContext: Zara asks: 'What's P(rolling 2 or 3)?' Aunt: 'Add: 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3. What's P(rolling 2 AND rolling odd)?' Zara: 'Multiply? But 2 is even, so P = 0.' Aunt grins: 'Right. Mutually exclusive events can't both happen.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Use addition for 'or' events; multiplication for sequential or independent 'and' events.

slides.title: Example: Addition Rule
slides.storyContext: From a deck, P(heart) = 1/4, P(spade) = 1/4. What's P(heart or spade)?

points.label: Are they mutually exclusive?
points.text: Yes—a card can't be both heart and spade.

points.label: Apply Addition
points.text: P(heart or spade) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.

slides.inSimpleWords: For mutually exclusive events, add probabilities directly.

slides.title: Example: Multiplication Rule
slides.storyContext: Roll a die, then flip a coin. P(die shows 3 AND coin shows heads)?

points.label: Are they independent?
points.text: Yes—die result doesn't affect coin.

slides.inSimpleWords: For independent events, multiply probabilities.

slides.title: Challenge: Combination Rule
slides.storyContext: Draw 2 cards without replacement. P(both hearts)?

example.problem: Find P(1st heart AND 2nd heart | 1st was heart).
example.solution: P(1st heart) = 13/52. P(2nd heart | 1st heart) = 12/51 (only 12 hearts left). P(both) = (13/52) × (12/51) = 156/2652 ≈ 0.0588 or 5.88%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Without replacement, the second probability depends on the first outcome.

slides.title: Conditional Probability

points.label: Definition
points.text: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B). Probability of A given that B has already happened.

points.label: Card Example
points.text: From a deck, draw a card without replacement. P(2nd is heart | 1st is heart) = 12/51 (only 12 hearts left out of 51 cards).

points.label: Bayes' Theorem
points.text: P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Used to revise probabilities with new information.

example.problem: In a class, 60% pass Math, 80% pass Science, 50% pass both. Find P(pass Science | pass Math).
example.solution: P(Science | Math) = P(both) / P(Math) = 0.50 / 0.60 = 5/6 ≈ 0.833 or 83.3%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Conditional probability updates likelihood when new information is given—vital for decision-making.

slides.title: Arjun's Cricket Analysis
slides.storyContext: Arjun says: 'If a batsman usually hits 6s 20% of the time, but he's up against a spin bowler (weaker against spin), does his odds change?' Aunt Savita: 'Yes! That's conditional probability. P(six | spin bowler) differs from P(six | pace bowler).'
slides.inSimpleWords: New information changes probabilities—use conditional probability to update estimates.

slides.title: Example: Bayes' Theorem
slides.storyContext: A disease test is 95% accurate. 1% of population has it. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have it?

points.label: Setup
points.text: P(disease) = 0.01, P(+|disease) = 0.95, P(+|no disease) = 0.05.

points.label: Surprising Result
points.text: Despite 95% accuracy, probability of having disease is only 16%—most positives are false!

slides.inSimpleWords: Bayes' theorem combines test accuracy with base rate to find true probability.

slides.title: Random Variables and Probability Distribution

points.label: Random Variable (X)
points.text: A function mapping outcomes to numbers. Example: rolling a die, X = number showing. X ∈ {1,2,3,4,5,6}.

points.label: Probability Distribution
points.text: Table/function showing P(X = x) for each outcome. For a fair die: P(X=1)=P(X=2)=...=P(X=6)=1/6.

points.label: Expected Value (Mean)
points.text: E(X) = Σ x × P(X=x). Average outcome over many trials. For a die: E(X) = 1/6 × (1+2+3+4+5+6) = 3.5.

example.problem: A game: roll a die, win ₹10 if even, lose ₹5 if odd. Find expected value.

slides.inSimpleWords: Random variables assign numbers to outcomes; expected value is the long-run average.

slides.title: Expected Value in Games
slides.storyContext: Zara asks: 'If the expected value is ₹2.50 per roll, should I play?' Aunt: 'Only if you're betting less than ₹2.50! Expected value is your average profit per game.' Arjun nods: 'Like cricket odds—if you're paid ₹15 for a ₹10 bet at 60% odds, you make ₹1 expected profit.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Expected value is average long-term outcome—basis for fair gambling and decision-making.

slides.title: Example: Probability Distribution
slides.storyContext: Spin a wheel: 50% red (win ₹50), 30% blue (win ₹0), 20% black (lose ₹30). Find E(X).

points.label: Setup
points.text: X: outcomes are {50, 0, -30} with probabilities {0.5, 0.3, 0.2}.

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: On average, you make ₹19 per spin.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply each outcome by its probability and sum—gives average payoff.

slides.title: Challenge: Binomial Distribution
slides.storyContext: Flip a coin 3 times. What's P(exactly 2 heads)?

example.problem: Using binomial: n=3, k=2, p=0.5. Find P(X=2).

slides.inSimpleWords: Binomial distribution counts successes in n independent trials—useful for repeated events.

slides.title: Full Problem: The Cricket Match
slides.storyContext: Arjun predicts: a batsman hits 3 sixes per 20 balls on average. In the next 3 balls, what's the probability he hits exactly 2 sixes?
slides.inSimpleWords: Binomial probability calculates outcomes in repeated trials—useful for sports, quality control, surveys.

image.alt: Full Problem: The Cricket Match — Probability

slides.title: Probability Powers Prediction
slides.storyContext: Arjun reflects: 'I used to say 'the team might win' by feeling. Now I calculate odds! Probability turns intuition into numbers.' Aunt smiles: 'Exactly. It's not fortune-telling—it's informed prediction.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability bridges intuition and logic—turning uncertainty into quantifiable risk.

slides.title: Your Challenge: The Lottery
slides.storyContext: A lottery draws 1 winning ticket from 1,000. You buy 5 tickets. What's the probability of winning at least one prize?

example.problem: Find P(at least 1 win out of 5 tickets from 1000).

slides.inSimpleWords: For 'at least one' problems, calculate the complement: P(at least 1) = 1 - P(none).

slides.title: Aunt Savita's Final Lesson
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Is probability just for games?' Aunt Savita shakes her head: 'No! Insurance, medicine, engineering, AI—every field needs probability. Weather forecasts? 70% chance of rain. Drug trials? 90% effective. All probability.' Zara grins: 'So we use math to handle real-world randomness!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the universal language for dealing with uncertainty in every field of knowledge.

slides.title: Probability Summary

points.text: Probability P(E) = (favorable outcomes) / (total outcomes). Range: 0 to 1.
Sample space = all outcomes. Event = subset of sample space.
Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).
Multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B|A).
Conditional probability: P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B).
Random variables map outcomes to numbers; expected value is the average over many trials.
Applications: gambling, weather forecasting, quality control, medical diagnosis, sports analytics.

slides.inSimpleWords: Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty—used to predict outcomes and make informed decisions under risk.

image.alt: Probability Summary — Probability

subject: Physics
title: Rohan's Market Quest: Measuring the World
hook: A shopkeeper's scales, a surveyor's tape, and why the whole world agrees on how to measure.

slides.title: Units and Measurements
slides.storyContext: Rohan visits the local vegetable market with his teacher Mr. Sharma and discovers why measurement matters.

image.alt: Units and Measurements — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Market Mystery
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks Anaya at the market: 'Why does your dad's scale show 1 kg, but the digital one shows 1000 grams?' Anaya's confused. Mr. Sharma steps in: 'Different units, same quantity. But here's the catch—if every shop used different units, chaos!' Rohan realizes: the whole world needs to agree on how to measure.

image.alt: The Market Mystery — Units and Measurements

slides.title: What is a Unit?
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma draws a line in the sand: 'A unit is a standard quantity we use to measure things.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: A unit is a standard quantity adopted by convention to measure a physical quantity.

points.label: Why?
points.text: Without units, '5' means nothing. 5 kg sugar ≠ 5 meters of rope ≠ 5 seconds of time.

points.label: Example
points.text: Length: meter (m), mass: kilogram (kg), time: second (s).

slides.inSimpleWords: A unit is like the answer to 'measuring what?' — it tells you if you're measuring kilos, meters, or seconds.

image.alt: What is a Unit? — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The SI Base Units (International Standard)
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out a reference card: 'In 1960, the world agreed on 7 fundamental units called SI base units. Every physical quantity is built from these 7.'

points.label: The 7 SI Base Units
points.text: Length (meter, m), Mass (kilogram, kg), Time (second, s), Current (ampere, A), Temperature (kelvin, K), Luminous intensity (candela, cd), Mole (mol).

points.label: Why SI?
points.text: Système International d'Unités — used by scientists worldwide. Ensures consistency.

points.label: Daily use in India
points.text: When you buy rice by kg, cook for minutes, measure cloth by meters—you are using SI.

slides.inSimpleWords: The whole world uses the same 7 building blocks to measure everything—like how all LEGO sets use the same-sized bricks.

image.alt: The SI Base Units (International Standard) — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Anaya's Confusion with the Scales
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father owns two scales: an old mechanical one and a new digital one. They show different numbers for the same tomato. Rohan and Anaya are baffled. Mr. Sharma grins: 'Not different numbers—different units! The old scale reads in 'ser' (an old Indian unit, about 900 g). The digital shows grams. It's the same tomato, just spoken in two languages.'

image.alt: Anaya's Confusion with the Scales — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Prefixes: Making Big and Small Numbers Easy
slides.storyContext: Rohan asks: 'Why do we say 1000 meters is 1 kilometer, not just 1000 meters?' Mr. Sharma smiles: 'Prefixes are shortcuts for big and small numbers.'

points.label: Large prefixes
points.text: kilo (k) = 10³, mega (M) = 10⁶, giga (G) = 10⁹, tera (T) = 10¹².

points.label: Small prefixes
points.text: milli (m) = 10⁻³, micro (μ) = 10⁻⁶, nano (n) = 10⁻⁹, pico (p) = 10⁻¹².

points.label: Real Indian examples
points.text: Your phone: gigabytes of data, nanoseconds to process. Monsoon rainfall: millimeters or centimeters. Distance to school: kilometers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prefixes are labels that multiply the unit. 1 km = 1000 m (kilo means ×1000).

image.alt: Prefixes: Making Big and Small Numbers Easy — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Land Surveyor's Challenge
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma mentions his weekend job: surveying land for a new school building. 'I measured 2500 meters. My colleague measured 2.5 kilometers. Same distance, different units. If we don't agree on units, we can't build the school straight!' Rohan nods: measurement errors destroy buildings.

image.alt: The Land Surveyor's Challenge — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Measurement Error & Significant Figures
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father measures sugar on an old scale (±50 g uncertainty) and a new digital scale (±1 g). Rohan asks: 'Which is correct?' Mr. Sharma: 'Both are, but one is more precise. And we only report as many digits as we can trust.'

points.label: Systematic error
points.text: The scale's zero mark is off—every reading is 10 g too high (always the same error).

points.label: Random error
points.text: The scale jiggles a bit—sometimes you read 100 g, sometimes 101 g.

points.label: Significant figures
points.text: Write only the digits you trust. If your scale reads ±1 g, write 250 g (3 sig figs), not 250.00 g (5 sig figs).

slides.inSimpleWords: Every measurement has tiny errors. Significant figures are the digits you can trust—don't pretend you're more precise than you really are.

image.alt: Measurement Error & Significant Figures — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Gold Scam
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma tells a cautionary tale: 'A jeweler cheated a customer by using an inaccurate scale. The customer bought 10 grams of gold but received only 9.5 grams. Thousands of rupees lost! That's why measurement standards matter.' Rohan shivers: careless measurement ruins lives.

image.alt: The Gold Scam — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Dimensional Analysis & Unit Conversion
slides.storyContext: Rohan needs to convert the market's rice price from rupees per kilogram to rupees per gram. Mr. Sharma teaches him a trick: treat units like numbers in a fraction.

points.label: The trick
points.text: Multiply by a conversion factor = 1. E.g., 1 kg = 1000 g, so (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 1.

points.label: Example
points.text: 100 rupees/kg = 100 rupees/kg × (1 kg)/(1000 g) = 0.1 rupees/g.

points.label: Dimensional check
points.text: Always cancel units. If you end with wrong units (e.g., m/kg when you want m/s), you made an error.

slides.inSimpleWords: To convert units, multiply by a fraction that equals 1. The unwanted units cancel, and only the units you want remain.

image.alt: Dimensional Analysis & Unit Conversion — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Rules for Significant Figures (Detailed)
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma pulls out examples: '250 has 2 or 3 significant figures depending on context. 0.0035 has 2. Leading zeros don't count; trailing zeros do if there's a decimal point.'

points.label: Nonzero digits
points.text: Always significant. 456 has 3 sig figs.

points.label: Zeros between nonzero digits
points.text: Always significant. 402 has 3 sig figs.

points.label: Leading zeros
points.text: Never significant. 0.0042 has 2 sig figs (only 4 and 2).

points.label: Trailing zeros
points.text: Significant only if there's a decimal point. 50 has 1 sig fig; 50. has 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: Counting sig figs: include all digits except leading zeros. Trailing zeros count only if there's a decimal point.

image.alt: Rules for Significant Figures (Detailed) — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Worked Example: Density Calculation
slides.storyContext: Anaya's father wants to know the density of his cooking oil. He fills a 1-liter bottle (volume = 1000 cm³) and weighs it on the market scale: 920 g (not counting the bottle).

example.problem: Calculate the density of cooking oil in kg/m³. Given: mass = 920 g, volume = 1000 cm³.
example.solution: Step 1: Convert to SI units. Mass = 920 g = 0.92 kg; Volume = 1000 cm³ = 1000 × 10⁻⁶ m³ = 10⁻³ m³. Step 2: Density = mass/volume = 0.92 kg / 10⁻³ m³ = 920 kg/m³.

slides.inSimpleWords: Oil is lighter than water (which has density 1000 kg/m³), so oil floats—and our calculation confirms it: 920 < 1000.

image.alt: Worked Example: Density Calculation — Units and Measurements

slides.title: The Market Scales Showdown
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma organizes a test. He brings certified 1 kg weights and checks each shop's scale. Anaya's father's scale reads 1.02 kg (2% error). Another shop reads 0.97 kg (3% error). Mr. Sharma explains: 'Every tool has limits. We account for that with uncertainty.'

image.alt: The Market Scales Showdown — Units and Measurements

slides.title: Absolute & Relative Errors
